on Your Rover

Lab 0 — Before you start

This lab trains nothing. You will write one file, common.py, about 170 lines long, check it with a few short commands, and run one test that takes about nine seconds. For a guide about three learning algorithms, that can feel like a slow start. It is the part everything else stands on.

Here is why. Every success rate and every error bar in Labs 1 to 3 comes out of one function you write here, evaluate(), and one formula, the Wilson interval. If evaluate() quietly scored two policies on different maps, or counted a timeout as a crash, every later conclusion would inherit the mistake, and nothing would look wrong. The only defense is to build the measuring tool slowly, understand every line of it, and test it on two policies whose answers you already know.

First, though, this lab shows where the three labs are going and why in this order (Section L0.1), how the guide works (L0.2), the three rules every experiment follows (L0.3), and the rover the way your code sees it: fifteen numbers in, two out, one reward, three ways to end (L0.4). Then you set up your folder (L0.5) and write common.py in three sittings (L0.6 to L0.8).

L0.1 What you are about to build, and why in this order

You already have a PPO policy that drives your rover. It is ppo_rover_v0.2_wheel_randomization: 5 million steps of Stable-Baselines3 PPO, trained by your train_rover.py and deployed on the hardware. At the end of this lab you will measure it on a fixed set of 100 episodes, and it will reach the goal in 76 of them. So why three more labs?

Because two questions stand between “I trained a policy once” and “I can do robot learning on purpose”:

  • When a run goes wrong, can you tell what went wrong from its curves? Without rerunning ten variations, and without guessing.
  • Can you learn from data you already have? A real robot cannot always afford the thing PPO needs most, which is a steady stream of fresh experience.

The three labs answer these two questions. Each lab also hands the next one exactly the input it needs, which is why the order is fixed.

This overview uses a handful of terms that the labs define properly when they arrive. You do not need the full definitions yet. Each term gets a short gloss the first time it appears, which is enough to follow the road map.

L0.1.1 Lab 1: PPO, broken on purpose

PPO is on-policy: it learns only from data collected by the current version of the policy. Make that concrete with your own settings. Each round, 8 environments drive 2,048 steps each, which gives 16,384 samples. PPO cuts them into minibatches of 64, so one pass over the batch is 256 minibatches. It makes 10 passes, so it takes 2,560 gradient steps on that one batch. Then it throws the batch away and drives again with the updated policy.

It has to throw the batch away. After 2,560 updates, the batch describes a driver who no longer exists. PPO’s clip (the clip_range setting, written \(\epsilon\) in book Section 3.4) is the mechanism that keeps those updates from carrying the policy too far from the driver who actually collected the data.

Lab 1 breaks that machinery twice, on purpose. One configuration sets clip_range=10, so the clip can never bind in practice.

The other configuration needs two words first. A critic is a second network, trained alongside the policy, that predicts how much reward is still to come from a given situation. An advantage is how much better a step turned out than the critic expected: positive when things went better than predicted, negative when worse. PPO computes its advantages with GAE (generalized advantage estimation, book Section 3.5). GAE blends a short-range estimate, which looks only one step ahead, with longer-range ones, which look further down the episode. The setting gae_lambda chooses the blend. Lab 1’s second broken configuration sets gae_lambda=0, so every advantage becomes a purely one-step estimate.

Each broken configuration runs with three seeds, next to three seeds of the healthy default, for 1 million steps per run.

Why break an algorithm that works? Because healthy runs all look alike. You only learn what a curve is telling you by watching it respond to a fault you planted yourself. This lab is rung E3 of the book’s experiment ladder (Appendix B rung E3).

Lab 1 also does two quieter things. It saves a checkpoint every 50,000 steps, which Lab 1 itself never uses: Lab 2 will need a mediocre policy, and the only way to have one later is to save it now. And it ends with you computing GAE advantages by hand, step by step, on one real episode, and checking your numbers against Stable-Baselines3’s (Section L1.8).

L0.1.2 Lab 2: AWR, learning from a file

Fresh data is cheap in simulation. On your workstation the raw rover environment runs about 12,000 random steps per second. On the real rover, every step costs battery, motor wear, and you walking across the room to reset it. Meanwhile you usually already own data: old training runs, teleoperation sessions, telemetry logs. PPO cannot use any of it, because none of it came from the current policy.

AWR (advantage-weighted regression, book Chapter 4) can. At heart it is behavior cloning, which means supervised learning that copies logged actions. AWR adds one extra number per sample: a weight saying how much better than expected that moment turned out.

Lab 2 records 500 episodes from one of Lab 1’s mediocre checkpoints into a file. From then on, the environment is used only to grade the result. On that one file you compare plain cloning with AWR at several values of its temperature \(\beta\). The temperature is a setting that controls how sharply the weight favors the better samples: a large \(\beta\) treats all samples almost equally, and a small \(\beta\) piles the weight onto the best ones. This is Appendix B rung E4.

L0.1.3 Lab 3: AWAC, a learned critic and then online

AWR’s weight has a weakness that you will be able to measure by the end of Lab 2. It compares the return that followed a step with what the collector’s critic expected. That comparison is computed once and frozen into the file. It describes the collector, not the policy you are training, and it never gets better.

AWAC (advantage-weighted actor-critic, book Section 4.5) keeps AWR’s kind of policy update: weighted regression onto the logged actions. What it changes is where the advantage comes from. AWAC trains its own critic, written \(Q(s, a)\): a network that predicts the reward still to come after taking action \(a\) in situation \(s\). Because it scores an action and not just a situation, it can compare the logged action with other actions the policy might have taken in the same spot.

AWAC trains that critic with temporal-difference (TD) backups. For each stored step, it nudges the critic’s prediction toward the reward that step actually earned plus the critic’s own prediction for the step after it (Section L3.3 works through this). A transition is one such stored step: an observation, the action taken, the reward, the next observation, and whether the episode ended there. The critic and the policy both learn from a replay buffer, a stored pool of past transitions that starts out holding Lab 2’s file. Because of that, AWAC can then take the wheel, add its own new transitions to the same buffer, and keep learning online, meaning while it drives. The book has no rung for this lab; the guide adds it.

An analogy, with its limit. PPO learns to drive by driving: every lesson uses the drives from the last hour, and older drives are thrown out because you are no longer that driver. AWR studies a box of dashcam recordings from a mediocre driver and copies the maneuvers that went better than that driver usually managed. AWAC watches the same box with a coach who scores each maneuver against what you would have done at that moment, and then hands you the keys so you can add your own recordings to the box.

Where it breaks down: a person watching a recording understands why a maneuver worked. AWR understands nothing. For each logged step it sees one number, saying whether the rest of that episode went better or worse than a critic predicted. Lab 2, Section L2.10 shows that on your data this number mostly reflects whether the whole episode was a lucky one, which no human viewer would confuse with good driving.

The coach is no expert either. It is a network that learns to score as it goes, from the same recordings. Early on, its scores can be confidently wrong, and it can even flatter a bad maneuver. Lab 3 spends Section L3.4 on exactly that problem and on the two fixes AWAC uses against it.

L0.1.4 The pipeline in one picture

L0.1.5 What you will find

Here are a few headline results from our run, so you know where the road goes. Don’t memorize them. The labs show how each one was earned, and how sure you can be of it.

  • Lab 1. With clip_range=10, PPO learns faster at first: its episode reward is around 40 by about 150,000 steps, while the healthy baseline is still around −50. Then it goes chaotic, and all three seeds end far below the baseline. The curve you would normally watch for trouble, clip_fraction (the share of samples that reached the edge of the clip), reads about 0.003 for the whole run; it is blind to exactly this failure. With gae_lambda=0, the critic looks better than the baseline’s: it has the lowest value loss, the critic’s training error, of the three configurations. Meanwhile the policy plateaus lower: final episode reward between −16 and +22, against 66 to 74 for the baseline.
  • Lab 2. The collector you end up using (the policy that drives while the dataset is recorded) is the 100,000-step checkpoint, and its 500 recorded episodes reach the goal only 15.4% of the time. Trained on that file, plain behavior cloning scores 24.0% success. AWR at \(\beta = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.3\) scores 36.7% and 37.3%. The book predicts that pushing \(\beta\) toward zero ends in “dead data”: almost all the weight lands on a handful of samples, so the rest of the file stops counting. By default, Lab 2’s AWR runs with a weight cap, which limits every sample’s weight to at most 20, as the book’s rung E4 recommends. With the cap in place you will see something different from the book’s prediction; with the cap removed, the collapse arrives on schedule (3.7% success at \(\beta = 0.03\)).
  • Lab 3. AWAC, trained offline on the same file, ends its offline phase at 48–58% success depending on the seed. A check that keeps AWAC’s policy update exactly as it is but feeds it Lab 2’s advantage instead of the critic’s lands back at AWR’s level, about 34%. AWAC’s final evaluation, after the online phase, pools to 58.3% [52.7%, 63.8%] over three seeds. The online phase did not measurably improve it within 100,000 steps. And counted in environment steps, PPO from scratch was the better deal on this cheap simulator. The case for offline methods is data you cannot cheaply collect again, not a fast simulator.

L0.2 How to use this guide

L0.2.1 Build it yourself, one piece at a time

You will write every script yourself. The guide never hands you a finished file. It hands you one piece at a time, and every piece follows the same rhythm:

  1. The problem. Why this piece has to exist, usually by showing what goes wrong without it.
  2. The code. A chunk of at most about 30 lines, with every line that is not obvious explained before or after it.
  3. Run it. The exact command.
  4. What you should see. The real output from our run, copied verbatim.
  5. How to read it. What the output says, what it does not say, and what would worry you.

Type the code rather than pasting it. That sounds old-fashioned, and it is slower. But typing is where you notice that a line divides by 8 and start wondering why, and that wondering is most of the learning. When a piece is small enough to attempt on your own, a box invites you to try it before you read the answer.
