L0.2.3 The answer key

A complete, tested version of every lab script lives in rl-rover/labs/ppo-awr-awac/, including this lab’s smoke test (also printed in full in Section L0.8.5). Every output in this guide came from running those files, the smoke test, or the short commands shown next to the output. Treat the folder as an answer key: finish a step your own way first, then compare. Appendix A.1 lists every file, what it does, and which section of this guide builds it. Appendix A.2 gives the whole run order with measured times.

The folder also holds our outputs: the PPO runs and checkpoints in runs/, the offline dataset in data/, the result files in results/, and the plots in figures/. That is useful when your own run has not finished yet. For instance, you may want to start Lab 2 while your Lab 1 grid is still training. Borrow an input from there if you need to, and write down in your notes that you did.

L0.2.4 A time budget

Computing is the cheap part of these labs. The table gives the measured compute time for each lab on the workstation this guide was written on: 12 CPU cores, 61 GB of RAM, everything on the CPU. The last column is a rough budget for the part that takes longer, which is reading, typing, debugging, and thinking about what came out.

LabWhat the computer doesCompute (measured)Your time (rough)
Lab 0smoke test: 300 evaluation episodesabout 9 s2–3 h (a guess)
Lab 1nine 1M-step PPO runs, 6 at a time; then plots and GAE by hand in secondsabout 10 minabout 5 h (the book’s estimate for a lighter rung E3)
Lab 2score 60 checkpoints (66 s), record 500 episodes (43 s), sweep 30 AWR and BC runs (about 2 min)about 4 minabout 7 h (the book’s estimate for a lighter rung E4)
Lab 3three AWAC seeds in parallel, about 19.5 min each on one coreabout 20 min6–8 h (a guess)

Two of the estimates in the last column come from the book, whose Appendix B budgets about 5 hours for rung E3 and about 7 for rung E4. Both of the book’s rungs are lighter than these labs. The book’s E3 is mostly reading, with short 300k-step runs, while Lab 1 has you write four scripts. The book’s E4 trains two policies, while Lab 2 adds a checkpoint search and a sweep. So read those two numbers as a floor. The other two estimates are guesses.

Taken together, the column adds up to about 20–23 hours (2–3, plus 5, plus 7, plus 6–8). At your 15–20 hours per week, plan on one to one and a half weeks.

The compute times depend on your core count. With fewer cores, run fewer jobs at once (the Lab 1 launcher’s docstring suggests --parallel 3 on a 4-core machine) and expect the waits to grow accordingly.

L0.2.5 Why your numbers may differ from ours

You will rerun code we already ran, with the same seeds, and your numbers can still come out different. That is normal, and knowing why saves you from hunting for a bug that is not there.

A seed pins down every random choice, but only for one exact combination of machine and software. Change the CPU, the thread count, or a library version, and the floating-point arithmetic inside a network can differ in its last digits. (Our runs used Python 3.12, gymnasium 1.3.0, stable-baselines3 2.9.0, torch 2.13.0, numpy 2.5.1 and matplotlib 3.11.)

Reinforcement learning then amplifies those digits. A slightly different network output means a slightly different wheel command, which puts the rover somewhere slightly different, which changes every observation after that. A few hundred steps later the two runs are driving different episodes.

A separate, more ordinary cause: outputs depend on which checkpoint you load. When Lab 1’s GAE-by-hand script was tested on an earlier checkpoint, the goal-reaching episode it found lasted 213 steps; on the final model it lasted 189. If you point a script at a different checkpoint than the guide does, expect different numbers for that reason alone.

So what should reproduce is the shape of each result, not its digits: which configuration is worse, whether two intervals separate, the direction of any difference larger than its error bar. Section L0.8 builds the tool for judging exactly that.

One line of output in this very lab samples its actions from an unseeded random number generator, so it will almost certainly differ from ours. Section L0.8.6 explains which one and why.

L0.3 Three rules for every experiment

Appendix B of the book opens with three rules that bind every experiment in it (Section B.1). They sound like bureaucracy. They are the difference between running code and finding something out. Here is each rule, and what it looks like in these labs.

L0.3.1 Rule one: one question per experiment

Write the question down before you touch the keyboard, as one sentence ending in a question mark. Then design the smallest run that answers it. The rule prevents a very common failure: you change three things, get a better number, and cannot say which change caused it.

Each lab in this guide is built around one question:

  • Lab 1: Can I diagnose, from TensorBoard curves alone, which knob a broken PPO run needs?
  • Lab 2: On the same logged data, does advantage weighting beat plain behavior cloning, and what does \(\beta\) do?
  • Lab 3: If the advantage comes from a learned Q-function instead of the collector’s frozen Monte Carlo estimate, and the policy keeps collecting its own data, does it improve beyond AWR?

One term in Lab 3’s question is new. A Monte Carlo estimate is one built from the return actually observed after a step, rather than from a learned prediction. AWR’s advantage is of that kind: the return that really followed, minus what the collector’s critic predicted, computed once when the file is recorded.

Look at how the runs follow from the questions. In Lab 1, each broken configuration changes exactly one setting from the healthy baseline: clip10 changes only clip_range, and lambda0 changes only gae_lambda. In Lab 2, every run trains on the identical file with identical code, and the only thing that changes is \(\beta\). The weight cap is removed too, but only in a separate, clearly labeled set of runs.

Lab 3’s question honestly bundles two changes: a learned critic, and online data. That is why the run keeps them apart in time. It does 50,000 updates offline first, then the online phase, with evaluations throughout, so each change can be read on its own stretch of the curve.

L0.3.2 Rule two: measure, don’t watch

Every experiment ends in a number or a plot, never an impression. Watching your rover in predict.py’s render window is great for building intuition and useless as evidence. “It looked smoother” is not a result, and neither is “it seemed to crash less”. That is why this lab builds evaluate() before anything else.

The rule has a second half that matters just as much: seeds. The book puts it bluntly: a single-seed RL result is noise wearing the costume of a finding, because two seeds of the same configuration can differ by more than two genuinely different configurations do. So every configuration in these labs runs with three seeds.

You will see why on real numbers. In Lab 3, three seeds of the identical AWAC run end at 48%, 65% and 62% success. Any one of them alone would have told a different story. Lab 1 shows the opposite case, and it is just as informative: the three baseline seeds agree closely on every curve, and that agreement is exactly what makes the broken configurations legible.

L0.3.3 Rule three: log it

Keep one dated note per experiment, in the NEXT.md style you already use in your repositories: question, setup, result, surprise. The surprise line is the valuable one. What surprised you is exactly what your mental model got wrong, and it is also the first thing you will forget.

Here is a template, filled in with this lab’s smoke test, so you can see the level of detail that pays off a month later:

## 2026-09-12 - Lab 0 smoke test​Question: Does my evaluate() tell a random driver from my deployed model,          and how wide are the error bars at 100 episodes?Setup:    common.py evaluate(), 100 episodes each, eval seeds 1,000,000-1,000,099.          Random driver: uniform wheel speeds, np.random.default_rng(0).          Model: ppo_rover_v0.2_wheel_randomization (5M PPO steps), on the CPU,          mean action (deterministic) and sampled actions (stochastic).Result:   random           success  0% [ 0%,  4%]  crash 33%  timeout 67%          v0.2 determ.     success 76% [67%, 83%]  crash 24%  timeout  0%          v0.2 stochastic  success 77% [68%, 84%]  crash 22%  timeout  1%Surprise: The random driver times out twice as often as it crashes.          Sampled vs mean action: 77% vs 76%, intervals almost identical;          no detectable difference at 100 episodes.

An analogy, with its limit. An experiment note is a commit message for a result. The diff tells future you what changed; only the message says why, and what you expected to happen. Where it breaks down: a commit deterministically produces the new code, while an experiment produces one draw from a noisy process. A note that records “76%” without “100 episodes, [67%, 83%], one trained model” will mislead you in a month, because you will remember the number and forget how little it was worth.

L0.4 The rover as the code sees it

You know rover-v0 well; you built it. This guide needs one particular view of it, though: the rover as a training script sees it. Every array in the labs has a shape that comes from here. Lab 2’s dataset stores 15 numbers per observation. Lab 3’s critic takes 17 inputs, because it reads an observation and an action together. It is worth ten minutes to have that view sharp.

L0.4.1 What the policy observes: 15 floats

An episode takes place in a 5 m × 5 m arena. Five circular obstacles of radius 0.30 m are placed at random every episode, along with a random start pose and a random goal at least 1.0 m from the start. The rover is a disc of radius 0.20 m, and one environment step lasts 0.2 simulated seconds.

None of that reaches the policy directly. What reaches it is this vector of 15 floats:

IndexNameWhat it holdsRange
0–4beam distancesthe last range reading of each of 5 beams, at −90°, −45°, 0°, +45° and +90° from the heading, divided by 1.5 m (the simulator’s maximum range; a beam that hits nothing reports 1.5 m)0 to 1
5–9beam ageshow many steps since each beam was last measured, divided by 80 to 1
10goal distancebelieved distance to the goal, divided by the arena diagonal (about 7.07 m)0 to 1
11goal bearing, sinesine of the believed angle from the heading to the goal−1 to 1
12goal bearing, cosinecosine of the same angle−1 to 1
13–14last actionthe left and right wheel commands sent on the previous step−1 to 1

Two things about this vector matter for everything that follows.

First, the sensor sweeps. The five beams are one ultrasonic sensor on a servo, and only one beam is measured per step. The servo walks back and forth across the fan, so the beams at the two ends are refreshed only once every 8 steps (1.6 simulated seconds). Between refreshes, an entry keeps its last reading, which may be stale by now. The five age numbers tell the policy how stale each reading is.

Second, the rover does not know where it is. Its position comes from dead reckoning: integrating the wheel speeds, with noise added, so the error grows as the episode goes on. The goal distance and bearing in the observation are computed from that believed pose. The reward, as you will see in a moment, is computed from the true one.

Together, these make the problem partially observable: the observation does not contain the full state of the world. You will see one symptom in Lab 1. Within a single goal-reaching episode, the critic’s estimate of how well things are going swings between about −12 and +91 (Section L1.8.7).

An analogy, with its limit. Picture crossing a dark room with a flashlight that you sweep slowly left and right, counting your steps to know where you are. You see one slice at a time, what you saw a moment ago may have shifted relative to you, and your step count drifts. Where it breaks down: you would build a mental map of the room as you go. The policies in these labs are plain feed-forward networks with no memory. Everything they know about the past has to fit into this one vector: the stale readings, their ages, and the last action sent.

On your rig

On the real rover, the five beams are your ultrasonic sensor on its sweeping servo, and the believed pose is what integrating your wheel encoders gives you. The simulator’s noise (2 cm range noise, 5% dropouts, 1% ghost echoes, odometry noise) and its per-episode randomization (motor lag, action delay, wheel base, wheel gains, sensor mount) are its stand-ins for exactly those imperfections of the hardware.

L0.4.2 What the policy does: two wheel speeds

The action is two floats: the normalized speeds of the left and right wheels, each in [−1, 1]. In Gymnasium’s terms the action space is Box([-1,-1],[1,1]). Roughly equal values drive straight ahead; opposite values turn the rover on the spot.

The environment clips any action to [−1, 1] itself, so a command of 1.7 behaves exactly like 1.0. That matters more than it looks. PPO’s policy is a Gaussian distribution, and a sample from a Gaussian can land anywhere, so a sampled command of 1.7 is perfectly possible. The environment silently turns it into 1.0. When Lab 2 records a dataset (Section L2.3), it has to decide which of those two numbers to store, and the choice changes what a cloned policy learns.

A command also does not take effect instantly. Each episode draws a motor lag and an action delay of 1 or 2 steps, so the wheels respond late, and only gradually, to what the policy asked for. The last-action entries in the observation are the policy’s only record of what is still in the pipe.

L0.4.3 What the policy is paid: the reward

The reward on each step is a sum of a few small terms, plus one large bonus or penalty on the very last step of an episode:

\[ \begin{aligned} r_t \;=\;& 33\,(d_{t-1} - d_t) \;-\; 0.05 \;-\; 0.01\,\big(|\Delta a^{L}_t| + |\Delta a^{R}_t|\big) \\ &-\; 1.5\,\max\!\big(0,\; 1 - c_t / 0.25\big) \;-\; 0.1\,[\text{backwards}] \\ &+\; 100\,[\text{goal}] \;-\; 100\,[\text{crash}] \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

\(r_t\) is the reward for step \(t\). \(d_{t-1}\) and \(d_t\) are the rover’s true distance to the goal, in meters, before and after the step, so \(33\,(d_{t-1} - d_t)\) pays 33 points per meter of progress and charges the same for moving away. \(0.05\) is a fixed charge per step, for taking time. \(\Delta a^{L}_t\) and \(\Delta a^{R}_t\) are how much the left and right wheel commands changed since the previous step; \(0.01\) times their sizes is a small charge for jerky driving. \(c_t\) is the clearance: the gap in meters between the rover’s disc and the nearest obstacle or wall. The clearance term is zero beyond 0.25 m and grows to 1.5 per step at contact. \([\text{backwards}]\) is 1 when the rover drives in reverse, else 0. \([\text{goal}]\) is 1 when the rover’s center comes within 0.15 m of the goal; \([\text{crash}]\) is 1 on a collision.

The first term deserves a closer look, because it explains something about returns that will matter when you read results. Add it up over a whole episode of \(T\) steps. Each step contributes 33 times the distance gained, and the distances cancel in a chain:

\[ 33(d_0 - d_1) + 33(d_1 - d_2) + \dots + 33(d_{T-1} - d_T) \;=\; 33\,(d_0 - d_T). \]

Every distance in the middle appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign. So the progress part of an episode’s return depends only on where the rover started and where it ended, not on the path in between.

Worked example (made-up teaching numbers: the formula is real, the four episodes are invented). Ignore the smoothness, clearance and reverse terms, and score four episodes:

  1. A far goal. The rover starts 3.00 m from the goal and ends 0.10 m from it, after 150 steps.
    Progress: \(33 \times (3.00 - 0.10) = 33 \times 2.90 = 95.7\). Time: \(150 \times 0.05 = 7.5\). Bonus: \(+100\).
    Return: \(95.7 - 7.5 + 100 = 188.2\).
  2. A near goal. It starts 1.20 m away and ends 0.10 m away, after 60 steps.
    Progress: \(33 \times (1.20 - 0.10) = 33 \times 1.10 = 36.3\). Time: \(60 \times 0.05 = 3.0\). Bonus: \(+100\).
    Return: \(36.3 - 3.0 + 100 = 133.3\).
  3. A crash. It starts 3.00 m away, gets to 0.40 m, and hits an obstacle on step 120.
    Progress: \(33 \times (3.00 - 0.40) = 33 \times 2.60 = 85.8\). Time: \(120 \times 0.05 = 6.0\). Penalty: \(-100\).
    Return: \(85.8 - 6.0 - 100 = -20.2\).
  4. A timeout. It starts 3.00 m away, dithers, and is still 2.50 m away when the 500-step limit arrives.
    Progress: \(33 \times (3.00 - 2.50) = 33 \times 0.50 = 16.5\). Time: \(500 \times 0.05 = 25.0\). No bonus or penalty.
    Return: \(16.5 - 25.0 = -8.5\).

Episodes 1 and 2 did the same job: both reached the goal. Their returns differ by \(188.2 - 133.3 = 54.9\) points, purely because one map put the goal further away. Episodes 3 and 4 failed in completely different ways, one by driving into something and one by never committing. Yet their returns are within 12 points of each other. Keep these four episodes in mind; Section L0.4.6 comes back to them.

L0.4.4 How an episode ends: goal, crash, timeout

Every episode ends in exactly one of three ways:

EndingWhenLast reward includesFlag setLabel in the labs
goalrover center within 0.15 m of the goal+100terminated=True"goal"
crashrover disc overlaps an obstacle or the wall−100terminated=True"crash"
timeout500 steps (100 simulated seconds) have passednothing extratruncated=True"timeout"

Gymnasium’s env.step(action) returns five things: obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info. The two flags are how an environment says an episode is over, and they mean different things.

The rover’s own code sets terminated=True at the goal and on a collision. Nothing inside the rover’s code ever sets truncated. That flag comes from a wrapper. The environment is registered with max_episode_steps=500, so gym.make wraps it in a TimeLimit wrapper, and the wrapper sets truncated=True once 500 steps have passed.

Notice that terminated alone cannot tell a goal from a crash. The info dictionary can: info["is_colliding"] is true when the rover’s disc overlaps an obstacle or the wall. There is one corner case. If a single step both reaches the goal and touches an obstacle, the environment adds the +100 and the −100 on the same step, and the labs count that episode as a crash.

L0.4.5 Terminated versus truncated

Why keep two flags at all, when both mean “stop”? Because they say opposite things about the future, and many computations in RL need an estimate of the future.

When an episode is terminated, the future really is over. The rover sits at the goal or against an obstacle, and no more reward will ever come. Any estimate of “reward still to come after this step” must be zero.

When an episode is truncated, the future is not over; you just stopped watching. The rover might be 0.3 m from the goal and about to arrive. Pretending its future is worth zero tells the learner that those last steps led nowhere, which is false.

The standard fix is bootstrapping: stand in for the missing future with the critic’s own estimate of it, \(\gamma\,V(s_{T+1})\). Here \(s_{T+1}\) is the observation after the last step, \(V\) is the critic (a network that predicts the discounted reward to come from a state), and \(\gamma\) is the discount factor, 0.99 in every lab.

This is not a corner case on your rover. In the file that Lab 2 records, 237 of the 500 episodes end in a timeout. Getting truncation wrong would corrupt the returns of nearly half the episodes.

And the damage is not limited to their last step. Each earlier step’s estimate of reward to come includes everything after it, discounted by \(\gamma = 0.99\) per step. So a wrong zero at the cut reaches back through the whole episode, shrinking only slowly. Ten steps before the cut it is still \(0.99^{10} \approx 0.90\) of its size. One hundred steps before, it is still \(0.99^{100} \approx 0.37\) of its size.

You will meet the distinction three times:

  • In Lab 1, Stable-Baselines3 handles it for you inside PPO: it adds \(\gamma\) times the critic’s value of the final observation to the last reward of a truncated episode.
  • In Lab 2, you add the same term by hand when you compute returns for the dataset (Section L2.3).
  • In Lab 3, the critic’s training target multiplies its look-ahead term by \((1 - \text{terminated})\) and deliberately ignores truncation (Sections L3.3.4 and L3.6).

An analogy, with its limit. A football match that ends at the final whistle has a final score. A match abandoned for rain in the 60th minute does not: the score so far is real, but it is not the result. Where it breaks down: an abandoned match gets replayed, or a committee decides it. In RL nobody replays the missing minutes. You guess them with the critic, and the guess is only as good as the critic is at that moment.

L0.4.6 Why success rate is the headline number

Your training curves in TensorBoard show episode return (ep_rew_mean), and Lab 1 reads them closely. Watching return while a run trains is fine. For judging a finished policy, though, these labs lead with success rate: the fraction of evaluation episodes that end at the goal. There are three reasons, and each connects to something you have just seen.

Success is the task. The rover’s job is to reach the goal. Return is a training signal designed to get it there, and its shaping terms are scaffolding.

Return carries map luck. Because the progress term telescopes, a goal far from the start is worth more return than a goal close to it. Episodes 1 and 2 of the worked example did the same job and differ by 54.9 points. Over 100 random maps this averages out to some extent, but it still adds spread that has nothing to do with how well the policy drives.

Return hides how a policy fails. Episodes 3 and 4 had nearly the same return and nothing else in common. On hardware, a crash and a timeout are different problems: one can break something, the other drains a battery. You will watch a real policy trade one for the other in Lab 2. There, AWR at \(\beta = 1\) cuts timeouts from 62% (behavior cloning) to 41%, and raises crashes from 14% to 22%.

So evaluate() reports all three outcome rates, plus the mean return with its own error bar. Success leads. Crash and timeout rates explain it. Return is a supporting number.

Words you will hear

On-policy / off-policy. On-policy methods (PPO) learn only from data the current policy collected. Off-policy methods (AWR, AWAC, SAC) can learn from data any policy collected.

Offline RL (older papers say batch RL). Learning a policy from a fixed dataset, with no further interaction. Lab 2 is offline; Lab 3 starts offline.

POMDP. Partially observable Markov decision process: the formal name for a problem like this rover’s, where the observation is not the full state.

Bootstrapping. Using a learned estimate, such as \(V(s')\), in place of rewards you have not observed. Unrelated to the statistical bootstrap.

Greedy evaluation. Scoring a stochastic policy by always taking its most likely action, which for a Gaussian is its mean. Stable-Baselines3 calls it deterministic=True.

L0.5 Setting up

L0.5.1 Your lab folder

The answer key sits in rl-rover/labs/ppo-awr-awac/. Don’t write your own code there, or you will overwrite the key the first time you save a file. Make a sibling folder for your version instead. This guide calls it labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/; the name is yours to choose.

Run it
cd /mnt/Storage/projects/rl-rover/labsmkdir my-ppo-awr-awaccd my-ppo-awr-awaccp ../ppo-awr-awac/.gitignore .   # keeps runs/, data/ and *.pt out of git

The last line copies the answer key’s .gitignore into your folder. The repository’s own .gitignore already ignores every runs/ folder and every *.pt file, but not a data/ folder in a new lab. Without the copy, the 500-episode dataset you record in Lab 2 would show up as an untracked file, one careless git add away from being committed.

Every command in this guide is run from inside a lab folder, and every path it mentions (runs/, data/, results/, figures/) is relative to that folder. Because your folder sits at the same depth as the answer key, paths that climb out to the repository root work from either one. Examples are ../../.venv and ../../ppo_rover_v0.2_wheel_randomization.

You do not need to create the four output folders by hand either. common.py provides a small function, ensure_dirs(), that creates them, and every lab script that writes files calls it first (Section L0.6.3). Importing common.py on its own creates nothing.

L0.5.2 The virtual environment

The labs use the repository’s shared virtual environment, rl-rover/.venv, the same one your training scripts use. It already contains everything the labs need: gymnasium, Stable-Baselines3, PyTorch, NumPy, matplotlib, the tensorboard package that Lab 1’s plotting script uses to read event files, and the rover_env package itself, installed from rover-v0/. That last one is what makes import rover_env work from any folder.

Activate the environment once per terminal, then check the versions:

Run it
source ../../.venv/bin/activate     # from now on, "python" means the venv's Pythonpython -c "import sys, gymnasium, stable_baselines3, torch, numpy, matplotlibprint(sys.version.split()[0], gymnasium.__version__, stable_baselines3.__version__,      torch.__version__, numpy.__version__, matplotlib.__version__)"
What you should see
3.12.7 1.3.0 2.9.0 2.13.0+cu130 2.5.1 3.11.0

Those are, in order, Python, gymnasium, Stable-Baselines3, PyTorch, NumPy and matplotlib. If you prefer not to activate, call ../../.venv/bin/python wherever the guide says python. If your versions differ, nothing is necessarily wrong, but Section L0.2.5 applies with extra force.

Notice the +cu130 at the end of PyTorch’s version. This is a CUDA-enabled build of PyTorch, and that detail sets up the next section.

L0.5.3 Everything on the CPU, and why the GPU still has to be hidden

Every script in these labs runs on the CPU, deliberately. The networks are tiny: PPO’s policy has two hidden layers of 64 units. For a network this small, a GPU typically brings no speedup, because shipping each small batch to the GPU and back costs about as much time as the fast arithmetic saves.

The CPU also scales the way these labs need: many small, independent runs at once. The training and scoring scripts each limit PyTorch to one thread with torch.set_num_threads(1); Lab 2’s recording script uses two. Small processes like that are what let Lab 1 run six PPO runs side by side on the 12-core workstation, each finishing in about 5 minutes.

So you pass device="cpu" everywhere, and the GPU is out of the picture. Except that it is not, and finding that out cost a batch of parallel runs.

Pitfall

CUDA out of memory in code that never uses CUDA. While the reference code was being written, parallel CPU-only runs died with torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: out of memory. Every tensor was on the CPU. The cause: in torch 2.13, torch.optim.Adam.step() calls an accelerator health check, torch.accelerator.current_stream(), which creates a CUDA context of about 386 MB per process whether or not anything uses the GPU. On this workstation a local llama-server permanently holds about 20.8 GB of the RTX 4090’s 24 GB, so parallel processes each claiming a context ran the card out of memory. device="cpu" does not prevent this. Hiding the GPU does.

The fix is two lines at the very top of every script, before anything imports torch:

import osos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""  # CPU only. Must run before torch is imported

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is an environment variable that lists which GPUs a process may see. An empty value means none. With no GPU visible, the health check has no device to open a context on, and the process leaves the card alone.

The order matters: the variable must be set before torch is imported. That includes indirect imports. Importing Stable-Baselines3, or your own common.py, also imports torch. This is why every reference script repeats the two lines as its very first statements, even though common.py contains them too. A script cannot count on common.py being the first thing that pulls in torch.

L0.6 Writing common.py, part 1: the header, paths, and the environment

L0.6.1 Why one shared file

Across the three labs you will write eleven scripts. Almost all of them build the rover environment, many of them score a policy, and all of them save results somewhere. The obvious approach is to write those few lines wherever they are needed.

That approach fails quietly. Suppose Lab 2’s checkpoint-scoring script seeded its evaluation episodes one way and the AWR script seeded them another way. Then “AWR beat the collector” might only mean “AWR was graded on easier maps”, and no error message would ever tell you.

So everything that more than one script needs goes into one file, common.py, and every script imports it. Its docstring states the design goal: nothing in it is clever. If a helper surprises you, that is a bug in the helper, not a gap in your understanding.

L0.6.2 The header

Create common.py in your lab folder. Start with the module docstring, the CPU-only lines from Section L0.5.3, and the imports.

"""Shared helpers for the three labs (PPO forensics, AWR, AWAC).​Everything that more than one script needs lives here, so each lab script canstay focused on the one idea it teaches:​  - where files go (RUNS, DATA, FIGS)  - how to build the rover environment  - how to score a policy fairly (evaluate) and put an error bar on the score  - the small Gaussian policy network that Labs 2 and 3 train by hand​Nothing in here is clever. If a helper surprises you, that is a bug in thehelper, not in your understanding."""​import os# Every script here runs on the CPU. Hiding the GPU matters even so (Section L0.5.3).# It must be set before torch is imported, which is why each lab script repeats# these two lines first.os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""​import jsonimport mathimport randomfrom pathlib import Path​import gymnasium as gymimport numpy as npimport torchimport torch.nn as nn​import rover_env  # noqa: F401  (importing it registers "rover_env/RoverEnv-v0")

Most of this is ordinary, but three details deserve a word.

The docstring lists four jobs. The last one, the Gaussian policy network, is not part of this lab; you add it in Lab 2, Section L2.4. The import torch.nn as nn exists for that same network. It does no harm to import it now.

The last line, import rover_env, looks unused, because nothing else in the file mentions rover_env. It is not unused. Importing the package runs its __init__.py, which registers the environment with Gymnasium under the id "rover_env/RoverEnv-v0", with max_episode_steps=500. Without that import, gym.make would not recognize the id. The # noqa: F401 comment tells a linter that this “unused import” is intentional, so it does not get deleted by a well-meaning cleanup.

L0.6.3 Paths and constants

Next, decide where files go and fix the three constants every lab shares.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------# Paths. Every script writes under this folder, never into the repo root, so# the lab can be deleted in one command without touching your real models.# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------LAB = Path(__file__).resolve().parentRUNS = LAB / "runs"      # PPO training runs: TensorBoard logs + checkpointsDATA = LAB / "data"      # the offline dataset collected in Lab 2RESULTS = LAB / "results"  # small JSON/CSV files with the numbers you reportFIGS = LAB / "figures"   # every plot the labs produce​ENV_ID = "rover_env/RoverEnv-v0"GAMMA = 0.99             # SB3's default discount; every lab uses the same one​# Episodes used for evaluation start from these seeds. Using the SAME seeds for# every policy means every policy faces the same 100 obstacle layouts and goals,# so a difference between two policies is not "one of them got easier maps".EVAL_SEED0 = 1_000_000​​def ensure_dirs():    for d in (RUNS, DATA, RESULTS, FIGS):        d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

Path(__file__).resolve().parent is the absolute path of the folder that contains common.py, and the / operator joins path pieces, so LAB / "runs" is the runs folder inside it. Every output of the labs lives in those four subfolders. Your real models in the repository root are never touched, and deleting the whole lab means deleting one folder.

GAMMA is the discount factor \(\gamma\). A reward \(k\) steps in the future counts \(\gamma^k\) as much as a reward now; 100 steps ahead (20 simulated seconds), that is \(0.99^{100} \approx 0.37\). It lives here, once, for a concrete reason. In Lab 2 you will compare returns that you compute with this \(\gamma\) against values predicted by a PPO critic that was trained with SB3’s default \(\gamma = 0.99\). If the two used different discounts, they would be measuring different quantities, and their difference would be meaningless.

EVAL_SEED0 is where evaluation episodes start: the first episode uses seed 1,000,000, the next 1,000,001, and so on. Section L0.7.4 explains why every policy gets the same seeds. The number is large on purpose, to keep evaluation far away from the seeds used elsewhere: Lab 2 records its dataset on episode seeds 0 to 499, and Lab 3’s online phase resets with seeds from 2,000,000 up. No policy is graded on a map that sits in its training file.

ensure_dirs() creates the four folders. parents=True creates any missing parent folders, and exist_ok=True makes it silent when a folder already exists, so every script can safely call it first thing.

L0.6.4 Seeding and building the environment

def set_seed(seed: int):    """Seed every random number generator a script touches."""    random.seed(seed)    np.random.seed(seed)    torch.manual_seed(seed)​​def make_env():    """One rover environment, with the 500-step time limit from the registration."""    return gym.make(ENV_ID)

set_seed seeds three separate random number generators, because different parts of the labs draw from different ones. Python’s random module is the first. NumPy’s global generator is the second; Lab 3’s replay buffer uses it to pick which stored transitions go into each batch. PyTorch’s generator is the third: it sets the initial network weights, shuffles minibatches in Lab 2, and samples actions from a Gaussian policy.

Just as important is what set_seed does not seed: the environment. The rover environment has its own private generator, and the only way to seed it is to pass a seed to env.reset(seed=...). When you do, the environment draws everything about the new episode from that generator: the obstacle layout, the start pose, the goal, and the per-episode randomization. After the reset, every per-step noise draw comes from the same generator too: the time-step jitter, the sensor noise, the dropouts and ghost echoes, and the odometry noise. So a seeded episode driven by the same actions repeats exactly. That is why evaluate(), next, passes an explicit seed to every reset.

make_env is one line, and it could look too small to deserve a function. It exists so that every script builds the environment the same way, including the TimeLimit wrapper that the registration adds. You can see the wrappers by printing the environment.

Run it
python -c "from common import make_envenv = make_env(); obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)print(obs.shape, obs.dtype, env.action_space); print(env)"
What you should see
(15,) float32 Box(-1.0, 1.0, (2,), float32)<TimeLimit<OrderEnforcing<PassiveEnvChecker<RoverEnv<rover_env/RoverEnv-v0>>>>>

The first line confirms the two shapes from Section L0.4: 15 observation floats, and a two-dimensional action box from −1 to 1. The second line shows the environment inside its wrappers, outermost first. TimeLimit is the one that sets truncated=True after 500 steps. OrderEnforcing and PassiveEnvChecker are two small safety wrappers that gym.make adds by default; they check, respectively, that reset is called before step and that the environment follows the Gymnasium API. If you see an import error instead, a likely cause is a python that is not the virtual environment’s.

L0.7 Writing common.py, part 2: how an episode ended, and a fair exam

L0.7.1 The problem: “how good is this policy?”

Soon you will compare policies constantly: nine PPO runs, sixty checkpoints, dozens of AWR runs, three AWAC seeds. Each comparison needs one question answered: how good is this policy?

There are two obvious ways to answer it, and you have used both.

The first is to watch. Run predict.py and look at the render window. That produces an impression, and Rule two rules it out.

The second is to read ep_rew_mean off TensorBoard at the end of training. That looks like a measurement, but it measures the wrong thing for comparing finished policies. It averages the returns of the most recent training episodes. Those episodes were driven with sampled actions, possibly by several slightly different versions of the policy as it kept updating, on whatever maps happened to come up. Two runs’ final values were therefore graded on different maps, with different amounts of action noise, by a metric that carries map luck (Section L0.4.6).

What you want instead is an exam: a fixed set of episodes, identical for every policy, scored by how each episode ended. That takes two functions.

L0.7.2 outcome_of: three endings, one word each

Try it yourself first

Write outcome_of(terminated, truncated, info). It returns "goal", "crash" or "timeout" for the last step of an episode. Everything you need is in Section L0.4.4. Two hints: only one of the three endings sets truncated, and info["is_colliding"] separates the other two.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------# Scoring a policy# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------def outcome_of(terminated: bool, truncated: bool, info: dict) -> str:    """How did the episode end? 'goal', 'crash' or 'timeout'.​    The env ends an episode (terminated=True) for two reasons: the rover reached    the goal, or it collided. info["is_colliding"] tells them apart. If the time    limit (500 steps) fires first, gymnasium sets truncated=True instead.    A step that both touches an obstacle and reaches the goal counts as a crash.    """    if terminated:        return "crash" if info["is_colliding"] else "goal"    return "timeout"

The function checks terminated first. If the episode really ended, the collision flag decides between crash and goal. Because a step that collides counts as a crash whether or not it also reached the goal, the corner case from Section L0.4.4 needs no special code. Anything else must be the time limit.

Why read info rather than the last reward? The last reward is not a clean signal: it mixes the +100 or −100 with the shaping terms, and on the corner-case step it contains both. The collision flag is the environment’s own statement of what happened. (Lab 2’s dataset does not store info, so Section L2.10, which needs each episode’s outcome from the file, falls back on the size of the last reward instead.)

L0.7.3 evaluate: the exam loop

Before the code, look at how evaluate receives the policy. It does not take a model object. It takes act_fn: any function that maps one observation (a NumPy array of shape (15,)) to one action (shape (2,)). That small contract is what lets one function score every kind of policy in this guide. A random driver is a one-line lambda. A Stable-Baselines3 model gets a thin wrapper (Section L0.8.4). Lab 2’s hand-written policy passes lambda o: policy.act(o, deterministic=True). evaluate never needs to know which one it is scoring.

def evaluate(act_fn, n_episodes: int = 100, seed0: int = EVAL_SEED0):    """Run `n_episodes` episodes with `act_fn` and summarize what happened.​    act_fn: a function obs (np.ndarray, shape (15,)) -> action (np.ndarray, shape (2,)).    Returns a dict with success/crash/timeout rates, the mean return and both    of their 95% intervals.    """    env = make_env()    returns, lengths, outcomes = [], [], []    for i in range(n_episodes):        obs, _ = env.reset(seed=seed0 + i)        total, steps = 0.0, 0        while True:            obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(act_fn(obs))            total += reward            steps += 1            if terminated or truncated:                break        returns.append(total)        lengths.append(steps)        outcomes.append(outcome_of(terminated, truncated, info))    env.close()

Walk through one episode. env.reset(seed=seed0 + i) starts episode i on its own fixed seed and returns the first observation plus an info dictionary, which the loop ignores (that is what the _ means). Inside the while True loop, the policy picks an action from the current observation, and env.step applies it and returns the five values from Section L0.4.4. The new observation replaces the old one, the reward is added to the running total, and the step is counted.

The loop stops as soon as either flag is set. When it stops, the variables terminated, truncated and info still hold the values from the episode’s last step, which is exactly what outcome_of needs. Each episode leaves behind three records: its return, its length in steps, and its outcome.

Two small details. One environment object serves all the episodes, because reset builds a completely new world each time. And total is the plain, undiscounted sum of rewards: the same kind of number as ep_rew_mean, not the discounted return-to-go you will compute in Lab 2.

L0.7.4 Paired evaluation seeds

The line that matters most in evaluate is the least exciting one: env.reset(seed=seed0 + i). Because the default seed0 is the same for every call, every policy you ever score faces the same first episode, the same second episode, and so on. Episode 0 of every evaluation has the same obstacle layout, the same start pose, the same goal, and the same motor lag, action delay, wheel base, wheel gains and sensor mount. Statisticians call this a paired comparison.

Here is the problem it solves. Maps differ a lot in difficulty: some put the goal in open space a meter away, others hide it behind two obstacles. Without pairing, a policy scored on 100 fresh random maps could beat another by a few points simply because its maps were kinder. With pairing, that explanation is gone. When two policies differ, they differ on identical situations.

Pairing controls how an episode starts, not how it unfolds. From the first action on, two different policies drive differently, so the rest of their episodes differ. That is the point: the only thing left to differ is the driving.

An analogy, with its limit. Every policy sits the same exam paper. If two students took different papers, a higher score might only mean an easier paper; giving everyone the same 100 questions removes that explanation. Where it breaks down: the paper is still only 100 questions drawn from an endless supply of possible maps. Pairing makes the comparison between two policies fairer, but it says nothing about how either would do on a different 100 maps; that uncertainty is what the intervals in the next section are for. And the more often you tune something against the same exam, the more you risk learning the exam rather than the subject.

On your rig

On the hardware you cannot reset to “seed 1,000,000”. The closest thing to pairing is taping start and goal marks to the floor and running every policy you compare from the same set of marks. Without that, a hardware comparison of two policies measures the policies and the course together.

L0.7.5 The summary, and an interval for the mean return

The rest of evaluate turns the three lists into numbers. Continue the function directly below env.close(), at the same four-space indentation. This is still the body of evaluate, not a new function; pasted at the left margin, the return would be outside any function and Python would refuse to load the file.

    returns = np.array(returns)    n = len(outcomes)    goals = outcomes.count("goal")    lo, hi = wilson_interval(goals, n)    # 95% interval for the mean return: mean +/- 1.96 * std / sqrt(n)    half = 1.96 * returns.std(ddof=1) / math.sqrt(n)    return {        "episodes": n,        "success_rate": goals / n,        "success_ci": [lo, hi],        "crash_rate": outcomes.count("crash") / n,        "timeout_rate": outcomes.count("timeout") / n,        "mean_return": float(returns.mean()),        "return_ci": [float(returns.mean() - half), float(returns.mean() + half)],        "return_std": float(returns.std(ddof=1)),        "mean_length": float(np.mean(lengths)),    }

The three rates are counts divided by the number of episodes, so they always add up to 1. success_ci is the 95% interval for the success rate, computed by wilson_interval, which you write in Section L0.8. In the reference file that function sits between outcome_of and evaluate. Python only needs it to exist by the time evaluate actually runs, so you can place it anywhere in the module.

The mean return gets its own interval, from the classic formula:

\[ \bar{R} \;\pm\; 1.96\,\frac{\sigma_R}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad \sigma_R = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(R_i - \bar{R}\big)^2} \]
In plain words

\(n\) is the number of episodes, 100 by default. \(R_i\) is the return of episode \(i\): its plain sum of rewards, the total from the loop. \(\bar{R}\) is the average of those returns. \(\sigma_R\) is their sample standard deviation: how far a single episode’s return typically lands from the average. (The subscript \(R\) marks it as the spread of returns, not the policy’s action spread.) Dividing by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\) (that is what ddof=1 does) corrects for measuring spread around the sample’s own average, which makes it look slightly too small. \(\sigma_R/\sqrt{n}\) is the typical error of the average itself, which shrinks as episodes accumulate. \(1.96\) makes the interval cover 95%, because an average of many independent episodes is approximately normally distributed.

You will put numbers into this formula when you read the smoke test in Section L0.8.6.

The remaining fields are simpler. return_std is \(\sigma_R\) itself, kept because it tells you how noisy single episodes are. mean_length is the average episode length in steps, a quick hint about how episodes end: a timeout always lasts 500. Every NumPy number is converted with float(...) because Python’s json module cannot write every NumPy number type, and these dictionaries end up in JSON files.

L0.8 Writing common.py, part 3: error bars, formatting, and the smoke test

L0.8.1 Why a success rate needs an interval

Your deployed model will reach the goal in 76 of 100 evaluation episodes. Is its true success rate 76%? Probably not exactly. The 100 maps are a sample. A different 100 would give a somewhat different count, and you need to know how different before you can say that 76% beats, say, 70%.

The obvious thing to try is the textbook formula for a proportion: \(p \pm 1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\), where \(p\) is the observed success rate and \(n\) the number of episodes. It fails exactly where you need it most, near 0% and near 100%.

Take the random driver you are about to test, which reaches the goal in 0 of 100 episodes. With \(p = 0\), the square root is \(\sqrt{0 \times 1 / 100} = 0\), so the interval is \([0\%, 0\%]\). The formula claims that 100 episodes proved the true rate is exactly zero, which no finite sample can prove.

Now take a made-up count: 2 successes out of 100, so \(p = 0.02\). The square root, 1.96 times it, and the interval are:

\[ \begin{aligned} \sqrt{0.02 \times 0.98 / 100} &= \sqrt{0.000196} = 0.014 \\ 1.96 \times 0.014 &= 0.02744 \\ 0.02 \pm 0.02744 &= [-0.7\%,\; 4.7\%] \end{aligned} \]

The lower end is a negative success rate.

Why does it break? The term \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\) is the standard error: how much an observed rate typically wobbles from sample to sample. But how much it wobbles depends on the true rate, which you do not know. The textbook formula plugs in the observed \(p\) instead. At \(p = 0\) that says “the rate never wobbles”, so the width is zero. Near 0 it underestimates the wobble, and because it also lays the same width on both sides of \(p\), the lower end falls below zero.

The Wilson score interval fixes this by turning the question around. Instead of asking “how far could the truth be from what I observed?”, it asks: which true rates would make what I observed unsurprising? Call a candidate true rate \(p^*\). With \(n\) episodes, a policy whose true rate is \(p^*\) produces observed rates with standard error \(\sqrt{p^*(1-p^*)/n}\), computed at \(p^*\), not at \(p\). The observed \(p\) is unsurprising if it lands within \(z = 1.96\) of those standard errors of \(p^*\). The interval is every \(p^*\) that passes that test.

The edges are the candidates that pass exactly, where the distance equals \(z\) standard errors:

\[ (p - p^*)^2 \;=\; z^2\,\frac{p^*(1 - p^*)}{n} \]

This is a quadratic equation in \(p^*\). Its two solutions are the interval’s two ends. They always lie inside [0, 1]: for any \(p^*\) outside that range, \(p^*(1 - p^*)\) is negative, so the right-hand side is negative, and the left-hand side, a square, can never be. And near the edges they sit lopsided around \(p\), because the wobble is computed separately at each candidate: a candidate closer to 50% wobbles more, so it can sit further away and still pass.

Try it on the random driver’s count, 0 out of 100, with \(z^2 = 1.96^2 = 3.8416\). With \(p = 0\), the left side is \((p^*)^2\), and the equation becomes \((p^*)^2 = 3.8416 \times p^*(1 - p^*)/100\). One solution is \(p^* = 0\): the lower end. For the other, divide both sides by \(p^*\): \(p^* = 0.038416\,(1 - p^*)\). Collect the \(p^*\) terms: \(p^* \times (1 + 0.038416) = 0.038416\). So \(p^* = 0.038416 / 1.038416 = 0.036995\), which you can also write as \(z^2/(n + z^2) = 3.8416/103.8416\). The upper end is 3.7%. A true success rate of up to 3.7% could plausibly produce zero goals in 100 episodes. Keep that number; the code and the smoke test will both give it back to you.

L0.8.2 The Wilson interval

For the general case, solve the quadratic from Section L0.8.1 once, with symbols. Three steps get you there. You can skim them on a first read, since you have already checked the result by hand at \(p = 0\).

Step 1: collect terms. Expand the left side, \((p - p^*)^2 = p^2 - 2p\,p^* + (p^*)^2\), multiply out the right side, and move everything to the left:

\[ \Big(1 + \frac{z^2}{n}\Big)(p^*)^2 \;-\; \Big(2p + \frac{z^2}{n}\Big)\,p^* \;+\; p^2 \;=\; 0 \]

Step 2: the quadratic formula. Apply it, then divide the top and the bottom by 2:

\[ p^* \;=\; \frac{p + \dfrac{z^2}{2n} \;\pm\; \sqrt{\Big(p + \dfrac{z^2}{2n}\Big)^2 - \Big(1 + \dfrac{z^2}{n}\Big)p^2}}{1 + \dfrac{z^2}{n}} \]

Step 3: tidy the square root. Expand the square; the two \(p^2\) terms cancel, and what is left factors neatly:

\[ \begin{aligned} &\Big(p + \frac{z^2}{2n}\Big)^2 - \Big(1 + \frac{z^2}{n}\Big)p^2 \\ &\quad= p^2 + \frac{p\,z^2}{n} + \frac{z^4}{4n^2} - p^2 - \frac{p^2 z^2}{n} \\ &\quad= z^2\Big(\frac{p(1-p)}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}\Big) \end{aligned} \]

So the square root is \(z\sqrt{p(1-p)/n + z^2/(4n^2)}\), and the two ends are a center minus a half-width and the same center plus it. Written out, that is the Wilson interval:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{center} &= \frac{p + \dfrac{z^2}{2n}}{1 + \dfrac{z^2}{n}} \\[6pt] \text{half} &= \frac{z\,\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} + \dfrac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \dfrac{z^2}{n}} \\[6pt] \text{interval} &= \big[\,\text{center} - \text{half},\;\; \text{center} + \text{half}\,\big] \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

\(n\) is the number of episodes and \(p\) the observed success rate, successes divided by \(n\). \(z = 1.96\) sets the coverage to 95%, as in the return interval. The shared denominator \(1 + z^2/n\) is just over 1 and shrinks the result slightly. The center (the code spells it centre) is not \(p\): the extra \(z^2/(2n)\) nudges it toward 50%, strongly when \(n\) is small and hardly at all when \(n\) is large. “half” is the half-width. Its square root holds the textbook term \(p(1-p)/n\) plus a small extra \(z^2/(4n^2)\), which keeps the width above zero even when \(p\) is exactly 0 or 1.

Try it yourself first

Write wilson_interval(successes, n, z=1.96) from the formula, returning a tuple (lo, hi). The formula leaves two decisions to you: what to return when n == 0, and what to do if floating-point rounding pushes an end a hair outside [0, 1].

def wilson_interval(successes: int, n: int, z: float = 1.96):    """95% confidence interval for a success rate (Wilson score interval).​    Unlike the textbook p +/- 1.96*sqrt(p(1-p)/n), it never leaves [0, 1] and    it stays honest when p is near 0% or 100%.    """    if n == 0:        return (0.0, 1.0)    p = successes / n    denom = 1 + z**2 / n    centre = (p + z**2 / (2 * n)) / denom    half = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z**2 / (4 * n**2)) / denom    return (max(0.0, centre - half), min(1.0, centre + half))

The two decisions, answered. With zero episodes you know nothing, and the honest interval is all of [0, 1]. And the max and min on the last line clamp the ends into [0, 1]. With 0 successes, for example, centre - half is mathematically zero, but floating-point rounding could make it a tiny negative number. The rest is the formula, line for line, with the same names (the reference code spells center the British way, centre).

You have now typed about 70 lines of common.py since the last time you ran anything. Check the new function before anything else leans on it. A typo in wilson_interval would otherwise surface only as a slightly wrong bracket in the smoke test, which is easy to miss. You already know two answers: the 3.7% upper end for 0 out of 100 from Section L0.8.1, and the example worked out in the next section, 33 out of 100.

Run it
python -c "from common import wilson_intervalprint(wilson_interval(33, 100))print(wilson_interval(0, 100))"
What you should see
(0.24562983793895452, 0.4269483966028862)(0.0, 0.03699480747600191)

The second line is the 0.036995 you solved for by hand in Section L0.8.1. The first line will match the hand computation of Section L0.8.3, which gets 0.245631 and 0.426951; the tiny differences in the sixth decimal come from rounding the intermediate steps by hand. If your digits disagree in the second or third decimal, compare your code with the formula one term at a time: the usual culprits are z**2 / 2 * n where z**2 / (2 * n) was meant, and a forgotten division by denom.

L0.8.3 Worked example: 33 successes out of 100

This example is not made up. In Lab 2 the data collector scores 33 successes in 100 episodes with its mean action, and evaluate prints its interval as [25%, 43%]. Here is where those two numbers come from, one step at a time, with \(z = 1.96\).

  1. The rate. \(p = 33 / 100 = 0.33\).
  2. The square of \(z\). \(z^2 = 1.96^2 = 3.8416\).
  3. The denominator. \(1 + 3.8416/100 = 1 + 0.038416 = 1.038416\).
  4. The center. The numerator is \(0.33 + 3.8416/200 = 0.33 + 0.019208 = 0.349208\). Divided by the denominator: \(0.349208 / 1.038416 = 0.336291\). The nudge moved the center from 0.33 to about 0.336, slightly toward 50%.
  5. Inside the square root. The textbook term is \(0.33 \times 0.67 / 100 = 0.2211 / 100 = 0.002211\). The extra term is \(3.8416 / (4 \times 100^2) = 3.8416 / 40000 = 0.00009604\). Their sum is \(0.002211 + 0.00009604 = 0.00230704\), and its square root is \(0.048032\).
  6. The half-width. \(1.96 \times 0.048032 = 0.094143\), and \(0.094143 / 1.038416 = 0.090660\).
  7. The interval. \(0.336291 - 0.090660 = 0.245631\) and \(0.336291 + 0.090660 = 0.426951\). So the interval is \([24.6\%, 42.7\%]\), which fmt_eval rounds to [25%, 43%].

For comparison, the textbook formula gives \(0.33 \pm 1.96 \times \sqrt{0.002211} = 0.33 \pm 0.0922\), which is \([23.8\%, 42.2\%]\). With 33 successes the two agree to within a point, because 33% is far from the edges. But notice the Wilson interval is lopsided: it reaches 8.4 points below 33% and 9.7 points above. The textbook interval is symmetric by construction.

Now the rules of thumb worth memorizing. Near a 50% success rate, the 95% interval is about \(\pm 14\) points with 50 episodes, about \(\pm 10\) with 100, and about \(\pm 6\) with 300. You will use them constantly. Lab 2 scores checkpoints and Lab 3 checks AWAC’s progress with 50 episodes per evaluation, so a jump from 50% to 60% between two of those evaluations is not evidence of anything. Lab 2’s sweep pools three seeds of 100 episodes each, 300 episodes in all, which is what lets it separate settings about 13 points apart.

Pooling has a limit, the same one you will meet in the poll analogy below. The pooled interval covers map luck for these three trained policies, treating the 300 episodes as if one policy had driven them all. It does not say what a fourth seed would score. So always read the per-seed numbers beside a pooled interval. For AWR at \(\beta = 0.3\) without the weight cap, the three seeds scored 51%, 40% and 51% (Section L2.9.2), a spread that the pooled interval [42%, 53%] does not show.

A practical reading rule follows, in three cases.

  • No overlap at all. The difference is very likely real.
  • Heavy overlap. Do not claim a difference; get more episodes or more seeds first.
  • Slight overlap, or ends that just touch. A gray zone, and one that leans toward “real”. Checking whether two separate intervals overlap is a conservative test: two rates can differ convincingly even when their intervals overlap a little. It is more conservative still when both policies faced the same evaluation maps, because a paired comparison removes the map-to-map differences that each interval still carries. So a gap whose intervals barely overlap is probably real. Say “probably”, and confirm with more episodes when the conclusion matters.

An analogy, with its limit. A success rate from 100 episodes is an election poll of 100 voters. The poll’s margin of error tells you how far the true share could plausibly sit from what you counted, and polling more people shrinks it. Where it breaks down: the margin of error covers only the luck of which voters, or maps, you happened to draw. It knows nothing about a bug in how you count, and nothing about training luck. A PPO run trained with a different seed is a different policy, so the interval around one seed’s 76% says nothing about what the next seed will score. That second kind of uncertainty is what Rule two’s seeds are for.

L0.8.4 The last four helpers

Four small functions finish common.py for this lab. (The Gaussian policy class from the docstring arrives in Lab 2, Section L2.4.)

def sb3_act_fn(model, deterministic: bool = True):    """Wrap a Stable-Baselines3 model as an act_fn for evaluate()."""    return lambda obs: model.predict(obs, deterministic=deterministic)[0]​​def fmt_eval(r: dict) -> str:    lo, hi = r["success_ci"]    return (f"success {r['success_rate']:.0%} [{lo:.0%}, {hi:.0%}]  "            f"crash {r['crash_rate']:.0%}  timeout {r['timeout_rate']:.0%}  "            f"return {r['mean_return']:.1f} "            f"[{r['return_ci'][0]:.1f}, {r['return_ci'][1]:.1f}]")​​def plot_style():    """Figure defaults for print: draw at about 7.5 inches wide    (the text width of an A4 page), so 9 pt labels are still 9 pt on paper    instead of shrinking to unreadable 4 pt."""    import matplotlib    matplotlib.rcParams.update({"font.size": 9, "axes.titlesize": 9.5,                                "axes.labelsize": 9, "legend.fontsize": 7.5,                                "xtick.labelsize": 8, "ytick.labelsize": 8,                                "savefig.dpi": 200})​​def save_json(obj, path: Path):    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)    path.write_text(json.dumps(obj, indent=2))

sb3_act_fn adapts a Stable-Baselines3 model to the act_fn contract. model.predict returns a pair: the action, and a hidden state that only recurrent policies use. The [0] keeps the action. The deterministic flag deserves your attention, because it is easy to get wrong without noticing. SB3’s predict defaults to deterministic=False, which samples an action from the Gaussian. Your predict.py passes deterministic=True and drives with the mean action. The demo loop at the end of your train_rover.py passes nothing, so it shows sampled behavior. This wrapper defaults to True, matching how you deploy, and the smoke test scores both ways.

fmt_eval turns an evaluate result into one line you can scan in a terminal. The format :.0% multiplies by 100, rounds to a whole number and adds a percent sign, so 0.245631 prints as 25%. The format :.1f prints one decimal place. Every script that prints a policy’s evaluation as one line uses this same format (Lab 2’s AWR runs and sweep, and Lab 3’s AWAC logs), which makes outputs from different labs easy to compare by eye. Lab 1’s scripts never call evaluate, and Lab 2’s checkpoint scorer prints its own compact table instead. Remember that it rounds: never copy a fmt_eval number into a calculation when the unrounded value is sitting in a JSON file.

plot_style is plotting housekeeping, not RL. Every script that draws a figure calls it first, so that labels stay readable when a figure is printed at page width. Nothing in this lab plots, but the plotting scripts of Labs 1 to 3 import it from common.py, so it belongs here. It imports matplotlib inside the function, so scripts that never plot never load matplotlib.

save_json writes any dictionary or list to a file, creating the parent folders first. indent=2 makes the file readable by a human. These JSON files in results/ are what the plotting scripts read later, and what your experiment notes should quote.

L0.8.5 The smoke test

Your common.py is complete for now. Before trusting it with three labs’ worth of conclusions, test it on two policies whose answers you already know. A random driver should almost never reach the goal. Your deployed model should reach it most of the time. If evaluate got either of those wrong, you would see it immediately.

Create lab0_smoke.py in your lab folder. Its full code is right here; the answer key has the same file as lab0_smoke.py.

"""Lab 0 smoke test: can evaluate() tell a random driver from your deployed model?"""import osos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""  # CPU only. Must run before torch is imported​import numpy as npfrom stable_baselines3 import PPO​from common import evaluate, fmt_eval, sb3_act_fn​# 1. A policy that ignores the observation: two uniform random wheel speeds per step.rng = np.random.default_rng(0)random_policy = lambda obs: rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=2)print(f"{'random policy':<19}: {fmt_eval(evaluate(random_policy, n_episodes=100))}")​# 2. Your deployed 5M-step model, driven by its mean action and then by sampled actions.#    (train_rover.py saved the file without a .zip extension; PPO.load accepts it as is.)model = PPO.load("../../ppo_rover_v0.2_wheel_randomization", device="cpu")for label, deterministic in [("v0.2, deterministic", True), ("v0.2, stochastic", False)]:    result = evaluate(sb3_act_fn(model, deterministic), n_episodes=100)    print(f"{label:<19}: {fmt_eval(result)}")

The random driver is a lambda that ignores the observation and draws two numbers uniformly from [−1, 1] using its own NumPy generator, seeded with 0. PPO.load reads your deployed model; device="cpu" keeps its tensors on the CPU. The format :<19 pads each label to 19 characters, so the three result lines line up in columns.

Run it
python lab0_smoke.py

It runs 300 episodes in total and takes about 9 seconds.

What you should see
random policy      : success 0% [0%, 4%]  crash 33%  timeout 67%  return -165.8 [-190.9, -140.7]v0.2, deterministic: success 76% [67%, 83%]  crash 24%  timeout 0%  return 97.5 [76.9, 118.1]v0.2, stochastic   : success 77% [68%, 84%]  crash 22%  timeout 1%  return 96.6 [75.5, 117.8]

L0.8.6 Reading the smoke test

First, the plumbing works. The environment builds, every episode ends, every outcome is counted (each line’s three rates add up to 100%), and both intervals are computed. That alone is worth the nine seconds.

The random driver. Zero goals in 100 episodes, as expected. Look at the interval, though: [0%, 4%], not [0%, 0%]. Check the upper end by hand, this time with the formula of Section L0.8.2. With \(p = 0\), the center, the half-width and the upper end are:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{center} &= (0 + 0.019208) / 1.038416 = 0.018497 \\ \text{half} &= 1.96 \times \sqrt{0 + 0.00009604} / 1.038416 = 1.96 \times 0.0098 / 1.038416 = 0.018497 \\ \text{upper end} &= 0.018497 + 0.018497 = 0.036994 \end{aligned} \]

The upper end, 0.036994, prints as 4%. It is the same 3.7% you solved for in Section L0.8.1 (0.036995 there; the last digit is hand rounding). Wilson is saying, correctly, that 100 episodes cannot rule out a true success rate of a few percent. Also notice the split: 33% crashes and 67% timeouts. If you expected a random driver to crash almost every time, that is your surprise line. Write down a guess at why; nothing later depends on it, and guessing is the practice.

Your deployed model. 76% success [67%, 83%] with the mean action. When it fails, it crashes (24%); it never runs out the clock (0% timeouts). For context, the healthy 1M-step PPO runs you will train in Lab 1 (and score in Lab 2) reach 62–70% with the mean action. So 5M steps probably bought something, but notice that 70% sits inside your model’s interval [67%, 83%]. The comparison is suggestive, not decisive.

Deterministic versus stochastic. 76% against 77%, with intervals [67%, 83%] and [68%, 84%]. They overlap almost completely. This is not evidence that sampling helps, and not evidence that it hurts: on this model and 100 episodes, the two ways of driving are indistinguishable. Don’t generalize it. In Lab 2 you will score a less-trained checkpoint where the gap is large, and very probably real: 33% with the mean action against 17% with sampled actions. Its intervals, [25%, 43%] and [11%, 26%], barely overlap, which puts it in the gray zone of Section L0.8.3, leaning toward real.

The returns. −165.8 [−190.9, −140.7] for the random driver against 97.5 [76.9, 118.1] for your model: the intervals are far apart, and they agree with the success rates. Now use the return formula from Section L0.7.5 backwards, to see how noisy a single episode is. The deterministic line’s half-width is \(118.1 - 97.5 = 20.6\), and the spread \(\sigma_R\) follows from it:

\[ 20.6 = 1.96 \times \frac{\sigma_R}{\sqrt{100}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \sigma_R = 20.6 \times 10 / 1.96 \approx 105 \]

One episode’s return typically lands about 105 points from the average. That is no surprise on this reward, where the terminal bonus and penalty alone are 200 points apart, and it is another reason the labs lead with success rate.

Which lines should repeat. With the same library versions as ours (Section L0.5.2), your first two lines should match ours exactly. The random driver draws from its own NumPy generator, seeded with 0. The mean action uses no randomness at all beyond the environment, which is seeded episode by episode. On other versions, judge those two lines against their intervals, as Section L0.2.5 explains.

Why your stochastic line will differ from ours. The third line samples its actions from PyTorch’s random number generator, and nothing in lab0_smoke.py seeds that generator. PPO.load does re-seed PyTorch when it loads a model, but only with the seed saved inside the model file. Your train_rover.py never passed a seed, so there is none to restore. Each run of the script therefore samples different actions and gets a slightly different third line.

How to judge yours. Compare it against the interval: a success rate a few points from 77% is the same result. Lab 1 shows the contrast. Its runs are trained with explicit seeds, so a sampled rollout right after loading one of their checkpoints does repeat exactly: two recordings of Lab 2’s dataset from the same checkpoint came out identical.

Before moving on, write your note, in the template from Section L0.3.3.

Checkpoint
