  • Name the groups in the 15-float observation, the terms of the reward, and why a far goal earns more return than a near one (L0.4.1 to L0.4.3).
  • For each of the three endings, say which flag it sets, and why a truncated episode’s future must not be treated as zero (L0.4.4, L0.4.5).
  • Explain why CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" must come before import torch in code that never uses the GPU (L0.5.3).
  • Say what paired evaluation seeds make fair and what they cannot tell you (L0.7.4).
  • Say which question the Wilson interval answers, compute one by hand, and quote roughly how wide it is at 50, 100 and 300 episodes. Say how to read two intervals that barely overlap, and what a pooled interval over three seeds leaves out (L0.8.1 to L0.8.3).

Where to go deeper. The three rules come from book Appendix B, Section B.1; reread it before each lab. Before Lab 1, read book Sections 3.4 to 3.6 (the clip, GAE, and the curves on the rover). Before Lab 2, read book Chapter 4 through Section 4.4; Section 4.5 is the background for Lab 3. The Wilson interval goes back to Wilson’s 1927 paper in the Journal of the American Statistical Association; any modern statistics text covers it.

Lab 1 — Break PPO on purpose, then read the damage

You have trained PPO on the rover many times, and you probably notice when a run’s TensorBoard looks off before you can say why. This lab turns that feeling into a skill you can explain. You will train the rover nine times, break two of PPO’s knobs on purpose, and learn to name the broken knob from the curves alone.

This is book rung E3 from Appendix B, “PPO forensics on the rover”, with one change explained where it comes up: runs are 1,000,000 steps long instead of 300,000. Each configuration gets three seeds, the low end of the 3–5 that Appendix B’s Rule two asks for. Book Chapter 3 holds the theory. This lab recaps only what it needs and names the book section to open for the full argument.

You need your own lab folder, labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/, the rover venv and common.py from Lab 0. Run every command from inside your lab folder with the venv active. The computer time is about ten minutes on 12 cores. The reading takes longer, and it should.

One note before you compare outputs. Every printed output in this lab came from the answer key, so any path it prints names labs/ppo-awr-awac/. Yours will name labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/. That difference is expected and does not mean you are writing into the answer key.

StepYou writeIt producesTime (12 cores)
1 (L1.3)lab1_train_ppo.pyone PPO run: TensorBoard log, a checkpoint every 50k steps, final.zip9 s smoke test
2 (L1.4)lab1_run_all.pynine runs: 3 configurations × 3 seeds × 1M stepsabout 10 min
3 (L1.5)lab1_plot_curves.pythree figures and results/lab1_summary.jsonseconds
4 (L1.8)lab1_gae_by_hand.pyone real episode’s advantages, by hand and checked against SB3seconds

Sections L1.2, L1.6 and L1.7 contain no code. They are where you learn to read, which is the point of the lab.

L1.1 The question

Appendix B’s Rule one says to write the question down first, as one sentence ending in a question mark:

Can I diagnose, from TensorBoard curves alone, which knob a broken PPO run needs?

“Curves alone”, because they are usually all you have. Nobody replays hundreds of episodes of an overnight run, or of a colleague’s run, to find out what went wrong. You open TensorBoard and look at six lines.

The trouble is that almost every PPO curve you have seen came from a run that mostly worked. You know what normal looks like. You have never seen a specific failure side by side with normal, and a symptom you have never seen is a symptom you cannot name.

So this lab runs in the other direction. You pick the cause, change nothing else, and record what every curve does. Once you have seen cause and symptom together, you can reason backward from a symptom to its knob.

An analogy. Software teams call this fault injection. You kill a database replica on purpose on a Tuesday afternoon, so the dashboard pattern of a dead replica has been seen and named before it happens for real at 3 a.m.

Where the analogy breaks down. A killed replica shows up within seconds and looks the same every time. A broken PPO knob does neither. Its damage can take hundreds of thousands of steps to appear; one break in this lab even looks like an improvement for the first third of training. And the same break looks different on different seeds. So this lab needs three things a fault-injection drill does not: a healthy baseline trained by the same code, three seeds per configuration, and runs long enough for slow damage to show.

L1.1.1 The design: one healthy configuration, two broken ones

There are three configurations. Each changes at most one knob, so any damage has exactly one possible cause (Rule one again).

  • baseline — SB3’s defaults, clip_range=0.2 and gae_lambda=0.95. This is your usual train_rover.py setup plus seeds and checkpoints, and every broken run is compared against it.
  • clip10 — clip_range=10. An action’s probability ratio compares how likely the policy now is to take an action from the stored batch with how likely the policy that collected the batch was; it equals 1 while nothing has changed (Section L1.2.2 defines it properly). PPO’s clip normally stops rewarding the policy for moving that ratio more than 20% away from 1 (book Section 3.4.1). With 10, the window is so wide that the clip almost never acts. You removed PPO’s brake and kept everything else.
  • lambda0 — gae_lambda=0.0. The advantage becomes the one-step TD error. You turned GAE’s dial all the way to “trust the critic” (book Section 3.5.3).

Each configuration runs with seeds 0, 1 and 2, for 1,000,000 steps. Appendix B suggests 300,000 steps. At 300,000 steps, though, both breaks would have looked harmless on the reward curve: clip10 was ahead of the baseline and lambda0 was level with it (Sections L1.6 and L1.7).

L1.1.2 What this lab hands to Lab 2

Lab 2 learns a policy from a file of logged episodes, recorded by a deliberately mediocre policy: one that reaches the goal sometimes, not usually. A finished run cannot give you back the version of itself from 100,000 steps ago. Either you saved it while training passed through that point, or it is gone.

So every run here saves a checkpoint every 50,000 steps, 20 per run. Lab 2 scores the baseline checkpoints and picks one. Keep the runs/ folder when you finish.

L1.2 Reading a healthy run: your own PPO_9

Before breaking anything, calibrate your eye on a run you trust. tb_rover_v0/PPO_9 is the 5M-step run that produced ppo_rover_v0.2_wheel_randomization, the model you deployed, which Lab 0 measured at 76% success. Figure L1.1 draws its curves with the script you will write in Step 3.

Two facts about these curves prevent confusion. First, SB3 writes one point per rollout, one round of collecting a batch: 8 environments × 2,048 steps = 16,384 environment steps, after which PPO trains on that batch. Over 5M steps that is 306 points. Each point summarizes one batch, which is why the lines are jagged.

Second, SB3’s defaults include n_epochs=10: every batch is reused for ten passes. Each pass cuts the 16,384 samples into minibatches of 64 and takes one gradient step per minibatch. Book Section 3.6.1 suggests 4 passes. Everything in this lab uses 10, so expect some curves to sit away from where the book says they should.

Below is one subsection per curve: what SB3 actually computes (checked in the SB3 2.9 source), and what healthy looks like on this rover.

L1.2.1 ep_rew_mean: the ground truth, as a moving average

rollout/ep_rew_mean is the average total reward of the last 100 finished episodes, across all 8 environments. The Monitor wrapper around each environment records each episode’s total, and SB3 logs the average once per rollout. Because it is a moving average, it smooths over luck and lags the policy a little.

For scale: ordinary steps earn about ±1, mostly 33 times the distance gained toward the goal, minus small penalties. An episode ends with +100 at the goal, −100 on a collision, or a cut-off after 500 steps. A policy that never reaches the goal sits far below zero; Lab 0’s random policy averaged −165.8.

PPO_9: −138 at the start, about 40 at 0.46M steps, about 90 at 0.92M, and about 100 over the last million, with most points between 90 and 115. This is the curve every other curve exists to explain (book Section 3.6.2). The other five never overrule it.

L1.2.2 approx_kl: how far did one batch move the policy?

The problem. PPO reuses each batch for 10 epochs, and after the first gradient step the policy is no longer the one that collected the data (book Section 3.2.1). You want one number for how far it has drifted.

In principle that number is the KL divergence (book Section 3.3.2). KL divergence is one number for how different two probability distributions are: zero when they are identical, and larger the more they differ. Here it compares the old policy with the current one, averaged over the actions the old policy took. SB3 estimates it from the samples it already has. For each sample it stored the old policy’s log-probability of the action; during training it computes the current one, and from the two it gets the ratio \(\rho_i\):

\[ \widehat{\mathrm{KL}} \;=\; \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\Big[\,(\rho_i - 1) - \log \rho_i\,\Big], \qquad \rho_i = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_i \mid s_i)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_i \mid s_i)} \]
In plain words

\(\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}\) is what TensorBoard shows as approx_kl. For stored sample \(i\), \(s_i\) is the state and \(a_i\) the action taken there. \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) is the policy that collected the batch, and \(\pi_\theta\) the policy as it is now, partway through training. The ratio \(\rho_i\) says how many times more likely the current policy is to take that same action. \(\log\) is the natural log. \(M\) is the number of samples averaged: SB3 uses the minibatches of the last epoch only, so this is the drift seen during the tenth pass. Each bracket is zero when \(\rho_i = 1\) and positive for any other ratio, so the average is never negative and grows as the policy moves.

Why that bracket? Take its two parts one at a time.

First, the samples were drawn by the old policy, so on average the ratios equal 1. One line shows it (for a single state, written with sums over actions):

\[ \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}}\big[\rho\big] = \sum_a \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a)\,\frac{\pi_\theta(a)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a)} = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a) = 1 \]

The old policy’s probability cancels, and any policy’s probabilities add up to 1. For the rover’s continuous actions the sums become integrals and the cancellation is the same. (This is book Section 3.2.2’s identity with \(f = 1\).) So the \((\rho_i - 1)\) part averages to zero.

Second, the \(-\log \rho_i\) part equals \(\log \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_i \mid s_i) - \log \pi_\theta(a_i \mid s_i)\). Its average over the old policy’s actions is exactly the KL definition of book Section 3.3.2, \(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}}[\log \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a) - \log \pi_\theta(a)]\).

So the first part changes nothing on average. Its job is to make every single term non-negative.

A worked example with made-up ratios. Take three samples with ratios 1.2, 0.8 and 1.0:

  • \(\rho = 1.2\): \((1.2 - 1) - \log 1.2 = 0.2 - 0.182322 = 0.017678\)
  • \(\rho = 0.8\): \((0.8 - 1) - \log 0.8 = -0.2 + 0.223144 = 0.023144\)
  • \(\rho = 1.0\): \(0 - 0 = 0\)

The average is \((0.017678 + 0.023144 + 0) / 3 = 0.040822 / 3 = 0.013607\). Add a fourth sample with ratio 11:

\[ \begin{aligned} (11 - 1) - \log 11 &= 10 - 2.397895 = 7.602105 \\ \text{average of four} &= (0.040822 + 7.602105) / 4 = 7.642927 / 4 = 1.910732 \end{aligned} \]

One runaway sample counts as much as about 430 samples with ratio 1.2, since \(7.602105 / 0.017678 = 430\). Remember that in Section L1.6.

A rule of thumb. For ratios near 1 the bracket is close to \((\rho - 1)^2 / 2\); for 1.2 that gives 0.02, against the exact 0.0177. So a small KL corresponds to typical ratio changes of about \(\sqrt{2 \times \mathrm{KL}}\): about 10% at a KL of 0.005 \((\sqrt{0.01} = 0.10)\), about 18% at 0.017 \((\sqrt{0.034} = 0.18)\). It is rough, and it fails for large values.

PPO_9: approx_kl rises smoothly from 0.005 to 0.017. The lab’s baseline runs have medians of 0.0059 to 0.0062, and their largest single values (0.0075 to 0.0082) are barely higher. Book Section 3.6.2 gives 0.01–0.03 as the healthy band. On this rover the healthy run spends millions of steps below that band, and nothing is wrong. Healthy here means small, smooth, and free of sudden jumps.

L1.2.3 clip_fraction: how often did a sample leave the window?

The problem. An average hides how many samples went far. You also want to know how many samples left PPO’s clip window \([1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon]\) from book Section 3.4.1.

\[ \text{clip fraction} \;=\; \frac{1}{E\,N}\sum_{e=1}^{E}\,\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\!\left[\,\big|\rho_i^{(e)} - 1\big| \gt \epsilon\,\right] \]
In plain words

\(\epsilon\) is clip_range, 0.2 by default. \(E\) is the number of epochs (10) and \(N\) the samples per batch (16,384), so the double sum visits every sample once per epoch: 163,840 visits. \(\rho_i^{(e)}\) is sample \(i\)’s ratio when its minibatch is used in epoch \(e\). \(\mathbf{1}[\ldots]\) counts 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise. So the clip fraction is the share of sample visits whose ratio was more than \(\epsilon\) away from 1. Unlike approx_kl, it averages over all epochs, including the first minibatch, where nothing has moved yet.

A worked example with made-up ratios. Take four samples with ratios 1.25, 0.7, 1.05 and 12. (A ratio is never negative, so with \(\epsilon = 10\) only ratios above 11 can count.) With \(\epsilon = 0.2\): \(|0.25| \gt 0.2\) counts, \(|-0.3| \gt 0.2\) counts, \(|0.05|\) does not, \(|11| \gt 0.2\) counts. That is 3 of 4, a clip fraction of 0.75. With \(\epsilon = 10\), only \(|11| \gt 10\) counts: 1 of 4, or 0.25. Same movement, very different reading.

PPO_9: the clip fraction rises from 0.05 to 0.195, with the same shape as approx_kl. By the end, typical ratio changes of about 18% meet a window edge at 20%. The baseline medians are 0.062 to 0.067. Book Section 3.6.2’s band is 0.1–0.3, which PPO_9 reaches only after about 2M steps. In a healthy run the two gauges move together, because they measure the same movement two ways. Section L1.6 shows what it means when they disagree.

L1.2.4 entropy_loss: a gauge, not a force (in your configuration)

SB3 logs train/entropy_loss as minus the average entropy of the policy’s action distribution. It is the term PPO would add to the loss to pay for exploration (book Section 3.4.5). But that term is multiplied by ent_coef, and SB3’s default, which you use, is 0.0. So in your runs it does nothing to training. It is a gauge of how spread out the actions still are.

Because of the minus sign, the curve rises as the policy becomes more certain. Reading that rise as “a loss getting worse” is the most common misreading of this panel.

The number has a physical meaning. The rover’s policy is a Gaussian per wheel, with a learned standard deviation \(\sigma\) that does not depend on the state. One Gaussian’s entropy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e) + \log\sigma \approx 1.4189 + \log\sigma\), and SB3 adds the two wheels. With the same \(\sigma\) on both wheels:

\[ \text{entropy loss} = -2 \times \big(1.4189 + \log \sigma\big) \]

  • At the start \(\sigma\) is close to 1, and \(\log 1 = 0\), so entropy loss \(= -2 \times 1.4189 = -2.84\). Every curve in this lab starts near −2.8.
  • The baseline at 1M steps has \(\sigma = 0.51\): \(\log 0.51 = -0.6733\); \(1.4189 - 0.6733 = 0.7456\); \(-2 \times 0.7456 = -1.49\). The baseline curves end near −1.5.
  • Zero is where \(\log \sigma = -1.4189\), that is \(\sigma = e^{-1.4189} \approx 0.24\). A positive entropy loss means the wheels’ standard deviation is below about 0.24.

A continuous distribution’s entropy may be negative, so nothing breaks at zero. PPO_9: a smooth rise from −2.8 to +0.9, so its final action noise is well below 0.24 per wheel, with no cliff-drop of the kind book Section 3.6.2 warns about. SB3 also logs train/std, the two wheels’ average \(\sigma\), which is easier to read; Step 3’s summary uses it.

L1.2.5 explained_variance: the critic’s grade, on a relative scale

The problem. PPO’s advantages are built from the critic’s predictions (Section L1.8), so a useless critic makes useless advantages. You want a grade for the critic that does not depend on how big the rewards are.

\[ \mathrm{EV} \;=\; 1 - \frac{\mathrm{Var}\big(\hat G_t - V(s_t)\big)}{\mathrm{Var}\big(\hat G_t\big)} \]
In plain words

EV is explained_variance. \(\hat G_t\) is the critic’s training target for step \(t\), stored as rollout_buffer.returns. \(V(s_t)\) is the critic’s prediction for that state, recorded while the batch was collected, before training on it. \(\mathrm{Var}\) is the variance over the batch’s 16,384 samples. The fraction is the share of the targets’ spread that the predictions fail to account for. EV = 1 means perfect predictions. EV = 0 means no better than one constant for every state. Negative means worse than a constant.

One detail decides Section L1.7. The target \(\hat G_t\) is not a pure record of what happened. SB3 builds it by adding the critic’s own prediction back onto the advantage: \(\hat G_t = \hat A_t + V(s_t)\) (book Section 3.4.5). The advantage is itself built from the critic’s predictions (Section L1.8 shows how). So the target is a mix of two things: real rewards the rover earned, and the critic’s guesses about the states those rewards led to.

These targets are called λ-returns, because \(\lambda\), gae_lambda, sets the mix. Written out, a real reward \(k\) steps ahead enters the target with weight \((\gamma\lambda)^k\) (Section L1.8.1 shows where that weight comes from). Put in the numbers:

  • At \(\lambda = 0.95\) the base is \(0.99 \times 0.95 = 0.9405\). The step’s own reward has weight 1, the next one 0.9405, the reward ten steps ahead \(0.9405^{10} \approx 0.54\), and the reward seventeen steps ahead \(0.9405^{17} \approx 0.35\).
  • Those weights, \(1 + 0.9405 + 0.9405^2 + \ldots\), add up to \(1 / (1 - 0.9405) = 1 / 0.0595 \approx 16.8\). So the target holds about as much real reward as seventeen steps counted in full.
  • At \(\lambda = 0\) the base is 0. The step’s own reward has weight 1, every later reward has weight 0, and the critic’s guess stands in for all of them.

That is what matters for grading. Explained variance grades the critic against an answer the critic partly wrote. At \(\lambda = 0.95\) the answer contains about seventeen steps of real rewards; at \(\lambda = 0\) it contains one.

PPO_9: EV climbs from 0 to about 0.76 by 0.5M steps, then settles near 0.55 while reward holds. The baseline runs end at 0.65 to 0.69. Healthy here is a fast early climb to a plateau somewhere around 0.5 to 0.8, not a value near 1.

L1.2.6 value_loss: the surprise — rising is healthy here

SB3’s train/value_loss is the mean squared error between the critic’s prediction \(V(s_t)\) and the λ-return \(\hat G_t\), averaged over all minibatches of all 10 epochs. Its units are reward squared.

Book Section 3.6.2 says value loss should fall early. On PPO_9 it rises, from about 100 to about 500 in the first 0.4M steps, then wanders between roughly 350 and 650. The critic is not broken. The targets changed.

At first nearly every episode ends in a crash or a timeout, and returns sit around −140. Those are similar numbers, and similar numbers are easy to predict. Once the rover starts reaching goals, returns grow toward +100. More importantly, they spread out, because some episodes now end with +100 and others with −100. Squared errors on bigger, more spread-out numbers are bigger, even for a critic that is doing relatively better. One approximate relation ties the two critic curves together:

\[ \text{value loss} \;\approx\; \mathrm{Var}\big(\hat G_t - V(s_t)\big) \;=\; (1 - \mathrm{EV}) \cdot \mathrm{Var}\big(\hat G_t\big) \]
In plain words

The value loss is roughly the variance of the critic’s errors \(\hat G_t - V(s_t)\), exactly so when the errors average to zero. The equals sign is the EV definition rearranged. So the loss is two factors multiplied: the share of the targets’ spread the critic misses, \(1 - \mathrm{EV}\), and the targets’ spread, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat G_t)\). It can grow because the critic got worse, or because the targets grew. In SB3 it is only approximate, since the loss is averaged while the critic trains and EV uses predictions from before training.

A worked example with made-up numbers. Early on, the targets have a standard deviation of 10, so \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat G) = 10^2 = 100\), and the critic is useless, EV = 0. The value loss is about \((1 - 0) \times 100 = 100\). Later, the targets have a standard deviation of 40, so \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat G) = 40^2 = 1{,}600\), and the critic is good, EV = 0.7. The value loss is about \((1 - 0.7) \times 1{,}600 = 0.3 \times 1{,}600 = 480\). The loss grew almost fivefold while the critic went from useless to good.

How to read it: never alone. Value loss rising while explained variance also rises and reward climbs, as in PPO_9, means the targets grew and the critic kept up. By the relation above, a rising loss with a falling explained variance would mean the critic is losing ground. Section L1.7 shows a third case, falling loss with rising explained variance, that still hides a real problem.

L1.2.7 What healthy looks like on this rover

CurvePPO_9 (5M steps)Lab baseline (3 seeds, 1M)Book, generic (section)
ep_rew_mean−138 → ~90 (0.92M) → ~100final 65.6 to 74.4climbs raggedly (3.1.2)
approx_kl0.005 → 0.017, smoothmedian 0.0059 to 0.00620.01–0.03 (3.6.2)
clip_fraction0.05 → 0.195, tracks KLmedian 0.062 to 0.0670.1–0.3 (3.6.2)
entropy_loss−2.8 → +0.9, no cliffends near −1.5 (std 0.51–0.53)entropy decays slowly (3.6.2)

Words you will hear

Rollout (SB3’s logs also say iteration) — one round of collecting a batch with the current policy, then training on it.

λ-return or TD(λ) return — the critic’s target \(\hat A_t + V(s_t)\), a blend of real rewards and the critic’s own predictions.

Entropy collapse — action noise shrinking so fast that the policy stops exploring before it has found good behavior.

KL early stopping — ending a batch’s epochs once approx_kl passes a limit; SB3’s target_kl, off (None) by default.

L1.3 Step 1: one training run, lab1_train_ppo.py

Why this script exists. train_rover.py trains one model and saves it at the end. Forensics needs more: the same configuration trained several times and told apart, the two knobs you will break exposed as flags, a run name the plot script can group by, and checkpoints for Lab 2. So lab1_train_ppo.py is train_rover.py plus --seed, --clip-range, --gae-lambda, --tag and a checkpoint every 50,000 steps. Everything else stays SB3’s default PPO. You will write it in five chunks.

L1.3.1 The first lines: CPU only

"""Lab 1, step 1: train one PPO run on the rover, optionally with one knob broken.​This is your train_rover.py with four additions: --seed, --clip-range and--gae-lambda, --tag, and a checkpoint every 50k steps. Everything else isSB3's default PPO, exactly as train_rover.py uses it.​    python lab1_train_ppo.py --tag clip10 --seed 0 --clip-range 10"""​import os# CPU only. Must run before torch is imported: see common.pyos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""​import argparseimport time​import torchfrom stable_baselines3 import PPOfrom stable_baselines3.common.callbacks import CheckpointCallbackfrom stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env​from common import ENV_ID, RUNS, ensure_dirs​N_ENVS = 8  # same as train_rover.py

The two statements after the docstring hide the GPU. They must run before anything imports torch, including common. Section L0.5.3 tells the whole story; in short, without them the parallel runs of Step 2 die with CUDA error: out of memory even though every tensor is on the CPU.

common.py supplies the environment’s registered name, the runs/ folder, and a helper that creates the output folders. N_ENVS is a named constant because it is used twice, and the second use (L1.3.4) is where a bug would hide.

L1.3.2 The flags

def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--tag", default="baseline",                   help="run name, e.g. baseline / clip10 / lambda0")    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=1_000_000,                   help="total environment steps")    p.add_argument("--clip-range", type=float, default=0.2,                   help="PPO's epsilon (SB3 default 0.2)")    p.add_argument("--gae-lambda", type=float, default=0.95,                   help="GAE's lambda (SB3 default 0.95)")    p.add_argument("--ckpt-every", type=int, default=50_000,                   help="save a checkpoint every N env steps")    args = p.parse_args()

Every default reproduces the baseline. Running with no flags trains baseline_s0, and a broken configuration is the baseline plus one flag. argparse turns dashes into underscores, so --clip-range arrives as args.clip_range. 1_000_000 is a million, written readably. --steps exists for smoke tests. --ckpt-every is in environment steps, the unit you think in, and L1.3.4 converts it to the unit SB3 counts in.

L1.3.3 The environment and the model

    ensure_dirs()    # A small MLP trains faster on the CPU than on a GPU (the data transfer costs    # more than the math). One thread per run lets you run several runs at once.    torch.set_num_threads(1)​    run_name = f"{args.tag}_s{args.seed}"    run_dir = RUNS / run_name​    # make_vec_env wraps each env in a Monitor, which is what produces the    # rollout/ep_rew_mean and rollout/ep_len_mean curves in TensorBoard.    vec_env = make_vec_env(ENV_ID, n_envs=N_ENVS, seed=args.seed)​    model = PPO(        "MlpPolicy",        vec_env,        clip_range=args.clip_range,        gae_lambda=args.gae_lambda,        seed=args.seed,        device="cpu",        tensorboard_log=str(RUNS / "tb"),        verbose=0,    )

torch.set_num_threads(1) is for Step 2: PyTorch normally uses several threads per process, and six runs doing that on 12 cores would fight over the cores. run_name, for example clip10_s1, names the checkpoint folder, the TensorBoard folder and the log file. make_vec_env builds 8 environment copies, each wrapped in the Monitor behind ep_rew_mean. Passing seed here and to PPO seeds the environments, the network’s initialization and the action sampling.

Compared with train_rover.py, the PPO(...) call adds the two knobs, the seed, device="cpu", a shared runs/tb/ log folder, and verbose=0, since nine log files do not need a table after every rollout. Everything else is SB3’s default: n_steps=2048, batch_size=64, n_epochs=10, learning_rate=3e-4, gamma=0.99, ent_coef=0.0, and a [64, 64] tanh network.

L1.3.4 Checkpoints, and the counting pitfall

Try it yourself first

SB3’s CheckpointCallback(save_freq=...) saves a file every save_freq calls, and it is called once per vec_env.step(), which advances all 8 environments by one step each. You want a checkpoint every 50,000 environment steps. What should save_freq be? If files are named ppo_<total env steps>_steps.zip, what is the second file called?

    # CheckpointCallback counts *calls*, and it is called once per vec_env.step(),    # which advances all N_ENVS environments at once. So "every 50k env steps"    # is every 50_000 / 8 = 6250 calls. Forgetting the division gives you    # checkpoints 8x further apart than you asked for.    checkpoints = CheckpointCallback(        save_freq=max(args.ckpt_every // N_ENVS, 1),        save_path=str(run_dir / "checkpoints"),        name_prefix="ppo",  # files: ppo_50000_steps.zip, ppo_100000_steps.zip, ...    )

The answer is \(50{,}000 / 8 = 6{,}250\) calls, and the second file is ppo_100000_steps.zip. Each call adds 8 to the step counter, so after 6,250 calls the counter reads 50,000, and SB3 writes that counter into the file name.

Now the mistake this chunk prevents. save_freq=50_000 looks right, and it saves every 50,000 calls: \(50{,}000 \times 8 = 400{,}000\) environment steps. A 1M-step run then gets two checkpoints, at 400k and 800k, and Lab 2 has nothing mediocre to choose from. Nothing warns you. The max(..., 1) only keeps a tiny --ckpt-every from rounding down to zero.

L1.3.5 Train, save, report

    t0 = time.time()    # tb_log_name is the folder inside runs/tb. SB3 appends "_1" to it.    model.learn(total_timesteps=args.steps, callback=checkpoints, tb_log_name=run_name)    model.save(run_dir / "final")    print(f"{run_name}: {args.steps:,} steps in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s "          f"-> {run_dir}/final.zip")​​if __name__ == "__main__":    main()

tb_log_name=run_name names the TensorBoard folder, and SB3 appends a counter: baseline_s0 logs to runs/tb/baseline_s0_1, and a second run with the same name would get _2. SB3 also finishes the rollout it has started. 1,000,000 steps is 61.03 rollouts, so it runs 62, and the last logged point is at \(62 \times 16{,}384 = 1{,}015{,}808\) steps. The twentieth checkpoint is at exactly 1,000,000; final.zip is the model at the very end. The printed line reports the number you asked for.

Run it

A smoke test: two rollouts (\(2 \times 16{,}384 = 32{,}768\)), with a checkpoint after each (\(16{,}384 / 8 = 2{,}048\) calls).

python lab1_train_ppo.py --tag smoke --seed 0 --steps 32768 --ckpt-every 16384ls runs/smoke_s0/checkpoints runs/tb
What you should see
smoke_s0: 32,768 steps in 9 s ->    /mnt/Storage/projects/rl-rover/labs/ppo-awr-awac/runs/smoke_s0/final.zipruns/smoke_s0/checkpoints:ppo_16384_steps.zip  ppo_32768_steps.zip​runs/tb:smoke_s0_1

Your seconds will differ. Throughout this lab, printed paths show our answer-key folder, ppo-awr-awac; yours will show my-ppo-awr-awac.

How to read it. The file names confirm the checkpoint arithmetic, and smoke_s0_1 confirms where the logs went. 32,768 steps in 9 seconds is about 3,600 steps per second, so a 1M-step run on its own would take about \(1{,}000{,}000 / 3{,}600 = 278\) seconds. If you see CUDA error: out of memory instead, the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES line is missing or runs too late.

Delete the smoke run now. The plot script in Step 3 reads every folder in runs/tb that matches *_s*_1, and smoke_s0_1 matches.

Run it
rm -rf runs/smoke_s0 runs/tb/smoke_s0_1
Pitfalls
  • Counting. save_freq counts calls, not environment steps. Divide by the number of environments.
  • Re-running a tag. A second baseline_s0 logs to baseline_s0_2, which the plot script ignores, so your figure silently shows the old run. Its checkpoints and final.zip, on the other hand, have the same file names as before and overwrite the old ones. The figure (old logs) and the checkpoints (new run) then no longer describe the same run. Delete runs/<name>/ and runs/tb/<name>_1/ before re-running.
  • Leftover smoke tests appear as extra gray marks near the start of the grid figure, and as an extra row in the printed summary.

L1.4 Step 2: the whole grid, lab1_run_all.py

Why this script exists. Nine runs back to back, at a little under five minutes each, take about 40 minutes. Each run uses one torch thread and the machine has 12 cores, so this script runs several at once and reports each run as it finishes.

L1.4.1 Why separate processes

  • Real parallelism. Threads inside one Python process take turns running Python code, and the rover simulator and SB3’s rollout loop are Python. Separate processes truly run at the same time.
  • Isolation. A crash, like the CUDA out-of-memory error, kills one run instead of nine, and leaves a log that says why.
  • No new code path. The grid runs exactly the script you just smoke-tested.

L1.4.2 Why three seeds

Appendix B’s Rule two asks for 3–5 seeds when runs are cheap, “because a single-seed RL result is noise wearing the costume of a finding”. So fix the decision rule before you look at anything: if all three broken seeds land below all three baseline seeds, that is a result. If they overlap, it is not.

Why is three enough for that rule to mean something, when one or two are not? Count how often the rule would pass by pure luck.

A worked example (teaching arithmetic, not a measurement). Suppose the broken knob changed nothing. Then the six final rewards, three baseline and three broken, come out in a random order, and every order is equally likely. The rule passes only if the three broken runs are the three lowest of the six.

  • The number of ways to choose which three of six runs are the lowest is \[ \binom{6}{3} = \frac{6!}{3! \cdot 3!} = \frac{720}{6 \times 6} = \frac{720}{36} = 20. \]
  • Exactly one of those 20 choices is “the three broken runs”. So the rule passes by luck 1 time in 20, or 5%.
  • With two seeds per configuration, \[ \binom{4}{2} = \frac{4!}{2! \cdot 2!} = \frac{24}{4} = 6, \] so luck passes the rule 1 time in 6, about 17%.
  • With one seed each there are only two orders, so luck passes it 1 time in 2, a coin flip.

The limits of that arithmetic. It assumes seeds are interchangeable, so that with no real effect every order is equally likely. And this lab tests two broken configurations, which gives luck two chances. The chance that at least one of them passes by luck is at most \(2 \times 5\% = 10\%\). Three seeds make a fluke unlikely, not impossible. Section L1.6 shows what they bought besides: the three clip10 seeds ended in very different places.

L1.4.3 The code

"""Lab 1, step 2: train the whole experiment grid, several runs at a time.​    baseline   clip_range=0.2  gae_lambda=0.95   (SB3 defaults: the healthy run)    clip10     clip_range=10   gae_lambda=0.95   (the clip almost never binds)    lambda0    clip_range=0.2  gae_lambda=0.0    (advantages = one-step TD only)​Why three seeds: two seeds of the SAME configuration can differ more than twodifferent configurations. If all three "broken" seeds land below all threebaseline seeds, that is a result. If they overlap, it is not.​    python lab1_run_all.py --parallel 6       (on 4 cores use --parallel 3)"""​import os# CPU only. Must run before torch is imported: see common.pyos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""​import argparseimport subprocessimport sysimport timefrom concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutorfrom pathlib import Path​HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent​CONFIGS = {    "baseline": [],    "clip10": ["--clip-range", "10"],    "lambda0": ["--gae-lambda", "0.0"],}SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]

The experiment design lives in CONFIGS and SEEDS. Each configuration is written as the flags it adds to the baseline, so “one knob per configuration” is visible at a glance. HERE, the script’s own folder, lets you start the launcher from any directory. This script never imports torch, but every lab script starts with the CPU-only lines, so you never have to remember which ones need them.

def run(cmd):    t0 = time.time()    # Each run's text output goes to its own log file instead of the terminal.    tag, seed = cmd[cmd.index("--tag") + 1], cmd[cmd.index("--seed") + 1]    log = HERE / "runs" / f"{tag}_s{seed}.log"    log.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)    with open(log, "w") as f:        code = subprocess.call(cmd, stdout=f, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, cwd=HERE)    return log.name, code, time.time() - t0

run launches one training process and waits for it. The log name is rebuilt from the command: cmd.index("--tag") + 1 is the position of the value after --tag, so --tag clip10 --seed 1 logs to runs/clip10_s1.log. subprocess.call returns the process’s exit code, where 0 means success. stderr=subprocess.STDOUT puts tracebacks into the same log. cwd=HERE runs the child where common.py can be imported.

def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--parallel", type=int, default=6,                   help="how many runs at the same time")    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=1_000_000)    args = p.parse_args()​    cmds = []    for tag, extra in CONFIGS.items():        for seed in SEEDS:            cmds.append([sys.executable, "lab1_train_ppo.py",                         "--tag", tag, "--seed", str(seed),                         "--steps", str(args.steps), *extra])​    print(f"launching {len(cmds)} runs, {args.parallel} at a time")    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=args.parallel) as pool:        for name, code, secs in pool.map(run, cmds):            status = "ok" if code == 0 else f"FAILED (exit {code}) - read runs/{name}"            print(f"  {name:<18} {secs / 60:5.1f} min  {status}")​​if __name__ == "__main__":    main()

sys.executable is the Python running the launcher, so every child uses the same venv. *extra appends the configuration’s flags. Threads are fine here, despite L1.4.1, because these threads run no simulation: each one starts a process and waits, and waiting does not compete for Python. pool.map returns results in the order the commands were listed. So the baseline lines print first, and a finished run is reported only after the runs listed before it.

Run it
python lab1_run_all.py --parallel 6

To watch curves arrive, run tensorboard --logdir runs/tb in a second terminal and open the address it prints.

What you should see
launching 9 runs, 6 at a time

Then nothing for about five minutes, while six runs train. Then one line per run: its log file name, its minutes, and ok. On our 12-core machine each run took 4.7 to 5.1 minutes, and the whole grid about 10 minutes. Each log file holds the single line the training script prints:

$ cat runs/baseline_s0.logbaseline_s0: 1,000,000 steps in 284 s ->    /mnt/Storage/projects/rl-rover/labs/ppo-awr-awac/runs/baseline_s0/final.zip

How to read it. The last three runs start as the first ones finish, so their lines arrive about five minutes later. 284 seconds is 4.7 minutes, a little more than the 278 seconds the smoke test predicts for a run alone. A FAILED line names the log to open. At the end, every run has runs/<name>/ with 20 checkpoints and final.zip, and runs/tb/<name>_1/ with its logs.

L1.5 Step 3: from event files to a figure, lab1_plot_curves.py

Why this script exists. TensorBoard is excellent for watching one run live. It is bad at this lab’s question, whether three seeds of one configuration differ from three seeds of another: you get nine overlapping lines and axes that rescale whenever you toggle one. Rule two also wants numbers, not impressions. So you will read the files TensorBoard reads, draw the panels you want with one color per configuration, and save a summary JSON.

Those files are event files, one per TensorBoard run folder, named events.out.tfevents. plus a timestamp, the machine name, a process id and a counter (for example events.out.tfevents.1789239407.lucas-ubuntu.152497.0). Each holds records of the form “tag, step, value”, and a few lines of Python can read them.

L1.5.1 The panels

"""Lab 1, step 3: turn TensorBoard logs into one figure you can reason about.​  python lab1_plot_curves.py                    # the 3x3 grid from lab1_run_all.py  python lab1_plot_curves.py --single ../../tb_rover_v0/PPO_9 --out lab1_your_ppo9_run.png"""​import os# CPU only. Must run before torch is imported: see common.pyos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""​import argparsefrom pathlib import Path​import matplotlibmatplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw to files, no window neededimport matplotlib.pyplot as pltimport numpy as npfrom tensorboard.backend.event_processing.event_accumulator import EventAccumulator​from common import FIGS, RESULTS, RUNS, ensure_dirs, plot_style, save_json​# (TensorBoard tag, panel title, what healthy looks like)PANELS = [    ("rollout/ep_rew_mean", "episode reward (ep_rew_mean)", "rises, then plateaus"),    ("train/approx_kl", "approx_kl", "small, ~0.005-0.03"),    ("train/clip_fraction", "clip_fraction", "~0.05-0.3"),    ("train/entropy_loss", "entropy_loss (= -entropy)", "rises slowly (entropy decays)"),    ("train/value_loss", "value_loss", "grows with the returns, no blow-up"),    ("train/explained_variance", "explained_variance", "climbs toward ~0.5-0.9"),]COLORS = {"baseline": "#4878a8", "clip10": "#b04a4a", "lambda0": "#4a8a5c"}

matplotlib.use("Agg") must come before pyplot is imported; it makes matplotlib draw into files rather than windows. plot_style is the helper you wrote in Lab 0 (Section L0.8.4); the main block calls it before drawing anything. PANELS is the figure’s design as data: for each panel, the tag, the title, and a reminder of healthy behavior. Those reminders describe this rover with SB3 defaults (Section L1.2.7), not PPO in general. COLORS gives each configuration one color, so its seeds read as a group.

L1.5.2 Reading an event file

Try it yourself first

Write load_scalars(event_dir), returning {tag: (steps array, values array)}. You need:

  • EventAccumulator(path, size_guidance={"scalars": 0}) creates a reader;
  • .Reload() reads the files;
  • .Tags()["scalars"] lists the tag names;
  • .Scalars(tag) returns events, each with .step and .value.

About ten lines.

def load_scalars(event_dir: Path):    """{tag: (steps array, values array)} for every scalar in one run folder."""    # size_guidance 0 = keep every point    ea = EventAccumulator(str(event_dir), size_guidance={"scalars": 0})    ea.Reload()    out = {}    for tag in ea.Tags()["scalars"]:        ev = ea.Scalars(tag)        out[tag] = (np.array([e.step for e in ev]), np.array([e.value for e in ev]))    return out

Three things here are easy to get wrong.

  • size_guidance={"scalars": 0}. By default the reader keeps at most 10,000 points per tag and silently subsamples the rest. Your runs have about 60 points per tag, so it would not bite here, but on a long, frequently logged run it could drop the very spike you are looking for. 0 keeps everything.
  • Reload(). Creating the reader reads nothing; without this line every tag list is empty.
  • Each tag has its own steps. SB3 writes the train/ tags one rollout late. In a 32,768-step run, the rollout/ tags have points at 16,384 and 32,768, but the train/ tags only at 32,768. So steps and values stay paired per tag. A run of a single rollout has no train/ tags at all, which the plot function in Section L1.5.3 has to guard against.

Check your function on one finished run before building on it. The short program below loads baseline_s0_1 and prints three lines: the number of tags and whether train/std is among them; the reward tag’s point count, first step and last step; and the same count and first step for train/approx_kl.

Run it
python - <<'EOF'from pathlib import Pathfrom lab1_plot_curves import load_scalarss = load_scalars(Path('runs/tb/baseline_s0_1'))print(len(s), 'train/std' in s)st = s['rollout/ep_rew_mean'][0]print(len(st), st[0], st[-1])kl = s['train/approx_kl'][0]print(len(kl), kl[0])EOF

This works once your file has the imports, PANELS and load_scalars; the rest of the script is not needed yet.

What you should see
13 True62 16384 101580861 32768

How to read it. 13 tags, including train/std, which the summary will use. The reward tag has 62 points, one per rollout, from step 16,384 to 1,015,808 (Section L1.3.5 explained the 62). train/approx_kl has one point fewer, 61, and starts one rollout later, at 32,768. That is the “one rollout late” rule from the last bullet, seen in your own data.

L1.5.3 The grid figure and the summary numbers

def plot_grid():    runs = sorted((RUNS / "tb").glob("*_s*_1"))    if not runs:        raise SystemExit("no runs in runs/tb - run lab1_run_all.py first")    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(7.5, 8.4))    summary = {}    for run in runs:        name = run.name[:-2]                 # "clip10_s1_1" -> "clip10_s1"        tag = name.rsplit("_s", 1)[0]        # -> "clip10"        s = load_scalars(run)        if any(key not in s for key, _, _ in PANELS):            # SB3 writes the train/* curves only after its second rollout, so a            # very short test run has none of them. Skip it instead of crashing.            print(f"  skipping {name}: too short to have logged every curve")            continue        for ax, (key, title, healthy) in zip(axes.flat, PANELS):            steps, vals = s[key]            label = tag if name.endswith("_s0") else None  # one legend entry per config            ax.plot(steps / 1e6, vals, color=COLORS.get(tag, "gray"), lw=1.2, alpha=0.85,                    label=label)        # ... (the loop continues in the next chunk)

The pattern *_s*_1 finds every folder from a first run of a name. run.name[:-2] drops the _1, and rsplit("_s", 1) splits once, at the last _s, to get the configuration.

plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(7.5, 8.4)) makes three rows by two columns, 7.5 by 8.4 inches, sized to fit the text width of an A4 page. zip(axes.flat, PANELS) walks the panels row by row and pairs each with its row of PANELS. So row 1 holds reward and approx_kl, row 2 clip_fraction and entropy_loss, and row 3 value_loss and explained_variance: the layout of Figures L1.1 and L1.2. Only seed 0 gets a legend label, so the legend lists each configuration once.

The if any(...) guard is the last bullet of Section L1.5.2 put to work. A run of a single rollout (16,384 steps with 8 environments) has no train/ tags, so s["train/approx_kl"] would stop the whole script with a KeyError. The guard prints a skipping line and moves on to the next run instead.

Still inside the loop over runs, each run’s curves become a few summary numbers:

        # Numbers for the write-up: averages over the last ~10% of training.        steps, rew = s["rollout/ep_rew_mean"]        tail = steps >= 0.9 * steps.max()        summary[name] = {            "final_ep_rew_mean": float(rew[tail].mean()),            "max_ep_rew_mean": float(rew.max()),            "median_approx_kl": float(np.median(s["train/approx_kl"][1])),            "max_approx_kl": float(s["train/approx_kl"][1].max()),            "median_clip_fraction": float(np.median(s["train/clip_fraction"][1])),            "final_explained_variance":                float(s["train/explained_variance"][1][-5:].mean()),            "final_std":                float(s["train/std"][1][-5:].mean()) if "train/std" in s else None,        }

The summary is Rule two in code. Each number is chosen to survive one noisy point:

  • final_ep_rew_mean averages the last 10% of steps, which is the last seven points of a 1M-step run. max_ep_rew_mean is the best point; next to the final value, it reveals a run that got somewhere and then lost it.
  • median_approx_kl and median_clip_fraction give the typical level and ignore spikes. max_approx_kl is there to catch the spikes.
  • final_explained_variance and final_std average the last five points. The if "train/std" in s check handles policies that log no std.

L1.5.4 Finishing the script, then running it

After the loop, plot_grid labels the panels, saves the figure and the JSON, and prints the summary table that you will read in Sections L1.6 and L1.7. That table is the lab’s main result, so write this part yourself.

    # (back at the indentation of plot_grid, after the loop over runs)    for ax, (key, title, healthy) in zip(axes.flat, PANELS):        ax.set_title(f"{title}\nhealthy: {healthy}", fontsize=10)        ax.set_xlabel("environment steps (millions)")        ax.grid(alpha=0.25)    axes.flat[1].set_yscale("log")  # KL spans orders of magnitude when a run breaks    axes.flat[0].legend(loc="lower right")    fig.tight_layout()    out = FIGS / "lab1_grid.png"    fig.savefig(out)    save_json(summary, RESULTS / "lab1_summary.json")    print(f"wrote {out} and {RESULTS / 'lab1_summary.json'}")    for name, v in summary.items():        print(f"  {name:<12} final reward {v['final_ep_rew_mean']:7.1f}"              f"   median KL {v['median_approx_kl']:.4f}"              f"   max KL {v['max_approx_kl']:.3f}"              f"   median clip_frac {v['median_clip_fraction']:.3f}")

Each panel’s title carries its “healthy:” reminder on a second line. axes.flat[1] is the KL panel, top right, and it gets a log scale: a broken run’s KL is a hundred times a healthy one’s, and on a linear axis the healthy lines would be flattened to zero. The legend goes on the reward panel only. The print loop writes one fixed-width line per run: {name:<12} pads the run name to 12 characters, and :7.1f prints the reward 7 characters wide with one decimal, so the columns line up.

Nine lines on six panels are too many to reason about one knob at a time. So plot_grid ends by drawing two smaller figures, one per broken knob, each with only the four curves that tell that knob’s story:

    # Two smaller figures, one per broken knob, with only the curves that tell    # that particular story. Nine lines on six panels is too much to read at once.    plot_pair(runs, "clip10", ["rollout/ep_rew_mean", "train/approx_kl",                               "train/clip_fraction", "train/entropy_loss"])    plot_pair(runs, "lambda0", ["rollout/ep_rew_mean", "train/explained_variance",                                "train/value_loss", "train/clip_fraction"])

The choice of curves is itself a forensics lesson:

  • For clip10 you watch how far the policy moves: reward, approx_kl, clip_fraction and entropy_loss.
  • For lambda0 you watch the critic: reward, explained_variance, value_loss, and clip_fraction once more.

Sections L1.6 and L1.7 explain why those are the telling curves.

Now copy two helpers from the answer key. plot_pair and plot_single are plotting boilerplate. Copy them from labs/ppo-awr-awac/lab1_plot_curves.py (lines 102–142) into your file, below plot_grid; without them, the calls above fail with a NameError. Here is what they do, so you can read them rather than just paste them:

  • plot_pair(runs, broken, keys) makes a 2×2 figure. It skips every run that is neither baseline nor broken, and every run missing one of the four keys. It draws the rest in their configuration’s color, puts the approx_kl panel on a log scale if it is one of the four, and saves figures/lab1_<broken>.png, which gives Figures L1.3 and L1.5.
  • plot_single(event_dir, out_name) draws the same 3×2 layout and titles for one run folder, in a single blue line, and saves it under figures/. That gives Figure L1.1.
Pitfall

plot_pair starts with axes = list(axes.flat), and the reference comment warns why. axes.flat is an iterator: it can be walked through only once. plot_grid gets away with using it directly because it asks for a fresh axes.flat on every pass of its loop. But store it once, axes = axes.flat, and zip it inside a loop over runs, and the first run uses it up. Every later run then draws nothing, with no error. list(...) copies the four panels into a list, which can be walked through any number of times.

Last, the main block. It reads the two flags, creates the output folders, and calls plot_style() from Lab 0 before anything is drawn. That sets print-sized fonts (9 pt) and 200 dpi, the settings the published PNGs use.

if __name__ == "__main__":    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--single", type=Path,                   help="plot one existing TensorBoard run folder instead of the grid")    p.add_argument("--out", default="single_run.png")    a = p.parse_args()    ensure_dirs()    plot_style()    if a.single:        plot_single(a.single, a.out)    else:        plot_grid()

With no flags, the script draws the grid. With --single, it plots one run folder from anywhere on disk into figures/, under the name given by --out. That is how Figure L1.1 was made.

Run it
python lab1_plot_curves.pypython lab1_plot_curves.py --single ../../tb_rover_v0/PPO_9 --out lab1_your_ppo9_run.png

The second path assumes the lab folder sits two levels below the rl-rover repo root, where tb_rover_v0/ lives. Adjust it if yours is elsewhere.

What you should see

These are our numbers. Yours will not match digit for digit; the patterns in Sections L1.6 and L1.7 are what should match.

How to read it. The printed lines are already a first diagnosis. In the “median KL” column, the clip10 rows are more than a hundred times the baseline’s. In “median clip_frac”, the same rows are the lowest. In “final reward”, every broken run is below every baseline run, which clears the bar set in Section L1.4.2. Figure L1.2 shows the whole experiment at once and is too dense to reason about in detail, so the next two sections use the focused figures.

L1.6 Reading the clip10 runs

Start with what the knob does to PPO’s objective. Book Section 3.4.1’s clipped objective takes, for each sample, the smaller of two terms: the plain ratio-times-advantage, and the same term with the ratio squashed into \([1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon]\). At \(\epsilon = 0.2\), a sample with a positive advantage stops pushing once its ratio reaches 1.2. That flat stretch in book Figure 3.1 is the brake.

At \(\epsilon = 10\), the flat stretch starts at a ratio of 11. On the negative side it would start below \(-9\), which no ratio can reach. So nearly every sample sees the plain surrogate of book Section 3.2.3: the ratio-times-advantage objective that PPO maximizes on the stored batch, with nothing squashed.

The book calls what the surrogate gets wrong its “lie”. The surrogate assumes that the new policy would visit the same states as the old one, since those are the only states in the batch. That assumption gets less true the further the policy moves, so the lie grows as the ratios move away from 1. The clip is what normally keeps the ratios near 1. Figure L1.3 shows what happened without it.

The table below lists the numbers behind Figure L1.3.

runfinal rewardmax rewardmedian approx_klmax approx_klmedian clip_fractionfinal action std
baseline s066.485.50.00620.00820.0670.51
baseline s165.682.20.00590.00750.0620.53
baseline s274.495.50.00610.00780.0640.52
clip10 s011.358.70.8610.40.00310.20
clip10 s1−75.357.61.3887.50.00340.23
clip10 s2−28.852.61.3170.00.00320.19

The story has five parts, in this order.

L1.6.1 First, it learns faster

By about 0.15M steps, clip10 reaches an ep_rew_mean of about 40 while the baseline is still near −50. At 0.3M steps the red lines are still above the blue ones. Had you stopped at Appendix B’s 300,000 steps, you would have called removing the clip an improvement.

Why faster? Count how hard each batch is used. \(16{,}384 / 64 = 256\) minibatches per epoch, and \(256 \times 10 = 2{,}560\) gradient steps on the same batch before new data arrives. (Book Section 3.4.5’s pseudo-code uses 4 epochs of 512-sample minibatches: \(16{,}384 / 512 = 32\), and \(32 \times 4 = 128\) steps.) Each sample takes part in ten of those steps, once per epoch. In the baseline, a sample whose ratio has passed the window’s edge, in the direction its advantage pushes, stops pushing. In clip10, almost every sample pushes in all ten epochs.

Is there another brake? The learning rate (3e-4) and SB3’s clipping of each gradient’s overall size (max_grad_norm=0.5) keep each of the 2,560 steps small. Neither of them looks at how far those steps have added up. SB3’s KL early stopping, target_kl, would look, but it is off by default. So nothing reacts to how far the policy has already moved during a batch.

A plausible reason for the faster start, not tested here: early in training the surrogate’s direction is roughly right, and moving further in a roughly right direction means faster progress.

L1.6.2 The gauge you would watch is blind

The red clip fractions sit near 0.003 all run: lower than healthy, flat, calm-looking. Book Section 3.6.2’s danger sign, “KL spiking with clip fraction above 0.4”, could never fire. The definition in Section L1.2.3 explains why. With \(\epsilon = 10\) the counter only sees ratios above 11. The gauge’s threshold moved with the knob.

An analogy. The clip fraction is a speed camera that flashes for cars above the limit. Set the limit to 1,000 km/h and it never flashes, however fast people drive. A dark camera then tells you about the limit, not about the traffic. The speedometer, approx_kl, still works.

Where the analogy breaks down. A speed camera only watches; it does not slow anyone down. PPO’s clip is the camera and the brake, because at \(\epsilon = 0.2\) the window the counter uses is the same window that switches a sample’s push off. So clip_range=10 removed the brake and blinded the camera with one number. The knob that causes the damage also hides it from the gauge designed to show it. Figure L1.4 draws one made-up batch of ten ratios against both windows.

What the nonzero 0.003 tells you. Every counted visit had a ratio above 11: the new policy made that logged action eleven or more times as likely as the policy that collected it. A batch has \(16{,}384 \times 10 = 163{,}840\) sample visits, and \(0.003 \times 163{,}840 \approx 490\). The “calm” gauge is reporting about 490 extreme events in a typical batch.

L1.6.3 The KL is a hundred times too large from the start, then it spikes

Now read the gauge that still works. The KL panel is logarithmic, so each gridline is ten times the one below. Blue sits near 0.006. Red starts between about 0.1 and 1 over the first few points and settles around 0.5 to 2: a hundred times the baseline, from the first updates on. The medians agree: 0.86 to 1.38 against 0.0059 to 0.0062.

From about 0.45M steps, and most violently after 0.6M, red spikes, up to 10.4, 87.5 and 70.0. Recall Section L1.2.2: one sample with a ratio of 11 adds as much as 430 calm ones. KL values in the tens mean some ratios are enormous; the policy after training is no longer the policy that collected the batch.

Book Section 3.1.2 says the KL spike usually comes first, a rollout or two before reward collapses. Here the warning was on from the first points, for hundreds of thousands of steps, while the reward looked better than the baseline’s. A fast start with a KL a hundred times healthy is not a win you can bank.

L1.6.4 The policy stops exploring

Red entropy loss climbs much faster than blue. Two red seeds end near +0.5 and one near 0, against about −1.5 for the baseline. Section L1.2.4’s formula translates it. clip10 s2 ends with \(\sigma = 0.19\):

\[ \log 0.19 = -1.6607, \qquad 1.4189 - 1.6607 = -0.2418, \qquad -2 \times (-0.2418) = +0.48 \]

That is the top red line.

The table’s last column says it directly: 0.19 to 0.23 per wheel, against 0.51 to 0.53 for the baseline. The clip10 runs reached the baseline’s final noise level, about 0.5, only about 0.3M steps in. About 95% of a Gaussian’s samples lie within two standard deviations of its mean. So a wheel with \(\sigma = 0.19\) tries commands within about \(\pm 0.38\) of what the policy already prefers, while \(\sigma = 0.51\) still spans about \(\pm 1.0\), as wide as the whole action range \([-1, 1]\).

That matters because a damaged policy recovers only by exploring (book Section 3.1.3). This lab did not isolate why the noise shrinks faster without the clip; for diagnosis, the pattern is enough.

L1.6.5 Then the reward collapses

From about 0.4M steps the red rewards stop improving, and after about 0.6M they turn chaotic. One seed collapses to about −100 near 0.75–0.8M steps; another falls to about −150 at 1.0M. Final rewards are 11.3, −75.3 and −28.8, against 65.6 to 74.4. Best points of 52.6 to 58.7 were reached and then lost, while the baseline’s best points are 82.2 to 95.5. In Figure L1.2, the clip10 value loss is also higher and noisier, roughly 400 to 900.

This is book Section 3.1.1’s self-feeding loop in slow motion. An oversized update makes a worse policy, the worse policy collects worse data, and the next update is computed on that data while the critic’s targets shift underneath it.

Notice how this differs from book Section 3.2.1’s compressed description, where reward “climbs for two or three rollouts, then falls to the floor and stays there”. On your rover the fast climb lasted about 0.4M steps, some two dozen rollouts. The collapse was uneven: one seed ended near the floor, one partway, and one (s0, final 11.3) still positive. clip_range=10 does not “never learn”. It learns fast, then destabilizes.

Seeds. The clip10 seeds ended at 11, −75 and −29; the baseline seeds at 66, 66 and 74. Any single clip10 seed would have told a different story, and that spread is itself a symptom of instability.

What knob does this point to? Check clip_range first; restoring 0.2 gives you the baseline. If clip_range is sane and you still see a KL far above healthy with unstable reward, book Section 3.6.2 names the next levers: a lower learning rate, or fewer epochs per batch. SB3’s target_kl is a third; it stops a batch’s epochs once approx_kl exceeds 1.5 times the target. This lab did not test those three. They are where to look, not measured fixes.

L1.7 Reading the lambda0 runs

With gae_lambda=0.0, GAE keeps only the first term of its sum (book Section 3.5.3), so the advantage is the one-step TD error, \(\hat A_t = \delta_t\). Section L1.8 builds \(\delta_t\) by hand. For now you need one consequence, for the critic’s target:

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat G_t &= \hat A_t + V(s_t) \\ &= \big(r_t + \gamma\, V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\big) + V(s_t) \\ &= r_t + \gamma\, V(s_{t+1}) \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

\(\hat G_t\) is the critic’s training target for step \(t\) (Section L1.2.5). With \(\lambda = 0\), the advantage \(\hat A_t\) is the TD error: the reward \(r_t\) of step \(t\), plus the discount \(\gamma = 0.99\) times the critic’s value \(V(s_{t+1})\) of the state the step led to, minus its value \(V(s_t)\) of the state it started from. Adding \(V(s_t)\) back cancels that last term. What remains is one real reward plus the critic’s own guess about everything after it. (At the final step of an episode that ended for real, the guess is zero.)

L1.7.1 The same early pace, then a lower plateau

Figure L1.5 and the table after it put the three lambda0 seeds against the baseline. Final rewards are −15.6 to +21.6, against 65.6 to 74.4, and seed 2 never gets above +5.9. All three seeds land below all three baseline seeds, so this is a result.

Look at when the damage appears. For about the first 0.4M steps the green and blue reward curves overlap; before 0.2M steps green is, if anything, slightly ahead. Then the gap opens: the baseline keeps climbing, to 65–75 by the end, while lambda0 stalls, wandering between about −40 and +40 for the remaining 0.6M steps.

lambda0 s0−1.533.60.01090.1290.870.40
lambda0 s121.642.80.01020.1240.840.38
