Appendix B’s rung predicted something else: “watch early learning starve while the critic is still bad”. The critic was bad early; green explained variance is still below about 0.15 at 0.2M steps, when blue is near 0.7. Yet early reward did not starve. A likely reason, not tested separately: the rover’s reward is dense. Every step pays about 33 times the distance gained toward the goal, so even a near-zero critic gives \(\delta_t \approx r_t\), which already says whether the step moved toward the goal. That is enough for the early lessons.

What one step cannot do is carry the +100 at the goal or the −100 at a collision back to the actions, many steps earlier, that caused them. Book Section 3.5.5’s toy episode shows the size of that effect: the first action’s advantage is 0.04 at \(\lambda = 0\) and 0.285 at \(\lambda = 0.95\). The book’s Section 3.5.2 example deliberately uses a sparse reward that pays nothing per step. Your rover pays something every step, and that changes when the damage shows.

L1.7.2 The critic that looks better

By its own metrics, lambda0 has the best critic in the experiment. Its value loss is the lowest of all runs, about 100 at the end against about 400. For two of its seeds, explained variance is the highest: 0.87 and 0.84, against 0.65 to 0.69. Judge critics by these two numbers and you would pick lambda0.

Look back at the equation above. The target is one real reward, about ±1 on ordinary steps, plus the critic’s own prediction for the next state. So the value loss mostly measures whether the critic agrees with itself one step later. A critic whose predictions change smoothly from state to state scores well on that exam, whether or not its predictions match what actually happens by the end of the episode. It is graded on predicting a slightly smoothed copy of itself. Explained variance shares the weakness, because the spread of these targets comes mostly from the critic’s own values.

You can see how easy the exam is at the start. In Figure L1.5, green value loss begins near 10 and blue near 100. An untrained critic outputs values near zero, so a one-step target is little more than one small reward, which a near-zero prediction nearly matches. The baseline’s targets hold about seventeen steps’ worth of real rewards (Section L1.2.5), a much harder exam.

An analogy. A student who writes most of the answer key for their own exam gets a high score. The score says the student is consistent with themself. It does not say the answers are right.

Where the analogy breaks down. The student could fill the key with anything. The critic cannot: every target contains one real reward, and the final step of every real ending contains the true +100 or −100 with no guess attached. Over many updates those real rewards seep backward through the chain of guesses, so a \(\lambda = 0\) critic is anchored to reality, just loosely and slowly. Nothing here is cheating; it is the structure of the target. The practical conclusion is narrower than “the metric lies”: a low value loss or a high explained variance is not evidence that the advantages are useful.

Pitfall

Never compare value_loss or explained_variance between runs with different gae_lambda. SB3 computes both against the λ-returns, and \(\lambda\) changes what those targets contain, so the runs are taking different exams. In this lab the runs with the “best” critic numbers learned a far worse policy than the baseline. When critic metrics and the reward curve disagree, believe the reward curve.

L1.7.3 The other lambda0 curves

  • Explained variance climbs slowly early. Green stays below about 0.15 for the first 0.2M steps, and seed 2 reaches 0.4 only at about 0.6M steps. A critic that takes hundreds of thousands of steps to become useful is part of this signature, even though it ends up looking good.
  • Clip fraction is about twice the baseline’s: medians of 0.124 to 0.144, and 0.2 to 0.4 in the first 0.1M steps. That sits inside book Section 3.6.2’s healthy band of 0.1–0.3, while the truly healthy baseline (0.062 to 0.067) sits below it. “In the band” does not mean healthy.
  • approx_kl is about twice the baseline’s, around 0.01 (medians 0.0102 to 0.0126), without large spikes. On its own it looks unremarkable.
  • Entropy also falls faster than the baseline’s, though far less than clip10’s. The final action std is 0.35 to 0.40 against 0.51 to 0.53, and in Figure L1.2 the green entropy_loss lines end between about −1.0 and −0.75, against about −1.5 for blue. By Section L1.2.4’s formula, \(\sigma = 0.40\) gives \(-2 \times (1.4189 - 0.9163) = -1.01\), and \(\sigma = 0.35\) gives \(-2 \times (1.4189 - 1.0498) = -0.74\).

This lab did not isolate why \(\lambda = 0\) raises these gauges. The signature is the combination: a low reward plateau, a slow critic that then scores unusually well, and mildly elevated movement and certainty gauges.

L1.7.4 Bias and variance, on your rover

Book Section 3.5 frames \(\lambda\) as a dial between two ways of being wrong. At \(\lambda = 1\), the Monte Carlo end, an action’s advantage adds up everything that really happened afterward. That is unbiased, but every random event later in the episode lands on that one action, so it is high variance, a noise that averaging over many samples cures. At \(\lambda = 0\), the TD end, the advantage uses one real reward and trusts the critic for the rest. Only one step of randomness enters, so it is low variance. But wherever the critic is wrong, the advantage is wrong in the same direction every time: it is biased, and more samples do not fix that.

The lambda0 runs are what the TD end of that dial looked like on this task: a policy that learned the easy early lessons at the normal pace, then stalled well below the baseline and did not catch up in 0.6M more steps. Section L1.8 lets you look at both kinds of advantage on the same real episode.

L1.8 Step 4: GAE by hand on a real episode, lab1_gae_by_hand.py

Why this script exists. The curves told you that \(\lambda = 0\) hurt, but they never showed you an advantage. Book Section 3.5.5 computes advantages on a made-up three-step episode, which teaches the arithmetic and says nothing about your robot. So here you let the trained baseline drive one real episode, record the critic’s value at every step, and compute the advantages yourself at \(\lambda = 0\) and \(\lambda = 0.95\). Then you check your loop against SB3’s own implementation. If they agree, you know exactly what PPO trains on.

L1.8.1 The two equations

Everything starts from the one-step TD error: how much better one step went than the critic expected.

\[ \delta_t \;=\; r_t \;+\; \gamma\,(1 - d_t)\,V(s_{t+1}) \;-\; V(s_t) \]
In plain words

\(\delta_t\) is the TD error of step \(t\). \(r_t\) is the reward that step earned. \(V(s_t)\) is the critic’s prediction, made before acting, of the discounted reward still to come from state \(s_t\), and \(V(s_{t+1})\) its prediction from the state the step led to. \(\gamma = 0.99\) is the discount, GAMMA in common.py. \(d_t\) is 1 if step \(t\) really ended the episode (goal or collision) and 0 otherwise; when it is 1, there is no next state to value and that term drops out. (This \(d_t\) is a “done” flag, not the distance to the goal that Lab 0’s reward formula also writes \(d_t\).) Positive \(\delta_t\): the step went better than expected. Negative: worse.

GAE adds up the TD errors ahead of each step, each discounted a little more. Inside one episode, before its last step, that sum is book Section 3.5.3’s formula:

\[ \hat A_t = \delta_t + (\gamma\lambda)\,\delta_{t+1} + (\gamma\lambda)^2\,\delta_{t+2} + \ldots \]

As a loop running backwards through the episode, it is one line:

\[ \hat A_t \;=\; \delta_t \;+\; \gamma\lambda\,(1 - d_t)\,\hat A_{t+1} \]
In plain words

\(\hat A_t\) is the advantage of step \(t\). \(\hat A_{t+1}\) is the next step’s advantage, which you already have because you walk from the end of the episode to the start. \(\lambda\) is gae_lambda. The product \(\gamma\lambda\) is the share of the next step’s advantage that flows back one step: \(0.99 \times 0.95 = 0.9405\) for the baseline, and \(0.99 \times 0 = 0\) for lambda0, which leaves \(\hat A_t = \delta_t\). \(d_t\) stops the flow at an episode’s end, so one episode’s outcome is never credited to another episode’s actions.

Why are the loop and the sum the same thing? Take a step where \(d_t = 0\), and apply the loop to \(\hat A_{t+1}\) as well: \(\hat A_{t+1} = \delta_{t+1} + \gamma\lambda\,\hat A_{t+2}\). Substitute that into the loop for \(\hat A_t\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat A_t &= \delta_t + \gamma\lambda\,\big(\delta_{t+1} + \gamma\lambda\,\hat A_{t+2}\big) \\ &= \delta_t + (\gamma\lambda)\,\delta_{t+1} + (\gamma\lambda)^2\,\hat A_{t+2} \end{aligned} \]

Do the same for \(\hat A_{t+2}\), then \(\hat A_{t+3}\), and so on, and the loop unrolls into exactly the sum above. The loop just computes that sum without re-adding the same terms for every step.

The sum also shows where Section L1.2.5’s weights come from. Each \(\delta_{t+k}\) contains exactly one real reward, \(r_{t+k}\), with coefficient 1. In the sum, \(\delta_{t+k}\) carries the weight \((\gamma\lambda)^k\), so the reward \(k\) steps ahead does too.

L1.8.2 Playing one episode

"""Lab 1, step 4: compute GAE advantages by hand on one real rover episode.​Book Section 3.5 computes advantages on a made-up three-step episode. Here youdo the same arithmetic on numbers your own critic produced, then check yourtwenty-line loop against Stable-Baselines3's implementation. If the two agreeto ~1e-5, you have understood exactly what PPO trains on.​    python lab1_gae_by_hand.py --model runs/baseline_s0/final.zip"""​import os# CPU only. Must run before torch is imported: see common.pyos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""​import argparse​import numpy as npimport torchfrom stable_baselines3 import PPOfrom stable_baselines3.common.buffers import RolloutBuffer​from common import GAMMA, RESULTS, ensure_dirs, make_env, outcome_of, save_json

New imports: SB3’s RolloutBuffer, where PPO stores a rollout and computes advantages; and from common.py, GAMMA, make_env, and outcome_of, which labels an ending "goal", "crash" or "timeout".

def play_one_episode(model, seed):    """Stochastic rollout: per-step rewards, critic values, and how it ended."""    env = make_env()    obs, _ = env.reset(seed=seed)    observations, actions, rewards, values = [], [], [], []    while True:        with torch.no_grad():            obs_t = torch.as_tensor(obs).unsqueeze(0)            # V(s_t) from the critic            values.append(model.policy.predict_values(obs_t).item())        # a_t sampled, as in training        action, _ = model.predict(obs, deterministic=False)        observations.append(obs)        actions.append(action)        obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)        rewards.append(reward)        if terminated or truncated:            return (np.array(observations), np.array(actions),                    np.array(rewards, dtype=np.float32),                    np.array(values, dtype=np.float32),                    outcome_of(terminated, truncated, info))

Each step records the observation, the action, the reward, and the critic’s value of the state before acting. model.policy.predict_values is the critic half of SB3’s network. It expects a batch, so unsqueeze(0) turns shape (15,) into (1, 15). .item() returns the result as a Python float. torch.no_grad() skips the bookkeeping for backpropagation, since you only read. The action is sampled, as in PPO training. Rewards and values are stored as float32, like SB3’s buffer, which matters for the comparison. The episode ends on terminated (goal or collision) or truncated (the 500-step limit).

On your rig

This episode samples its actions on purpose, because PPO trains on sampled actions. As Section L0.8.4 showed, your predict.py drives with the mean action instead, while your train_rover.py demo loop samples. Neither is wrong, but they are different policies to evaluate, and Lab 2 measures how different.

L1.8.3 The advantages, by hand

Try it yourself first

Write gae_by_hand(rewards, values, gamma, lam) for one episode that ended for real, returning the TD errors and the advantages. Walk backwards from the last step. After the last step there is no next state, so use 0 for its value, and start with a next advantage of 0. About a dozen lines.

def gae_by_hand(rewards, values, gamma, lam):    """Advantages for ONE episode that ended for real (goal or crash, not a timeout)."""    T = len(rewards)    deltas = np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float32)    advantages = np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float32)    next_advantage = 0.0    for t in reversed(range(T)):             # walk backwards: A_t needs A_{t+1}        # nothing comes after the last step        next_value = values[t + 1] if t + 1 < T else 0.0        deltas[t] = rewards[t] + gamma * next_value - values[t]        advantages[t] = deltas[t] + gamma * lam * next_advantage        next_advantage = advantages[t]    return deltas, advantages

Match it to the equations. reversed(range(T)) visits \(t = T-1, \ldots, 0\). next_value is \(V(s_{t+1})\), except after the final step, where it is 0. That one line is the whole \((1 - d_t)\) factor, because in a single episode that really ended, only the last step has \(d_t = 1\). The next two lines are the two equations. next_advantage carries \(\hat A_{t+1}\) into the next iteration, starting at 0 so the last step’s advantage equals its TD error. Note the docstring’s demand, an episode that ended for real; Section L1.8.8 explains why.

L1.8.4 The same advantages, by SB3

def gae_by_sb3(model, observations, actions, rewards, values, gamma, lam):    """The same episode pushed through SB3's own RolloutBuffer, for comparison."""    T = len(rewards)    buf = RolloutBuffer(T, model.observation_space, model.action_space, device="cpu",                        gae_lambda=lam, gamma=gamma, n_envs=1)    for t in range(T):        buf.add(observations[t][None], actions[t][None], np.array([rewards[t]]),                np.array([t == 0]),                       # episode_start flag                torch.tensor([values[t]]), torch.zeros(1))    # dones=True: the step after the buffer is a real ending, so no bootstrap.    buf.compute_returns_and_advantage(last_values=torch.zeros(1), dones=np.array([True]))    return buf.advantages.flatten()

The buffer is one episode long, for one environment, with the same \(\gamma\) and \(\lambda\). buf.add takes, per step: observation, action, reward, an “episode starts here” flag, value, and log-probability. The [None] adds a leading axis of size 1, for one environment. SB3 stores no per-step “done” flag. It finds boundaries by checking whether the next step starts an episode, and only step 0 does here. The log-probability is zero because advantages never use it.

compute_returns_and_advantage runs SB3’s backward loop:

delta = r + gamma * V_next * (1 - done) - VA     = delta + gamma * lambda * (1 - done) * A_next

These are your two equations. For the buffer’s last step it needs last_values, the critic’s value of the following observation, and dones, whether that step ended the episode. With dones=True the bootstrap is multiplied by zero, so last_values is just a placeholder.

L1.8.5 Find a goal episode and compare

def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--model", default="runs/baseline_s0/final.zip")    p.add_argument("--first-seed", type=int, default=0)    args = p.parse_args()    ensure_dirs()​    model = PPO.load(args.model, device="cpu")    for seed in range(args.first_seed, args.first_seed + 50):        obs, acts, rewards, values, outcome = play_one_episode(model, seed)        if outcome == "goal":            break    T = len(rewards)    print(f"episode seed {seed}: {T} steps, ended at the {outcome}, "          f"return {rewards.sum():.2f}\n")​    report = {"seed": seed, "T": T, "gamma": GAMMA,              "rewards": rewards.tolist(), "values": values.tolist()}    for lam in (0.0, 0.95):        deltas, adv = gae_by_hand(rewards, values, GAMMA, lam)        adv_sb3 = gae_by_sb3(model, obs, acts, rewards, values, GAMMA, lam)        diff = float(np.abs(adv - adv_sb3).max())        print(f"lambda = {lam}:  max |mine - SB3| = {diff:.2e}")        report[f"lambda_{lam}"] = {"deltas": deltas.tolist(), "advantages": adv.tolist(),                                   "max_abs_diff_vs_sb3": diff}    # ... (the table and the report: next chunk)

PPO.load brings back the trained baseline: its actor drives, its critic supplies the values. Loading also re-seeds PyTorch and NumPy from the model file, so the same file gives the same sampled episode every time. The loop keeps the first episode, from seed 0 upward, that ends at the goal. If 50 pass without one it keeps the last anyway, so always read the first printed line. The comparison is the largest absolute difference between your advantages and SB3’s.

Next, main prints a few rows side by side, so you can check the arithmetic yourself in Section L1.8.6, and saves the report:

    d0, a0 = report["lambda_0.0"]["deltas"], report["lambda_0.0"]["advantages"]    a95 = report["lambda_0.95"]["advantages"]    print("\nlast five steps of the episode (the goal bonus arrives on the final one):")    print(f"{'t':>4} {'r_t':>9} {'V(s_t)':>9} {'V(s_t+1)':>9} "          f"{'delta_t':>9} {'A(l=0)':>9} {'A(l=.95)':>9}")    for t in range(T - 5, T):        v_next = values[t + 1] if t + 1 < T else 0.0        print(f"{t:>4} {rewards[t]:>9.3f} {values[t]:>9.3f} {v_next:>9.3f} "              f"{d0[t]:>9.3f} {a0[t]:>9.3f} {a95[t]:>9.3f}")    print("\nfirst three steps:")    for t in range(3):        print(f"{t:>4} {rewards[t]:>9.3f} {values[t]:>9.3f} {values[t+1]:>9.3f} "              f"{d0[t]:>9.3f} {a0[t]:>9.3f} {a95[t]:>9.3f}")    save_json(report, RESULTS / "lab1_gae_episode.json")    print(f"\nwrote {RESULTS / 'lab1_gae_episode.json'}")    # ... (the figure: copy from the reference file)

The first two lines pull the TD errors and both advantage arrays back out of the report. {'t':>4} right-aligns a column 4 characters wide, and :>9.3f prints a number 9 wide with three decimals, so the columns line up. Look at v_next: it is the same rule as in gae_by_hand. After the final step there is no next state, so the table prints 0 there, which is exactly the value your loop used. The first-three-steps loop can use values[t+1] directly, since those steps are never the last. save_json writes the rewards, values, TD errors and advantages, so you can study the episode later without replaying it.

The rest of main draws Figure L1.6: two stacked panels, the critic’s values and the rewards on top, the two advantage estimates below. It is matplotlib boilerplate, so copy it from the end of the reference file, labs/ppo-awr-awac/lab1_gae_by_hand.py (lines 116–137).

Your episode will differ unless your final.zip is identical to ours; an earlier test on the 300k-step checkpoint picked a 213-step episode. What must match is the pattern: a goal episode, and differences of zero or very close to it.

L1.8.6 Reading the table, one row at a time

The agreement lines. A maximum difference of exactly zero means bit-for-bit identical advantages on all 189 steps, at both \(\lambda\) values, because both loops do the same float32 operations in the same order. If yours uses float64, expect tiny differences; the docstring you typed in Section L1.8.2 treats about \(10^{-5}\) as a pass. A difference of 0.1 or more is a bug, usually a wrong last-step value or an off-by-one.

Row \(t = 188\), the last step. The rover reaches the goal: \(r_{188} = 100.521\), the +100 bonus plus an ordinary 0.521. The episode really ended, so \(d_{188} = 1\) and the next value is 0.

\[ \delta_{188} = 100.521 + 0.99 \times 0 - 87.250 = 100.521 - 87.250 = 13.271 \]

Nothing comes after, so both advantages equal the TD error: \(\hat A_{188} = 13.271\) at \(\lambda = 0\) and at \(\lambda = 0.95\).

The goal paid more than 100, yet the advantage is only 13.271. Standing one step from the goal, the critic already predicted 87.25. Most of the bonus was expected, and only the surprise counts as “better than expected”. A working critic makes good news less surprising, and the advantage measures surprise.

Row \(t = 187\), one step earlier. An ordinary step: \(r_{187} = 0.521\), \(V(s_{187}) = 88.197\), \(V(s_{188}) = 87.250\), and \(d_{187} = 0\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \delta_{187} &= 0.521 + 0.99 \times 87.250 - 88.197 \\ &= 0.521 + 86.3775 - 88.197 \\ &= -1.2985 \end{aligned} \]

The table shows −1.298, the same number rounded. At \(\lambda = 0\), \(\hat A_{187} = \delta_{187} = -1.2985\). At \(\lambda = 0.95\), add the share of the next step’s advantage:

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat A_{187} &= -1.2985 + 0.99 \times 0.95 \times 13.271 \\ &= -1.2985 + 0.9405 \times 13.271 \\ &= -1.2985 + 12.4814 \\ &= 11.1829 \end{aligned} \]

The table shows 11.183.

Same step, same data, same critic, and the two estimates disagree about the sign. At \(\lambda = 0\), step 187 looks slightly bad, because the critic’s value dipped from 88.2 to 87.25 and one step is all this estimate sees. At \(\lambda = 0.95\), it looks clearly good, because it led straight into the step that reached the goal, and 94% of that step’s surprise flows back to it. This is book Section 3.5.5’s toy example, happening on your robot.

Try it yourself first

Compute row \(t = 186\): \(r_{186} = 0.548\), \(V(s_{186}) = 90.949\), \(V(s_{187}) = 88.197\), and \(\hat A_{187} = 11.183\) at \(\lambda = 0.95\). You should get the printed \(\delta_{186} = -3.086\) and \(\hat A_{186} = 7.432\). The worked answer follows.

The answer, which the table prints as −3.086 and 7.432:

\[ \begin{aligned} \delta_{186} &= 0.548 + 0.99 \times 88.197 - 90.949 \\ &= 0.548 + 87.3150 - 90.949 \\ &= -3.0860 \end{aligned} \]

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat A_{186} &= -3.086 + 0.9405 \times 11.183 \\ &= -3.086 + 10.5176 \\ &= 7.4316 \end{aligned} \]

The first three rows show something no toy example can. The rewards are ordinary, about −1 each. The critic’s values are not: 17.681, then 27.628, then 26.710, then 1.873. At \(t = 2\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \delta_2 &= -1.089 + 0.99 \times 1.873 - 26.710 \\ &= -1.089 + 1.8543 - 26.710 \\ &= -25.945 \end{aligned} \]

The reward was an ordinary −1.089, so the step itself earned nothing unusual. What changed was the critic’s opinion of the new observation, which fell by about 25. The sensor measures one sonar beam per step, so a single new reading can change what the critic believes about the whole situation. At \(\lambda = 0\), step 2’s action takes the full blame, −25.945. At \(\lambda = 0.95\) it gets −1.624, because over the next few steps the value climbs back, to about 20 by step 7, and GAE adds those upcoming positive TD errors to this negative one.

L1.8.7 The whole episode, and what \(\lambda\) does to it

Read the bottom panel against the top one, in three stretches.

Steps 0 to 25: a jumpy start. The rewards are ordinary, yet the critic’s value leaps by tens from one step to the next: from −7.9 at step 12 to 50.9 at step 13, and from 58.8 at step 17 to 7.5 at step 18. This lab did not test why. A plausible reason is the one from the first three rows: the sensor measures one sonar beam per step, so each new reading can change the critic’s picture of the whole situation.

Both estimators swing hardest here, in different ways. Green swings on the spot, because each TD error is one jump: +58.0 at step 12 and −50.8 at step 17. Red peaks at +63.4 at step 12 and stays positive from step 3 to step 22, often above +30, because it sums a run of those jumps. Over this stretch they add up to a climb, from about 2 at step 3 to about 70 at step 23.

Steps 75 to 150: a slow slide. The critic’s value drifts from the 80s down to single digits. Each step lowers it only a little, so each step’s own TD error is usually small, and the green line stays within about \(\pm 5\) of zero for most of the stretch. The red line is negative from about step 65 to about step 125, reaching about −40 near step 100, because each of its values adds up the many small disappointments that lie ahead. At \(\lambda = 0\) the actions that led into the slide are barely blamed; at \(\lambda = 0.95\) they are blamed clearly.

Steps 152 to 178: the recovery. From its lowest point, about −12 at step 152, the value climbs to about 51 within seven steps and peaks at about 91 at step 178. The red line is already above +50 at step 152, before most of that climb: GAE credits the actions that started the recovery with the recovery. The green line gives those same actions mostly single-digit advantages.

Two numbers from results/lab1_gae_episode.json sum it up, over the whole episode, jumpy start included. About two thirds of the \(\lambda = 0\) advantages lie within \(\pm 5\) of zero, against about one in six at \(\lambda = 0.95\). Their standard deviations over this episode are 9.7 and 23.5. The long sums carry real outcomes back to the actions that caused them, and collect more of the episode’s luck on the way. That is Section L1.7.4’s trade in one picture: \(\lambda = 0\) is quiet because it mostly repeats the critic’s step-to-step opinion.

PPO does not use these numbers raw. SB3 rescales each 64-sample minibatch’s advantages to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (normalize_advantage=True). What survives is the shape in Figure L1.6: which actions stand out from their neighbors.

L1.8.8 Why a goal episode, and what SB3 does with a cut-off one

The hand loop uses 0 for the value after the last step. That is right only if the episode really ended, because only then is there truly no future reward. A goal and a collision both qualify. The script waits for a goal because the +100 bonus makes the backward flow of credit easy to see.

A timeout is different (Section L0.4.5 introduced the two flags). When the 500-step limit fires, gymnasium sets truncated=True, but the task did not end: the rover could have kept driving. Using 0 for the next value would pretend its future was worth nothing. The last step of every timed-out episode, and through GAE the steps before it, would be scored as if that future were worth exactly zero: too harshly when the critic expects reward ahead, and too kindly when it expects penalties.

The fix is to bootstrap: use the critic’s value of the final observation, the state the last step led to, as the stand-in for everything that would have come next.

SB3 does this during PPO rollouts. When an environment reports a time-limit truncation, SB3 adds \(\gamma\) times the critic’s value of the final observation to that episode’s last reward (the source comment reads “Handle timeout by bootstrapping”, GitHub issue #633) and then treats the step as an ending. If the last step is step \(t\) and the final observation is \(s_{t+1}\), its TD error becomes \(r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\), as if the episode had continued for one bootstrapped step. To handle a timeout in your own loop, set the last step’s next_value to the critic’s value of the final observation instead of 0.

A second kind of cut happens when a rollout’s 2,048 steps per environment fill up mid-episode. That is what last_values and dones=False handle in compute_returns_and_advantage: SB3 bootstraps the unfinished episode from the critic’s value of the next observation. Your episode is complete, which is why the script passes zeros and True.

L1.9 Diagnosis cheat-sheet

Back to the question of Section L1.1. For these two knobs on this rover, each break left a distinct signature that all three seeds repeated. Telling those signatures apart from other causes, such as a learning rate that is too high or too many epochs per batch, is the next experiment, not something this lab showed. Here is the evidence as a table. Every row is a pattern seen in this lab’s runs, not a general catalog of PPO failures. The middle column says where to look first, not a guaranteed fix.

What you seeWhat it points toSeen in
approx_kl about 100× healthy from the first updates (0.5–2 against 0.006), spiking to 10–87 laterUpdates far larger than one batch supports; nothing limits how far a batch moves the policy. Check clip_range first.clip10
clip_fraction near zero (about 0.003) while approx_kl is hugeA clip window so wide that nothing reaches its edge. Near-zero clip fraction means “calm” only if the KL is small too. Nonzero at clip_range=10 means ratios above 11.clip10
Reward rising faster than healthy, then turning chaotic and collapsing in some seedsThe same oversized updates: early progress bought with instability. Do not judge a huge-KL run by its first 300k steps.clip10
entropy_loss rising much faster than healthy; action std 0.19–0.23 against 0.51–0.53, reaching the healthy final value about 0.3M steps in; lambda0 shows a milder version, std 0.35–0.40The policy growing confident too fast, with little exploration left for recovery. Read it with the KL.clip10, lambda0 (milder)
Seeds of one configuration ending far apart (11, −75, −29) while healthy seeds agree (66, 66, 74)Instability. One seed would have told any of three stories.clip10 vs baseline
value_loss rising early while explained_variance rises and reward climbsHealthy on this rover: the returns grew and spread out.PPO_9, baseline
Lowest value_loss and highest explained_variance of all runs, with a reward plateau well below healthyA critic graded against targets built mostly from its own predictions. Suspect gae_lambda too low. Never compare critic metrics across different \(\lambda\).lambda0
explained_variance below about 0.15 for the first 0.2M steps (one seed reaches 0.4 only at about 0.6M); reward level with healthy early, then stallingAdvantages that look one step ahead. A dense reward still teaches the early lessons; long-range credit does not arrive.lambda0
clip_fraction about twice healthy (0.12–0.14; 0.2–0.4 in the first 0.1M steps) and approx_kl about twice healthy, no spikesConsistent with \(\lambda = 0\) here. It sits inside the book’s 0.1–0.3 band: “in band” is not the same as healthy.lambda0

Three habits make the table usable on a run you did not train. Compare against a healthy run of the same environment and settings, never against generic bands; this rover’s healthy KL and clip fraction sit below the book’s. Read the gauges in pairs, approx_kl with clip_fraction and value_loss with explained_variance, because the diagnosis lives in each pair’s disagreement. And when a critic metric and the reward curve disagree, believe the reward curve.

Checkpoint
  • You can say what SB3 computes for approx_kl, clip_fraction, entropy_loss, explained_variance and value_loss, and why a healthy rover run’s value loss rises early. (If not: Section L1.2.)
  • You can explain why CheckpointCallback’s save_freq is divided by 8, and what goes wrong when you re-run a tag. (Section L1.3.)
  • You can explain why the grid runs as separate processes, and which outcome across three seeds counts as a result. (Section L1.4.)
  • Looking at Figure L1.3, you can explain why a clip fraction of 0.003 is a warning rather than reassurance, and what its being nonzero says about the ratios. (Section L1.6.)
  • You can explain why the lambda0 critic’s better value loss and explained variance are not evidence of better advantages. (Section L1.7.)
  • Given one row of a real episode, you can compute \(\delta_t\) and \(\hat A_t\) at \(\lambda = 0\) and \(\lambda = 0.95\), and say why a timed-out episode needs a bootstrap. (Section L1.8.)

Where to go deeper. Book Sections 3.1 to 3.6 are the theory this lab exercised: step size (3.1), importance ratios and the surrogate (3.2), TRPO and KL divergence (3.3), the clipped objective (3.4), advantage estimation from Monte Carlo to GAE (3.5), and PPO on the rover (3.6). The primary sources the book names are short and readable: Schulman et al. (2017) for PPO, Schulman et al. (2016) for GAE, and Schulman et al. (2015) for TRPO. For the gap between those papers and code that actually trains, the book points to Engstrom et al. (2020) and Andrychowicz et al. (2021). Finally, read the train() method in SB3’s ppo/ppo.py. It is about a hundred lines, every curve in this lab is computed there, and its comment on approx_kl links to John Schulman’s note on approximating the KL divergence, the estimator of Section L1.2.2.

Lab 2 — Learn a better policy from a file (AWR)

In Lab 1 every piece of learning happened with the simulator running. PPO drove the rover, learned from what it had just seen, threw that batch away, and drove again. This lab changes the rules. You will use the simulator once, to record a file of driving. After that, the learning happens from the file alone, the way it has to on a real robot whose every episode costs a person’s time.

You will train two kinds of policy on that file. The first, behavior cloning, copies every recorded action. The second, advantage-weighted regression (AWR), copies every recorded action too, but makes the ones that turned out better than expected count for more. Book Chapter 4 derives AWR from first principles. This lab builds it with your own hands, on your own rover, and then measures what it really does, including one place where the measurement disagrees with the book’s own recipe.

The compute is small: every step in this lab runs in seconds to a couple of minutes on the CPU. The time goes into understanding. The one place most people slow down is Section L2.6, where an exponential turns advantages into weights. Go slowly there; everything after it depends on it.

Before you start, check these five things.

  • From Lab 0: common.py. This lab uses its make_env, set_seed, evaluate, wilson_interval, sb3_act_fn, fmt_eval, save_json, ensure_dirs, plot_style and outcome_of, the discount GAMMA, and the folder constants RUNS, DATA, RESULTS and FIGS. You will add one class to it in Section L2.4.
  • From Lab 1: the three baseline PPO runs, with their checkpoints in runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/, runs/baseline_s1/checkpoints/ and runs/baseline_s2/checkpoints/.
  • Where to work: run every command from inside your own lab folder (labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/), with the virtual environment active.
  • The first two lines of every script: the same as in Lab 0, import os and os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "", before anything imports torch.
  • Whose outputs you are reading: the printed outputs below came from the answer key in labs/ppo-awr-awac/, so paths in them name that folder instead of yours. When you are done, compare your files with the answer key.

If you do not have the Lab 1 runs, you can borrow the answer key’s, as Lab 0 suggests. Knowing that the answer key has them is not enough, though. Every script in this lab looks for checkpoints only in your runs/ folder, because that is where RUNS in your common.py points. So copy the three folders in, from your lab folder:

mkdir -p runscp -r ../ppo-awr-awac/runs/baseline_s0 \      ../ppo-awr-awac/runs/baseline_s1 \      ../ppo-awr-awac/runs/baseline_s2 runs/

Each folder is about 3 MB. Write down in your notes that you borrowed them. One caution: if your own Lab 1 grid is still training, let it finish first (the whole grid took about 10 minutes on the reference machine). Copying into a folder that a run is still writing to would mix its checkpoints with the answer key’s.

L2.1 The question

Appendix B’s Rule one is one question per experiment, written down before you touch the keyboard. Here it is:

On the same logged data, does advantage weighting beat plain behavior cloning — and what does \(\beta\) do?

The question has two halves. The first half asks whether weighting helps at all. The second half asks about \(\beta\) (the Greek letter beta), the temperature: one number that decides how strongly the weights favor the better samples. You will meet it properly in Section L2.6. For now, hold on to the idea that a large \(\beta\) makes every weight close to 1 (so AWR turns back into behavior cloning), and a small \(\beta\) makes the weights extreme.

L2.1.1 What “offline” means

Start with what you already know. PPO is on-policy: it learns only from data produced by the current policy, or something very close to it. Each batch is collected, used for a few epochs, and discarded, because after the update the policy has changed and the batch no longer describes it.

Offline learning is the opposite extreme. Someone, or something, drove the robot at some point in the past. That driver is called the behavior policy (the book writes it \(\pi_\beta\)). It left behind a file: what the robot saw, what it did, and what happened next. An offline method learns a new policy from that file with zero interaction with the environment during training.

In this lab the environment is used in three places: to score Lab 1’s checkpoints and choose a collector, to record the file, and at the very end to score each finished policy. Once the file is recorded, training never touches the environment again. Nothing from the scoring episodes is ever fed back into training.

An analogy. Imagine learning a delivery route only from a box of dashcam recordings made by a trainee driver, each one labeled with how the trip ended: delivered, crashed, or ran out of time. You can study which moves came before good trips, and copy those more. But you cannot take the van out to test an idea of your own. Where the analogy breaks down: a human watching the footage can imagine a maneuver the trainee never made and reason about whether it would work. AWR cannot do that at all. It can only turn the recorded moves up or down; book Section 4.4.3 calls this reshuffling, not exploring. If the trainee never once took the left lane, AWR will never take it either.

L2.1.2 Why robots need it, and why the rover does not

Book Section 4.1 prices out a one-million-step on-policy run on the SO-101 arm, counting the human reset after each episode, and arrives at about 16 hours of a person standing next to the arm for a single run. PPO then discards each batch after its update. Meanwhile your disks hold hours of logs: teleoperation, interventions, rollouts of old policies. Offline methods exist to learn from data like that, data you already paid for and cannot cheaply collect again.

Now the honest note. Your rover simulator runs about 12,000 random steps per second, and PPO trains on it at about 3,600 steps per second (Lab 1). On this simulator you would never need offline learning: collecting fresh data is nearly free. Lab 3 counts the total environment steps honestly, and on this simulator PPO from scratch wins that count. So why do this lab here? Because the rover is a safe, fast and fully measurable place to learn the mechanism. You can score every policy on the same 100 episodes in seconds, run three seeds of everything, and sweep \(\beta\) across ten settings in two minutes. None of that is affordable on the arm, and all of it is what you need to trust the method before you use it where it matters.

On your rig

Everything in this lab has the same shape on your SO-101 logs: a file of (observation, action, outcome) steps from some past driver, a baseline that says what that driver usually achieved, and one weight per step. The difference is that on the arm you will not be able to re-score a policy on 100 identical episodes. That is exactly why you practice the reading of the results here, where you can.

L2.1.3 What you will build

Figure L2.1 is the whole lab as one picture. Keep it in mind as you go: steps 1 and 2 use the simulator, steps 3 to 7 use only the file, and scoring uses the simulator again but learns nothing from it.

filewhat it doestime on the reference machine
lab2_pick_checkpoint.pyscores 60 Lab 1 checkpoints, stochastic and deterministic, 50 episodes each66 s with --parallel 8
lab2_collect.pydrives 500 episodes with the chosen checkpoint, writes data/rover_offline.npz43 s

lab2_awr.pybehavior cloning (--beta inf) or AWR on the file, then scoringabout 10–25 s per run

L2.2 Step 1: choose the data collector

L2.2.1 Why a mediocre driver

AWR’s whole promise is to learn a policy better than the one that collected the data. To test that promise, the data has to leave room for it.

Think about the two extremes. If the collector already reaches the goal 95% of the time, there is almost nothing to improve, and any difference between cloning and weighting drowns in the noise of the evaluation. If the collector reaches the goal 0% of the time, the file contains no good behavior to turn up. The interesting regime sits in between: a driver who succeeds sometimes and fails often, so the file holds plenty of both. The reference script’s docstring puts that regime at roughly 30–60% success, and it will pick a checkpoint automatically by that rule. As you will see in Section L2.2.4, that rule turned out to pick the wrong checkpoint for this question, and the way you find that out is the most useful habit in this lab.

Where do candidates come from? Lab 1 saved a checkpoint every 50,000 environment steps for each baseline run, named ppo_<steps>_steps.zip. That is 20 checkpoints per seed (50k, 100k, …, 1M) and 60 in total. You already own a whole range of drivers from terrible to decent; this step measures them.

L2.2.2 Two ways to score a checkpoint

A PPO policy on this rover is a Gaussian: for each wheel it outputs a mean action and has a standard deviation (its “noise”). You can drive it in two ways, and they answer different questions.

  • Stochastic: sample each action from the Gaussian. This is how the policy behaves while it collects data, so it tells you what the file will contain. Note that Stable-Baselines3’s model.predict(obs) samples by default (deterministic=False).
  • Deterministic: use the Gaussian’s mean action and ignore the noise. This is how you deploy a policy; your predict.py passes deterministic=True. It is also how every policy you train in this lab will be scored.

Here is the first piece of lab2_pick_checkpoint.py: the function that scores one checkpoint both ways.

import osos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""  # CPU only. Must run before torch is imported​import argparseimport refrom concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor​import matplotlibmatplotlib.use("Agg")import matplotlib.pyplot as pltimport torchfrom stable_baselines3 import PPO​from common import (FIGS, RESULTS, RUNS, ensure_dirs, evaluate, plot_style, save_json,                    sb3_act_fn)​SEEDS = [0, 1, 2]​​def steps_of(path):    return int(re.search(r"ppo_(\d+)_steps", path.name).group(1))​​def score_checkpoint(job):    seed, path, episodes = job    torch.set_num_threads(1)    model = PPO.load(path, device="cpu")    stoch = evaluate(sb3_act_fn(model, deterministic=False), n_episodes=episodes)    det = evaluate(sb3_act_fn(model, deterministic=True), n_episodes=episodes)    return {"seed": seed, "steps": steps_of(path), "path": str(path.relative_to(RUNS.parent)),            "stochastic": stoch, "deterministic": det}

A few lines deserve a word.

matplotlib.use("Agg") tells matplotlib to draw into files without opening a window, which is what you want in a script; it must come before pyplot is imported. plot_style is the helper from Lab 0’s common.py that sets font sizes so the figures stay readable when printed at page width.

steps_of reads the step count out of the file name, so the checkpoints can be sorted by number. Sorting the names as text would put ppo_1000000_steps.zip before ppo_150000_steps.zip, because the character 0 comes before 5.

score_checkpoint takes a single tuple, job, rather than three arguments. That is because it will run inside a pool of worker processes, and pool.map hands each call exactly one item from a list. torch.set_num_threads(1) keeps each worker to one CPU thread, so eight workers share twelve cores instead of each one trying to use all of them.

The two evaluate calls are the heart of it. evaluate (Lab 0) plays the episodes with seeds 1,000,000, 1,000,001 and so on, so every checkpoint, in both modes, faces exactly the same obstacle layouts and goals. A difference between two checkpoints is therefore not “one of them got easier maps”.

The second piece builds the list of jobs and runs them in parallel.

def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--episodes", type=int, default=50,                   help="episodes per checkpoint per mode")    p.add_argument("--parallel", type=int, default=10)    p.add_argument("--plot-only", action="store_true",                   help="redraw the figure from results/lab2_checkpoints.json")    args = p.parse_args()    ensure_dirs()    plot_style()​    if args.plot_only:        import json        rows = json.loads((RESULTS / "lab2_checkpoints.json").read_text())        args.episodes = rows[0]["stochastic"]["episodes"]    else:        rows = score_all(args)    draw_and_report(rows, args)​​def score_all(args):    jobs = []    for seed in SEEDS:        for path in sorted((RUNS / f"baseline_s{seed}" / "checkpoints")                           .glob("ppo_*_steps.zip"), key=steps_of):            jobs.append((seed, path, args.episodes))    print(f"scoring {len(jobs)} checkpoints x 2 modes x {args.episodes} episodes")    with ProcessPoolExecutor(args.parallel) as pool:        rows = sorted(pool.map(score_checkpoint, jobs), key=lambda r: (r["seed"], r["steps"]))    save_json(rows, RESULTS / "lab2_checkpoints.json")    return rows

Scoring and drawing are split into two functions so that --plot-only can redraw the figure from the saved JSON without replaying 6,000 episodes. score_all also sorts the results by seed and step count before saving; the job list is already in that order, so the sort is only a safety net.

The third piece draws the figure and prints the table.

def draw_and_report(rows, args):    # ... the two-panel figure, figures/lab2_checkpoints.png (see lab2_pick_checkpoint.py)​    print(f"\n{'seed':>4} {'steps':>9} {'stoch success':>14} "          f"{'det success':>12} {'det crash':>10}")    for r in rows:        print(f"{r['seed']:>4} {r['steps']:>9,} {r['stochastic']['success_rate']:>14.0%} "              f"{r['deterministic']['success_rate']:>12.0%} "              f"{r['deterministic']['crash_rate']:>10.0%}")    mediocre = [r for r in rows                if r["seed"] == 0 and 0.3 <= r["stochastic"]["success_rate"] <= 0.6]    if mediocre:        print(f"\nsuggested collector (seed 0, stochastic success in 30-60%): "              f"{mediocre[0]['path']}")    print(f"wrote {RESULTS / 'lab2_checkpoints.json'} and {FIGS / 'lab2_checkpoints.png'}")​​if __name__ == "__main__":    main()

The mediocre line is the automatic pick: among seed 0’s checkpoints, the first one whose stochastic success lies between 30% and 60%. The figure code, which the chunk elides, draws two panels (stochastic and deterministic), one line per seed, shades seed 0’s 95% Wilson interval, and shades the 30–60% band in gray. Copy it from the reference file; it teaches nothing new. The if __name__ == "__main__": guard at the bottom matters more than it looks. The sweep script in Section L2.8 imports run from lab2_awr.py, and without the guard in that file the import would start a whole run. Every script in this lab gets the same guard, so the habit is automatic.

Run it
python lab2_pick_checkpoint.py --episodes 50 --parallel 8

60 checkpoints × 2 modes × 50 episodes is 6,000 episodes. On the reference machine this took 66 seconds.

What you should see
scoring 60 checkpoints x 2 modes x 50 episodes​seed     steps  stoch success  det success  det crash   0    50,000             4%           2%         8%   0   100,000            14%          30%        12%   0   150,000            28%          58%        30%   0   200,000            48%          58%        36%   0   250,000            38%          52%        34%   0   300,000            48%          52%        38%...   0   500,000            54%          64%        20%...   0   750,000            64%          62%        14%...   0 1,000,000            74%          70%        24%   1    50,000             2%           6%        22%...   1 1,000,000            74%          64%        24%...   2 1,000,000            66%          62%        38%​suggested collector (seed 0, stochastic success in 30-60%): runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/ppo_200000_steps.zipwrote /mnt/Storage/projects/rl-rover/labs/ppo-awr-awac/results/lab2_checkpoints.json and /mnt/Storage/projects/rl-rover/labs/ppo-awr-awac/figures/lab2_checkpoints.png

The paths in the last line will name your own lab folder. If the first line says scoring 0 checkpoints, your runs/ folder has no baseline checkpoints: the script then prints an empty table and no error. See the note on borrowing at the start of this chapter. If you trained your own Lab 1 runs, your percentages will differ from ours; look for the broad pattern described next, not the same numbers.

L2.2.3 Reading the checkpoint table

Read the table and the figure together, and look for four things.

First, where PPO plateaus. By 1M steps the three seeds reach 74%, 74% and 66% with sampled actions, and 70%, 64% and 62% with the mean action. Crash rates stay between 20% and 40% even at 1M steps. PPO on this rover, at this budget and network size, levels off around 60–70% success. Keep that ceiling in mind; it will explain a lot in Section L2.2.4 and again in Lab 3.

Second, deterministic beats stochastic early. At seed 0’s 100k checkpoint the mean action succeeds 30% of the time and the sampled actions only 14%. At 150k it is 58% against 28%. Early in training the policy’s noise is large, and random swerves near obstacles cost episodes.

Third, the noise shrinking. This is the observation worth pausing on. The deterministic curve is roughly flat from 150k to 1M steps (about 50–70%), while the stochastic curve keeps climbing, from 28% at 150k to 66–74% at 1M. If the mean action barely improved over those 850,000 steps, what made the sampled driving improve? Largely the noise itself getting smaller. Lab 1’s summary shows the final action standard deviation of the baseline runs at 0.51–0.53 at 1M steps; at the 100k checkpoint it is about 0.93 per wheel (Section L2.5 uses that number). A large part of PPO’s later “improvement” in sampled behavior is the Gaussian narrowing around a mean that was already decent, not the mean getting much better.

An analogy: a darts player whose aim is settled in the first week, but whose hand tremor calms down over months. The average score keeps rising even though the point they aim at barely moves. Where the analogy breaks down: a tremor has nothing to do with the aim, whereas PPO’s mean and noise are trained by the same gradient and do influence each other; and the mean action does still improve a little here (seed 0 goes from 58% at 150k to 70% at 1M).

Fourth, how much to trust one number. Each point is 50 episodes, so its 95% interval is about ±14 points wide. A checkpoint at 58% and another at 52% are not distinguishable. That is why the figure shades the interval, and why you should read trends, not individual dots.

Seeds disagree too, and most of all early in training. At 100k steps the three seeds’ checkpoints succeed 14%, 22% and 30% of the time with sampled actions, and 30%, 54% and 54% with the mean action. Keep that in mind in the next subsection: a “100k checkpoint” is not one kind of driver.

L2.2.4 The pilot that changed the choice

The script suggested the 200k checkpoint: seed 0’s first checkpoint with stochastic success in the 30–60% band (48%). That sounds reasonable. Before spending a sweep on it, we ran a pilot: a small, cheap version of the experiment whose only job is to tell you whether the real experiment can answer your question. The pilot recorded a dataset with each of two candidate collectors, the suggested 200k checkpoint and the earlier 100k checkpoint, and trained four policies on each with seed 0: behavior cloning and AWR at three temperatures. Each was scored on 100 episodes.

You cannot run this pilot yet: it needs the recording script and the training script that you write in Steps 2 to 6. Section L2.8.2 gives the commands, as an optional step just before the sweep. For now, read what it found.

collectorBCAWR \(\beta = 1\)AWR \(\beta = 0.3\)AWR \(\beta = 0.1\)
200k checkpoint (data: 47% goal)58%60%61%58%
100k checkpoint (data: 15% goal)23%38%43%30%

All AWR runs in the pilot use the default weight cap of 20 (Section L2.6 explains the cap).

Read the first row. All four policies land between 58% and 61%. With 100 episodes each, the 95% interval is about ±10 points, so those four numbers are indistinguishable. A full sweep on the 200k data would most likely have found no difference it could resolve.

That would not have been a false result, but it would have answered a different question from the one this lab asks. It would say something like “weighting adds nothing measurable to data from a collector that is already near PPO’s ceiling”. That is a statement about the setup, not about whether advantage weighting can improve on cloning.

Why did the 200k data leave no room? Here is the most likely reason. It is an inference from two collectors with one seed each, not a measured cause. Look back at the checkpoint table. The 200k checkpoint’s mean action already succeeds 58% of the time, and PPO’s own ceiling at 1M steps is only about 60–70%. Cloning its data seems to land near that ceiling already, which would leave weighting nothing to add that 100 episodes can resolve. The automatic rule looked at stochastic success. But the policies you train are scored by their mean action, so the room between the collector’s mean action and the ceiling is a plausible thing to watch.

One observation, not a rule: among seed 0’s checkpoints, the first whose mean action succeeds 30–60% of the time is exactly the 100k one (30%).

Now read the second row. At 100k the four numbers spread from 23% to 43%. There is room, and the pilot already hints that weighting uses it. This lab uses the 100k checkpoint, runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/ppo_100000_steps.zip, even though its 14% stochastic success sits below the band the script aimed for. For comparison, the 200k checkpoint’s dataset had 134,526 steps, 47% goals, 33.4% crashes and 19.6% timeouts; the 100k dataset you are about to record looks very different.

This choice is specific to seed 0 of our Lab 1 grid. As Section L2.2.3 showed, the 100k checkpoints of seeds 1 and 2 already have mean actions that succeed 54% of the time, close to the ceiling. If you use checkpoints from your own Lab 1 run, do not assume their 100k checkpoint behaves like ours: run the pilot of Section L2.8.2 on your candidates.

The lesson is short: pilot before you sweep. A heuristic band is a guess about what makes the experiment informative. A pilot on one seed is a measurement of it, and it costs a few minutes.

Pitfall

Trusting a selection rule you have not tested. The 30–60% rule is sensible and was still wrong for this question. It looked at the collector’s sampled driving, while what seems to have mattered was how close the collector’s mean action already was to PPO’s ceiling. That explanation is itself a guess from two collectors, so do not turn it into a new rule either. Whenever an automatic choice decides what a long experiment measures, spend one seed checking that the experiment can show a difference at all. Measure; do not replace one guess with another.

L2.3 Step 2: record the dataset

Here is the problem this step solves. After this script finishes, AWR never touches the environment again until scoring. Anything the learner will need later must be written into the file now, because there is no going back to ask. So before writing any code, decide what the learner needs.

L2.3.1 What goes into the file, and why

Behavior cloning needs to know what the rover saw and what it did. AWR needs that too, plus one number per step saying how much better or worse than usual things went from there. Computing that number needs the rewards, where each episode ended and how, and a baseline. Lab 3 will need a little more. The file stores one row per environment step, with these fields:

fieldper stepwhat it iswho needs it
obs15 floats\(s_t\), the observation the policy sawthe input of BC and AWR
act2 floats\(a_t\), clipped to \([-1, 1]\): what the wheels actually receivedthe target of BC and AWR
rew1 float\(r_t\), the reward for that stepthe returns
next_obs15 floats\(s_{t+1}\), the observation after the stepthe time-limit bootstrap here; Lab 3’s Q-learning
terminatedbooltrue if the episode really ended at this step (goal or crash)the returns
truncatedbooltrue if the 500-step time limit cut the episode off herethe returns
episodeintegerwhich of the 500 episodes this step belongs tothe diagnostic of Section L2.10
value1 float\(V(s_t)\) from the checkpoint’s own criticthe baseline of the advantage
ret1 float\(G_t\), the discounted reward-to-go from step \(t\)the advantage

The last two fields combine into the number AWR runs on. Stable-Baselines3’s PPO trains a critic next to the policy: a network \(V(s)\) that predicts how much discounted reward the policy usually collects from observation \(s\) onward. The checkpoint you load contains that critic. So for every logged step you can ask two questions. What did the rest of this episode actually pay? That is \(G_t\). And what did the collector’s critic expect it to pay? That is \(V(s_t)\). The difference is the advantage estimate:

\[ \hat{A}_t \;=\; G_t \;-\; V(s_t) \]
In plain words

\(t\) indexes one logged step. \(G_t\) is the return that actually followed that step: its own reward plus the discounted rewards of the rest of the episode (defined exactly in Section L2.3.4). \(V(s_t)\) is the collector’s critic’s prediction of that same quantity, made from the observation \(s_t\) alone, before it knew how the episode would go. \(\hat{A}_t\) (read “A-hat”; the hat marks an estimate) is positive when things went better than the collector usually does from there, and negative when they went worse. Because the critic belongs to the policy that made the data, this is an estimate of the behavior policy’s advantage, the \(A^{\pi_\beta}\) of book Section 4.4.2.

The book computes this very quantity in Section 3.5.1, where it calls it the Monte Carlo advantage. “Monte Carlo” means that the return part is estimated from the rewards that actually happened in one sampled episode, rather than predicted by a model. The book also warns that it is noisy: \(G_t\) charges every random event from step \(t\) to the end of the episode to the action at step \(t\). Keep that warning in your pocket. Section L2.10 measures exactly how noisy it is on your file.

L2.3.2 The recording loop

Create lab2_collect.py. The first chunk loads the checkpoint and sets up empty lists, one per field.

import osos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""  # CPU only. Must run before torch is imported​import argparsefrom pathlib import Path​import numpy as npimport torchfrom stable_baselines3 import PPO​from common import DATA, GAMMA, ensure_dirs, make_env, outcome_of, save_json, set_seed​# ... compute_returns(...) goes here: Section L2.3.4​​def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--checkpoint", required=True)    p.add_argument("--episodes", type=int, default=500)    p.add_argument("--out", default=str(DATA / "rover_offline.npz"))    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0,                   help="seeds the action sampling, so a re-run gives the same file")    args = p.parse_args()    ensure_dirs()    # model.predict(deterministic=False) draws from torch's global generator    set_seed(args.seed)    torch.set_num_threads(2)​    model = PPO.load(args.checkpoint, device="cpu")    env = make_env()    buf = {k: [] for k in ["obs", "act", "rew", "next_obs",                           "terminated", "truncated", "episode"]}    outcomes, returns = [], []

GAMMA comes from common.py and is 0.99, the same discount PPO used. buf is a dictionary of Python lists; appending to a list is cheap, and the lists become NumPy arrays once, at the end. value and ret are missing from buf on purpose: they are computed after the driving, in one go.

A note on --seed, because it surprised us. The help text says it seeds the action sampling. But PPO.load re-seeds PyTorch and NumPy with the seed saved inside the checkpoint, and it runs after set_seed. So the action sampling always starts from the checkpoint’s own seed, whatever you pass, and --seed has no effect on the file. The good news is that the file is reproducible: two collections from the same checkpoint produced identical datasets. The thing not to expect is a different dataset from a different --seed.

The second chunk is the driving loop.

    for ep in range(args.episodes):        # seeds 0..499; evaluation uses seeds from 1,000,000 up        obs, _ = env.reset(seed=ep)        total = 0.0        while True:            action, _ = model.predict(obs, deterministic=False)            next_obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)            buf["obs"].append(obs)            buf["act"].append(np.clip(action, -1.0, 1.0))            buf["rew"].append(reward)            buf["next_obs"].append(next_obs)            buf["terminated"].append(terminated)            buf["truncated"].append(truncated)            buf["episode"].append(ep)            total += reward            obs = next_obs            if terminated or truncated:                outcomes.append(outcome_of(terminated, truncated, info))                returns.append(total)                break        if (ep + 1) % 100 == 0:            print(f"  {ep + 1} episodes, {len(buf['rew']):,} steps")

Walk through it once, slowly, because three decisions here change the results.

env.reset(seed=ep). Episode 0 uses seed 0, episode 499 uses seed 499. Every obstacle layout, start and goal in the file is therefore reproducible. And none of them is an evaluation layout: evaluate uses seeds from 1,000,000 up. This is an ordinary train/test split. If you recorded on the evaluation seeds, a policy could score well partly by having seen those exact maps.

deterministic=False. This is the decision most worth understanding. AWR can only prefer one recorded action over another if the file contains different actions in similar situations. A deterministic collector records one action per situation: in similar states it does nearly the same thing every time. Then there is nothing to choose between, and weighting cannot pick a better action that was never tried. Book Section 4.4.3 says the same thing in its own terms: the tilt reweights actions the data contains and can never invent one. Sampled actions give the file variety, and variety is the raw material of AWR.

np.clip(action, -1.0, 1.0). The file must hold what the wheels actually received. The rover env clips actions to \([-1, 1]\) itself, so an action of 1.6 drives exactly like 1.0. (Stable-Baselines3’s predict already clips into the action box, so here the line is a guarantee rather than a change: the file’s promise does not depend on a library detail.) Remember this line; Section L2.5 shows that clipping has a real effect on what behavior cloning learns.

The rest is bookkeeping. obs is appended before obs = next_obs, so each row pairs the observation the policy acted on with the action it took. When either flag is set, outcome_of (Lab 0) turns the flags and info["is_colliding"] into "goal", "crash" or "timeout", and the loop moves to the next episode.

L2.3.3 Ask the critic, once

With all the driving done, the third chunk turns the lists into arrays and asks the checkpoint’s critic for its predictions.

    data = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in buf.items()}    data["obs"] = data["obs"].astype(np.float32)    data["next_obs"] = data["next_obs"].astype(np.float32)    data["act"] = data["act"].astype(np.float32)    data["rew"] = data["rew"].astype(np.float32)​    # Ask the checkpoint's critic for V(s_t) at every step, in one batch.    with torch.no_grad():        data["value"] = model.policy.predict_values(            torch.as_tensor(data["obs"])).numpy().ravel()        v_next = model.policy.predict_values(            torch.as_tensor(data["next_obs"])).numpy().ravel()    data["ret"] = compute_returns(data["rew"], data["terminated"], data["truncated"],                                  v_next).astype(np.float32)    np.savez_compressed(args.out, **data)

The astype(np.float32) lines store the big arrays in 32-bit floats, which is what PyTorch uses by default and half the size of NumPy’s default 64-bit floats. The finished file is about 12 MB compressed.

model.policy.predict_values runs only the critic half of the PPO network. Asking it about all 182,658 observations in one call, inside torch.no_grad() (no gradients needed, we are only reading), takes a moment instead of 182,658 separate calls. It returns one value per row in a column of shape (N, 1); .ravel() flattens that to shape (N,). The Lab 1 runs used no observation normalization (no VecNormalize), so the raw observations are exactly what this critic was trained on and can go in as they are.

v_next is the critic’s opinion of every next observation. Only 237 of those numbers will be used, one for each episode the time limit cut off, but computing all of them in one batch is simpler than picking out the right rows. Why they are needed is the next subsection.

L2.3.4 Returns, and the time-limit trap

Now define \(G_t\) exactly. The return from step \(t\) is the reward at \(t\), plus 0.99 times the return from step \(t+1\). That recursion needs an ending, and an episode can end in two very different ways (Section L0.4.5 introduced the two flags; here they decide a formula).

  • Terminated: the rover reached the goal (+100) or collided (−100). The episode is truly over. Nothing comes after, so the return of the last step is just its reward.
  • Truncated: the 500-step clock ran out while the rover was still driving. The world did not end; the recording did. The rewards the rover would have collected next are missing, not zero.

For a truncated episode, the honest stand-in for the missing future is the critic’s estimate of it, \(V(s_{T+1})\), evaluated at the observation right after the last recorded step. Using an estimate in place of rewards you never observed is called bootstrapping. Stable-Baselines3 does the same thing for PPO’s own rollouts, by adding \(\gamma V\) of the final observation to the last reward of a truncated episode.

\[ G_t \;=\; \begin{cases} r_t + \gamma\, G_{t+1} & \text{the episode continues after } t \\[2pt] r_t & \text{terminated at } t \\[2pt] r_t + \gamma\, V(s_{t+1}) & \text{truncated at } t \end{cases} \]
In plain words

\(G_t\) is the discounted reward-to-go from logged step \(t\). \(r_t\) is that step’s reward. \(\gamma = 0.99\) is the discount: each step further into the future counts 1% less. \(G_{t+1}\) is the return of the next step in the same episode, which is why the computation runs backwards, from each episode’s last step to its first. “Terminated at \(t\)” means step \(t\) reached the goal or crashed; then nothing is added. “Truncated at \(t\)” means the 500-step limit cut the episode off at step \(t\); then the critic’s value \(V(s_{t+1})\) of the observation that followed stands in for all the rewards the recording is missing.

Here is the function. Put it above main(), where the placeholder comment was.

def compute_returns(rew, terminated, truncated, value_after_truncation):    """G_t = r_t + gamma * G_{t+1}, computed backwards through the whole file.​    Where the next step belongs to the same episode, G_{t+1} is simply the next    entry. At an episode's last step there are two cases:      terminated -> nothing comes after: G_T = r_T      truncated  -> the rover was still driving when the clock stopped, so we                    stand in for the missing future with the critic's estimate:                    G_T = r_T + gamma * V(s_{T+1})    """    ret = np.zeros_like(rew)    running = 0.0    for t in reversed(range(len(rew))):        if terminated[t]:            running = rew[t]        elif truncated[t]:            running = rew[t] + GAMMA * value_after_truncation[t]        else:            running = rew[t] + GAMMA * running        ret[t] = running    return ret

One loop runs backwards through all 182,658 rows, across all 500 episodes at once. How does it avoid mixing one episode’s return into the previous episode? Every episode’s last step has terminated or truncated set, and at such a step running is replaced, not added to. So the running sum restarts at every episode boundary. Episodes are stored one after another, so “the next row” is always “the next step of the same episode” except at those boundaries.

The order of the if matters in one corner case. If the rover reaches the goal on exactly its 500th step, both flags are set. Checking terminated first means the real ending wins, which is right: the episode really is over.

L2.3.5 A worked example: the same three steps, ending two ways

The numbers below are made up for teaching; they do not come from the rover. Take a three-step episode with rewards \(r_0 = 1.0\), \(r_1 = 2.0\), \(r_2 = 3.0\), and \(\gamma = 0.99\). Step 2 is the last recorded step. Suppose the critic values the observation after it at \(V(s_3) = 50.0\).

Ending one: terminated at step 2. Work backwards.

G_2 = r_2                     = 3.0G_1 = r_1 + 0.99 * G_2 = 2.0 + 0.99 * 3.0  = 2.0 + 2.97   = 4.97G_0 = r_0 + 0.99 * G_1 = 1.0 + 0.99 * 4.97 = 1.0 + 4.9203 = 5.9203

Ending two: truncated at step 2. Same rewards; only the last line changes, and the change flows backwards.

G_2 = r_2 + 0.99 * V(s_3) = 3.0 + 0.99 * 50.0 = 3.0 + 49.5 = 52.5G_1 = r_1 + 0.99 * G_2    = 2.0 + 0.99 * 52.5   = 2.0 + 51.975   = 53.975G_0 = r_0 + 0.99 * G_1    = 1.0 + 0.99 * 53.975 = 1.0 + 53.43525 = 54.43525

Identical rewards, and the return of the first step differs by 48.5. Which one is right depends entirely on why the recording stopped. If you forget the bootstrap and treat a timeout like a real ending, every timed-out episode looks as if its last steps led nowhere, and their advantages \(\hat{A} = G - V\) come out wrong by an amount that is largest at the final step and fades backwards by a factor of 0.99 per step. On your file this is not a corner case: 237 of the 500 episodes end by truncation.

Pitfall

Treating truncation as termination. Gymnasium gives you two flags for a reason. A time limit is a fact about the recording, not about the world; bootstrap through it. The same mistake in a real robot log is easy to make, because a logger that stops at a fixed duration writes an ending that looks exactly like a finished task.

L2.3.6 Run it and read the summary

The last chunk of main() computes the advantage once more, for a summary, and prints it.

    adv = data["ret"] - data["value"]    summary = {        "checkpoint": args.checkpoint,        "episodes": args.episodes,        "steps": int(len(data["rew"])),        "goal": outcomes.count("goal") / len(outcomes),        "crash": outcomes.count("crash") / len(outcomes),        "timeout": outcomes.count("timeout") / len(outcomes),        "mean_episode_return": float(np.mean(returns)),        "advantage_mean": float(adv.mean()),        "advantage_std": float(adv.std()),        "fraction_positive_advantage": float((adv > 0).mean()),    }    summary_path = Path(args.out).with_name(Path(args.out).stem + "_summary.json")    save_json(summary, summary_path)    print(f"\nwrote {args.out} and {summary_path}")    for k, v in summary.items():        print(f"  {k:<28} {v}")​​if __name__ == "__main__":    main()

summary_path puts rover_offline_summary.json next to the data file. The float(...) and int(...) calls turn NumPy scalars into plain Python numbers, which the JSON writer can handle.

Run it
python lab2_collect.py --checkpoint runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/ppo_100000_steps.zip

500 episodes; 43 seconds on the reference machine.
