With the reference checkpoint file these numbers should repeat to the last digit, because the collection is reproducible. If you borrowed the answer key’s runs, the command above already uses that file.

Do not expect the same from your own Lab 1 checkpoint. At 100k steps PPO checkpoints vary a lot between seeds (Section L2.2.3), so another run’s 100k checkpoint can record a very different file, and every later number in this chapter would shift with it. If you want the downstream numbers to match, record from the answer key’s checkpoint: --checkpoint ../ppo-awr-awac/runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/ppo_100000_steps.zip (the first summary line then shows that path). If you use your own checkpoint, run the pilot of Section L2.8.2 before trusting the choice.

How to read it: the outcomes. 182,658 steps over 500 episodes is about 365 steps per episode. The collector reached the goal in 15.4% of episodes, crashed in 37.2%, and timed out in 47.4%. Counted as episodes: 77 goals, 186 crashes, 237 timeouts, so 263 episodes terminated and 237 were truncated. The mean episode return is −84.4. This is a poor driver, on purpose, and a file with plenty of both good and bad endings.

How to read it: the advantage. Its mean is −0.59, close to zero next to its standard deviation of 35.4. That is what you should expect: if the critic were perfect, advantages would average to zero over the collector’s own data. A mean this close to zero says the critic’s predictions are, on average, calibrated to this driver. (For contrast, the 200k checkpoint’s dataset gave a mean of +8.5 and a standard deviation of 40.8: its episodes paid more, on average, than its critic predicted.)

How to read it: the skew. 64.1% of the advantages are positive, yet the mean is slightly negative. That can only happen if the negative ones are larger. Computing a few more statistics makes the shape clear:

statistic of \(\hat{A}\)value
median+7.0
10th percentile / 90th percentile−56.6 / +29.5
minimum / maximum−117.5 / +135.0
average of the positive ones / of the negative ones+19.3 / −36.2

Many moderate positives, fewer but larger negatives. The \(\pm 100\) terminal rewards explain it. A crash is a large, sudden negative surprise. Through the discount it lands on every step before it in that episode, most heavily on the last ones. And crashes are common in this file (37% of episodes), so a long negative tail forms. This lopsided shape will matter when you standardize the advantages in Section L2.6.

Try it yourself first

Load the file in a Python shell and reproduce the table above. You need np.load, d["ret"] - d["value"], np.median, np.percentile(adv, [10, 90]), boolean masks such as adv[adv > 0], and d["terminated"].sum() and d["truncated"].sum() for the endings (263 and 237). While you are there, print {k: d[k].shape for k in d} and check that every field has 182,658 rows.

L2.4 Step 3: the policy network

L2.4.1 What the learner needs from a policy

You are about to train a fresh policy on the file. What kind of network should it be?

The obvious choice is a plain regression network: observation in, two wheel speeds out, trained with mean-squared error against the recorded actions. It would work for cloning. But it cannot answer the question both BC and AWR are built on: how likely would this policy have been to produce this recorded action? A network that outputs one action has no notion of “likely”. It also has nowhere to store how spread out the recorded actions are, and Section L2.5 shows that the spread tells you something real about the data.

So the policy will be a probability distribution, the same shape Stable-Baselines3’s PPO uses. Five terms describe it; take them one at a time.

  • Gaussian. For each observation \(s\), the policy describes a bell curve over each wheel’s speed. A Gaussian is that bell curve.
  • Mean action \(\mu(s)\). The center of the bell, where the policy’s preferred action sits. A small network computes it from the observation.
  • Standard deviation \(\sigma\). The width of the bell: how far from the mean the policy’s actions typically land. Here it is one learned number per wheel.
  • Probability density \(\pi(a \mid s)\). The height of the bell at the action \(a\): high near the mean, low far away. It is a density, not a probability, so it can exceed 1. What matters is how it compares between actions.
  • Log-probability \(\log \pi(a \mid s)\). Simply the natural logarithm of that density. Section L2.4.4 explains why the logarithm is the form you want.

L2.4.2 The code

Add this class to common.py, below the other helpers. Labs 2 and 3 both use it. common.py already imports numpy as np, torch and torch.nn as nn at the top.

class GaussianPolicy(nn.Module):    """pi(a | s) = Normal(mean(s), std), the same shape of policy SB3's PPO uses.​    - mean(s): a small MLP, 15 inputs -> 64 -> 64 -> 2 outputs, tanh hidden layers.    - std: one learned number per action dimension, NOT a function of the state.      Stored as log_std so it can never go negative.    """​    def __init__(self, obs_dim: int = 15, act_dim: int = 2, hidden: int = 64):        super().__init__()        self.mean_net = nn.Sequential(            nn.Linear(obs_dim, hidden), nn.Tanh(),            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.Tanh(),            nn.Linear(hidden, act_dim),        )        self.log_std = nn.Parameter(torch.full((act_dim,), -0.5))​    def distribution(self, obs: torch.Tensor) -> torch.distributions.Normal:        return torch.distributions.Normal(self.mean_net(obs), self.log_std.exp())​    def log_prob(self, obs: torch.Tensor, act: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:        """log pi(a | s), summed over the two wheels -> one number per sample."""        return self.distribution(obs).log_prob(act).sum(dim=-1)​    @torch.no_grad()    def act(self, obs: np.ndarray, deterministic: bool = True) -> np.ndarray:        """Numpy in, numpy out, for driving the env. Clipped to the action box."""        o = torch.as_tensor(obs, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(0)        d = self.distribution(o)        a = d.mean if deterministic else d.sample()        return a.squeeze(0).clamp(-1.0, 1.0).numpy()

Take it one piece at a time.

mean_net maps the 15 observation numbers through two hidden layers of 64 units with tanh activations to 2 outputs, one mean per wheel. That is the architecture of SB3’s default PPO policy network (64, 64, tanh). With the two log_std numbers the whole policy has 5,316 parameters.

log_std is a learnable parameter with one entry per wheel, and it does not depend on the observation: the policy is equally noisy everywhere. It stores the logarithm of the standard deviation because the optimizer may push it to any real number, and \(\exp\) of any real number is positive, so the standard deviation can never become zero or negative. It starts at −0.5, which means a standard deviation of \(e^{-0.5} \approx 0.607\) per wheel.

distribution(obs) builds a torch.distributions.Normal whose mean has shape (batch, 2) and whose standard deviation has shape (2,). PyTorch broadcasts the two, so every row of the batch shares the same pair of standard deviations.

log_prob(obs, act) asks that distribution for the log-density of each wheel’s recorded action, shape (batch, 2), then adds the two columns, giving shape (batch,): one number per logged step. Adding is correct because the two wheels are modeled as independent, and the density of two independent events is the product of their densities; the log of a product is the sum of the logs.

act(obs) is only for driving the environment. @torch.no_grad() switches off gradient tracking. unsqueeze(0) turns one observation of shape (15,) into a batch of one, shape (1, 15), because the network expects batches. It returns the mean when deterministic=True (how every policy in this lab is scored) or a sample otherwise, removes the batch dimension, and clips to \([-1, 1]\).

L2.4.3 What a log-probability is, with numbers

For one wheel with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), the Gaussian log-density has a closed form. The policy adds it over the two wheels:

\[ \begin{aligned} \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{2} \Bigg[ & -\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{a_k - \mu_k(s)}{\sigma_k}\Big)^{2} \\ & -\; \log \sigma_k \;-\; \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi) \Bigg] \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

\(\theta\) stands for all of the policy’s parameters: the weights of mean_net and the two log_std numbers. \(s\) is the 15-number observation and \(a\) the recorded action. \(k\) counts the wheels, 1 and 2. \(a_k\) is wheel \(k\)’s recorded speed, \(\mu_k(s)\) is the network’s mean for that wheel, and \(\sigma_k\) is its standard deviation: \(e\) raised to wheel \(k\)’s entry of log_std. The first term measures how far the action is from the mean in units of standard deviations, squares it and halves it: far-away actions are penalized quadratically. The second term, \(-\log \sigma_k\), is larger for narrow bells, because a narrow bell is taller at its center. The last term is a constant, about 0.919 per wheel, that makes the density integrate to 1. One notation clash to watch: the \(\pi\) inside \(\log(2\pi)\) is the number 3.14159, not the policy. The clash is standard.

Here is a worked example with made-up teaching numbers. One wheel, mean 0.2, standard deviation 0.5, recorded action 0.7.

distance in standard deviations:   (0.7 - 0.2) / 0.5 = 1.0first term:    -1/2 * 1.0^2      = -0.5second term:   -log 0.5          = +0.693147constant:      -1/2 * log(2*pi)  = -0.918939log N = -0.5 + 0.693147 - 0.918939 = -0.725792

If the other wheel had exactly the same numbers, log_prob would add them:

\[ -0.725792 + (-0.725792) \;=\; -1.451584 \]

Now move the action further away, to 1.7, with the same mean and standard deviation. The distance becomes \((1.7 - 0.2)/0.5 = 3.0\), the first term becomes \(-\tfrac{1}{2} \times 9 = -4.5\), and the log-density is \(-4.5 + 0.693147 - 0.918939 = -4.725792\). Three standard deviations away costs 4 more nats than one standard deviation away. (A nat is the unit of a natural logarithm, so “4 more nats” means the log-density is lower by 4.)

That quadratic growth has a consequence worth remembering. Far-away actions pull hard on the fit: for a recorded action three standard deviations away, the first term costs nine times as much as at one standard deviation, and (as Section L2.4.4 shows) its pull on the mean is three times as strong. And with a squared penalty, the best-fitting mean at a given state is the average of the actions recorded there, not the location of their bulk. Keep that in mind for Section L2.5.5, where some recorded actions are not where the collector meant them to be.

Before trusting your class, check it against this arithmetic. Predict what each line below prints, then run it.

Run it

Start python in your lab folder (so that from common import GaussianPolicy finds your file) and type:

import torchfrom common import GaussianPolicyprint(torch.distributions.Normal(0.2, 0.5).log_prob(torch.tensor(0.7)))pol = GaussianPolicy()print(pol.log_std.exp())print(pol.log_prob(torch.zeros(4, 15), torch.zeros(4, 2)).shape)
What you should see
tensor(-0.7258)tensor([0.6065, 0.6065], grad_fn=<ExpBackward0>)torch.Size([4])

The first line is the hand result, −0.725792, rounded to four digits. The second is \(e^{-0.5}\), the starting standard deviation of each wheel; grad_fn only says that PyTorch is tracking how it was computed, for the gradient. The third says log_prob returns one number per sample, not per wheel. If you see torch.Size([4, 2]) instead, the .sum(dim=-1) is missing.

L2.4.4 Why weighted regression needs log-probabilities

Three reasons, from the most practical to the deepest.

Sums, not products. Behavior cloning wants the recorded actions to be as probable as possible under the policy, all of them together. “All together” is a product of 182,658 densities, a number too small or too large for any floating-point type. Its logarithm is a sum, which is easy to compute and to split into minibatches (book Section 4.3).

A sum has a slot for a weight. Once the objective is a sum of one term per logged step, AWR’s entire change is to multiply each term by its own number \(w_i\). A weight of 3 means “count this step three times”; a weight of 0.01 means “whisper”. That is all “weighted regression” means.

The gradient does the right thing for both the mean and the spread. Take the negative of the per-wheel log-density as the loss, and look at the mean and the width separately.

The mean. The derivative of the loss with respect to the mean is \(-(a - \mu)/\sigma^2\). With the toy numbers above that is \(-(0.7 - 0.2)/0.25 = -0.5/0.25 = -2.0\). Gradient descent subtracts the derivative, so the mean moves up, toward the recorded action. An action three times as far away gives a derivative three times as large, which is the “pulls hard” of Section L2.4.3.

The width. Write \(z = (a - \mu)/\sigma\) for the distance in standard deviations. The code stores \(\log \sigma\), so take the derivative with respect to that. Start from the loss, dropping the constant, which has no derivative:

loss  = 1/2 * z^2  +  log sigma  +  constz     = (a - mu) / sigma = (a - mu) * exp(-log sigma)​d z / d(log sigma)                 = (a - mu) * exp(-log sigma) * (-1) = -zd (1/2 * z^2) / d(log sigma)       = z * (d z / d(log sigma)) = z * (-z) = -z^2d (log sigma) / d(log sigma)       = 1​d loss / d(log sigma)              = 1 - z^2

Now put in three cases. At \(z = 1\) the derivative is \(1 - 1 = 0\): this sample is exactly as far away as the bell’s width says it should be, and it leaves the width alone. At \(z = 3\) it is \(1 - 9 = -8\). Descent subtracts a negative number, so \(\log \sigma\) goes up and the bell widens. A sample closer than one standard deviation, say \(z = 0.5\), gives \(1 - 0.25 = +0.75\), and the bell narrows.

Averaged over the data, the width settles where these pushes cancel: where the average of \(1 - z^2\) is 0, so the average of \(z^2\) is exactly 1. That is where the root-mean-square distance of the recorded actions from the mean equals one standard deviation. In other words, the learned \(\sigma\) measures how spread out the recorded actions are around the policy’s mean. You will read exactly that number in the next section.

If you froze \(\sigma\), the first term of the log-density would be the squared error scaled by a constant, and you would be back at mean-squared-error regression. The Gaussian gives you that plus a learned spread, and a sampling method that Lab 3 needs.

L2.5 Step 4: behavior cloning first

L2.5.1 Why the baseline comes first

Suppose AWR reaches 37% success on this file. Is that good? You cannot say. Maybe any policy trained on this file reaches 37%. Maybe it is worse than simply copying the file. A number means something only next to the right comparison, and the right comparison here is behavior cloning (BC): the same file, the same network, the same number of updates, the same scoring episodes, and every weight equal to 1. If AWR beats that, the weights did it, because nothing else differs.

Book Section 4.3 states BC’s objective and its ceiling. The objective is ordinary supervised learning: make the recorded actions as likely as possible under the policy. The ceiling is that BC treats every recorded action as equally worth imitating, and so it copies the collector’s mistakes as faithfully as its successes. In code, BC minimizes this, one minibatch at a time:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}}(\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{i \in B} \Bigl( -\log \pi_\theta(a_i \mid s_i) \Bigr) \]
In plain words

\(B\) is a minibatch: 512 logged steps drawn at random from the file, and \(|B|\) is how many steps it holds. \(i\) indexes one of those steps; \(s_i\) and \(a_i\) are its recorded observation and action. \(\pi_\theta\) is the GaussianPolicy with parameters \(\theta\), and \(\log \pi_\theta(a_i \mid s_i)\) is what its log_prob method returns. The minus sign turns “make the recorded actions likely” into a quantity to make small; the average of these terms is called the negative log-likelihood (NLL). Notice what is absent: no reward, no return, no advantage. BC never asks how an episode went.

L2.5.2 The training loop

Create lab2_awr.py. It will hold both methods, because they are the same program with a different weight per sample. Start with the imports, and with a first version of awr_weights that only handles \(\beta = \infty\), which is behavior cloning. You will fill in the other branch in Section L2.6.

import osos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""  # CPU only. Must run before torch is imported​import argparseimport mathimport time​import numpy as npimport torch​from common import (DATA, RESULTS, GaussianPolicy, ensure_dirs, evaluate, fmt_eval,                    save_json, set_seed)​​def awr_weights(adv: np.ndarray, beta: float, max_weight: float):    """One weight per sample, plus the diagnostics that tell you if beta is sane."""    adv_std = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)       # zero mean, unit spread    if math.isinf(beta):        w = np.ones_like(adv_std, dtype=np.float64)    else:        ...  # the exponential weights: you write this branch in Section L2.6    ess = w.sum() ** 2 / (w ** 2).sum()                      # effective sample size    info = {        "ess": float(ess),        "ess_fraction": float(ess / len(w)),        "fraction_at_cap": (float(np.isclose(w, w.max()).mean())                            if not math.isinf(beta) else 0.0),        "top1pct_weight_share": float(np.sort(w)[-max(1, len(w) // 100):].sum() / w.sum()),    }    return w / w.mean(), info                                # rescale so the mean weight is 1

For BC this returns an array of ones, one per logged step, plus a small dictionary of diagnostics that Section L2.6 explains. For now, note only that “ESS” will be 182,658, the number of steps, when every weight is equal.

Until you fill in the else: branch, always pass --beta inf when you run this script. The default you are about to give --beta is 1.0, which reaches the unfinished branch. There, ... does nothing, w never gets a value, and Python stops at the ess line with an UnboundLocalError.

Next, the training loop. It is written once, for any weights; for BC every weight is 1.

def train_policy(data, weights, seed, epochs=30, batch_size=512, lr=1e-3, log=print):    set_seed(seed)    obs = torch.as_tensor(data["obs"])    act = torch.as_tensor(data["act"])    w = torch.as_tensor(weights, dtype=torch.float32)    policy = GaussianPolicy()    opt = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=lr)    n = len(obs)    history = []    for epoch in range(epochs):        perm = torch.randperm(n)        total = 0.0        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):            idx = perm[start:start + batch_size]            # -log pi(a_i | s_i), one per sample            nll = -policy.log_prob(obs[idx], act[idx])            # Weights have mean 1 over the WHOLE dataset, so this is an unbiased            # mini-batch estimate of the full weighted loss. (Dividing by this            # batch's own sum instead would secretly re-inflate batches that            # happen to contain only low-weight samples.)            loss = (w[idx] * nll).mean()            opt.zero_grad()            loss.backward()            opt.step()            total += loss.item() * len(idx)        history.append(total / n)        if epoch % 10 == 0 or epoch == epochs - 1:            log(f"  epoch {epoch:3d}  weighted NLL {history[-1]:.4f}  "                f"std {policy.log_std.exp().detach().numpy().round(3)}")    return policy, history

Read it top to bottom.

set_seed(seed) fixes the network’s random initial weights and the order of the minibatches. That is all a seed changes in this lab. The file is identical for every seed, and so are the scoring episodes. When you later see three seeds disagree, the disagreement comes only from initialization and shuffling, which is a useful thing to know about how fragile a result is.

The tensors. The whole file fits in memory: the observations are 182,658 × 15 floats, about 11 MB. torch.as_tensor wraps the NumPy arrays without copying them where it can.

Adam with learning rate \(10^{-3}\) is a standard choice for a network this small.

One epoch is one pass over the file in a random order. torch.randperm(n) shuffles the row numbers, and the inner loop slices them into minibatches of 512. \(182{,}658 / 512 = 356.75\), so each epoch has 356 full minibatches and one last minibatch of 386 steps: 357 updates per epoch, and \(357 \times 30 = 10{,}710\) updates in a run.

The loss line multiplies each step’s negative log-likelihood by its weight and averages. For BC every weight is 1, so this is exactly \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}}\). The comment above it matters for AWR, and Section L2.7 is devoted to it.

total += loss.item() * len(idx) accumulates the loss weighted by the minibatch’s size, so that the smaller last minibatch counts correctly; dividing by n gives the epoch’s average. The log line prints that average and the policy’s current standard deviation per wheel, at epochs 0, 10 and 20 and at the last epoch, 29.

L2.5.3 Running a whole experiment: run and main

run ties the pieces together: load the file, compute the weights, train, score, save.

def run(beta, max_weight, seed, epochs, eval_episodes, dataset, quiet=False):    torch.set_num_threads(1)    log = (lambda *a, **k: None) if quiet else print    data = dict(np.load(dataset))    adv = data["ret"] - data["value"]    weights, winfo = awr_weights(adv, beta, max_weight)    name = ("bc" if math.isinf(beta)            else f"awr_b{beta:g}" + ("" if max_weight > 0 else "_nocap"))    log(f"{name} seed {seed}: {len(adv):,} samples, "        f"ESS {winfo['ess_fraction']:.1%} of the data, "        f"top 1% of samples carry {winfo['top1pct_weight_share']:.1%} of the weight")    t0 = time.time()    policy, history = train_policy(data, weights, seed, epochs=epochs, log=log)    ev = evaluate(lambda o: policy.act(o, deterministic=True), n_episodes=eval_episodes)    log(f"  {fmt_eval(ev)}   ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")​    # Histogram of the (mean-1) weights on log-spaced bins, for the plot script.    bins = np.logspace(-6, 3, 46)    counts, _ = np.histogram(np.clip(weights, 1e-6, 1e3), bins=bins)    out = {"name": name, "beta": beta, "max_weight": max_weight, "seed": seed,           "epochs": epochs, "weights": winfo, "eval": ev, "train_loss": history,           "hist_bins": bins.tolist(), "hist_counts": counts.tolist()}    # save_json creates results/lab2/    save_json(out, RESULTS / "lab2" / f"{name}_s{seed}.json")    torch.save(policy.state_dict(), RESULTS / "lab2" / f"{name}_s{seed}.pt")    return out

A few details. quiet swaps print for a function that does nothing; the sweep in Section L2.8 runs thirty of these, ten at a time, and their logs would otherwise interleave. dict(np.load(dataset)) reads every array out of the .npz file into an ordinary dictionary. name becomes bc, or for example awr_b1 and awr_b0.3_nocap; the :g format writes 1.0 as 1 and 0.3 as 0.3.

The scoring line is the one to notice: policy.act(o, deterministic=True), 100 episodes, on the evaluation seeds. Every trained policy in this lab is scored by its mean action, exactly like the collector’s “deterministic” column.

The histogram block stores, for the plotting script, how many steps received a weight in each of 45 bins spaced evenly on a logarithmic scale from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{3}\). np.clip first moves any weight below \(10^{-6}\) into the lowest bin; remember that when you see a pile at the left edge of Figure L2.4. The JSON file keeps every number, and the .pt file keeps the trained network’s parameters in case you want to drive it later.

def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--beta", type=float, default=1.0,                   help="temperature; 'inf' = behavior cloning")    p.add_argument("--max-weight", type=float, default=20.0, help="cap on w_i; 0 = no cap")    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)    p.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=30)    p.add_argument("--eval-episodes", type=int, default=100)    p.add_argument("--dataset", default=str(DATA / "rover_offline.npz"))    a = p.parse_args()    ensure_dirs()    run(a.beta, a.max_weight, a.seed, a.epochs, a.eval_episodes, a.dataset)​​if __name__ == "__main__":    main()

Two argparse details. type=float accepts the string inf, because Python’s float("inf") is infinity, so --beta inf reaches math.isinf as you want. And argparse turns the flag --max-weight into the attribute a.max_weight, dash replaced by underscore.

Run it
python lab2_awr.py --beta inf

Behavior cloning, seed 0, 30 epochs, scored on 100 episodes. One run took about 10–25 seconds on the reference machine.

What you should see
bc seed 0: 182,658 samples, ESS 100.0% of the data, top 1% of samples carry 1.0% of the weight  epoch   0  weighted NLL 2.0921  std [0.691 0.68 ]  epoch  10  weighted NLL 2.0813  std [0.688 0.682]  epoch  20  weighted NLL 2.0809  std [0.692 0.679]  epoch  29  weighted NLL 2.0808  std [0.689 0.676]  success 23% [16%, 32%]  crash 15%  timeout 62%  return -55.7 [-85.4, -26.0]   (NN s)

NN stands for the run’s wall-clock time in seconds, which depends on your machine and on what else it is doing; expect something in the 10–25 s range. The other numbers depend on which checkpoint recorded your file (Section L2.3.6).

L2.5.4 How to read the BC run

The first line confirms that every step counts the same: the effective sample size is 100% of the data, and the top 1% of steps (1,826 of them) carry 1.0% of the total weight, as they must when every weight is equal.

The loss barely moves. It goes from 2.0921 in the first epoch to 2.0808 in the last. Is something broken? No, and you can check why with the formula from Section L2.4.3. If the recorded actions really were spread around the policy’s mean like a Gaussian with the learned standard deviation, the average of \(z^2\) would be 1, and the average negative log-likelihood per wheel would be \(\tfrac{1}{2} + \log\sigma + \tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)\). With the final standard deviations that is:

wheel 1:  0.5 + log(0.689) + 0.918939 = 0.5 - 0.3725 + 0.918939 = 1.0464wheel 2:  0.5 + log(0.676) + 0.918939 = 0.5 - 0.3916 + 0.918939 = 1.0274sum                                                             = 2.0738

That is within 0.01 of the printed 2.0808. The small gap has two measured causes. First, the learned \(\sigma\) sits a hair below the actual root-mean-square distance of the recorded actions from BC’s mean (0.6890 against 0.6903 on the first wheel, 0.6763 against 0.6791 on the second), so the average of \(z^2\) is 1.004 and 1.008 rather than exactly 1. Second, the printed loss is an average over the last epoch, taken while the weights were still moving; the loss over the whole file at the end of training is 2.0803.

The lesson: almost the entire loss is set by how spread out the recorded actions are around the mean this network learns. Most of that spread is the collector’s own sampling noise (a standard deviation of about 0.93 per wheel, then clipped, as Section L2.5.5 shows), and no network can predict noise from the observation. All 29 epochs of learning after the first one moved the loss by about 0.01. Never judge these policies by their training loss; score them.

The standard deviation started at 0.607 and is already about 0.69 per wheel after the first epoch. By the argument at the end of Section L2.4.4, that is the typical distance of the recorded actions from BC’s mean. The policy does not use its standard deviation when scored, but the number tells you how noisy the file is.

The score: 23% success, 95% interval [16%, 32%], 15% crashes, 62% timeouts, mean return −55.7. The sweep in Section L2.8 will give seeds 1 and 2 as well: 24% and 25%, and 24.0% pooled over the 300 episodes, with interval [20%, 29%]. BC on this file is a steady, cautious, mostly timing-out driver.

L2.5.5 The surprise: BC scores below the policy it copied

The sweep also scores the collector itself on the same 100 evaluation episodes:

collector, deterministic: success 33% [25%, 43%]  crash 12%  timeout 55%  return -39.0 [-70.8, -7.1]collector, stochastic:    success 17% [11%, 26%]  crash 38%  timeout 45%  return -74.5 [-96.4, -52.6]

BC beats the collector’s sampled driving (24% against 17%). That part is expected: BC is scored by its mean action, so it drops the collector’s noise. But BC is below the collector’s mean action, 24% against 33%. That part is strange. BC learns to imitate the collector, and it is scored by its mean; shouldn’t its mean end up near the collector’s mean, and its score near 33%?

Be careful with the numbers first. The collector was scored on only 100 episodes, and its interval [25%, 43%] overlaps BC’s pooled interval [20%, 29%] a little, between 25% and 29%. The gap alone is suggestive, not conclusive. What makes it credible is that we found the mechanism, and the mechanism is the clipping line from Section L2.3.2.

Here is the clue. At the 100k checkpoint, the collector’s Gaussian has a standard deviation of about 0.93 per wheel, inside an action box that is only 2 wide, from −1 to +1. A bell that wide lands outside the box often, and every such sample is recorded as exactly −1 or +1. Measured on the file: about 30.5% of one wheel’s logged actions and 30.2% of the other’s sit exactly at \(\pm 1\).

Now see what clipping does to an average, with made-up teaching numbers. Say that at one state the collector’s mean for a wheel is 0.6, and five of its samples there are the mean plus \(-1.2, -0.6, 0, +0.6, +1.2\):

intended samples:   -0.6   0.0   0.6   1.2   1.8     average = 3.0 / 5 = 0.6recorded (clipped): -0.6   0.0   0.6   1.0   1.0     average = 2.0 / 5 = 0.4

The collector meant 0.6 on average. The file says 0.4. BC fits the file, so its mean lands near 0.4, and when you score BC by its mean it drives that wheel at 0.4 where the collector would have driven 0.6. Why toward zero? When the mean is positive, the upper edge of the box is closer than the lower one, so more of the upper side of the bell gets cut off than of the lower side. The same happens in mirror image for a negative mean. Only a mean of exactly zero is left alone.

The measurements on the real policies match that story on every count:

  • On the same states, BC’s mean action has an average size of 0.14 and 0.17 (first and second wheel), against 0.21 and 0.24 for the collector’s mean action. BC’s driving is smaller.
  • Averaged over the file, BC’s mean action on the first wheel is 0.113, almost exactly the average recorded action on that wheel (0.115). The collector’s own mean action on that wheel averages 0.164 (0.143 on the other). BC matched the file, not the collector.
  • None of the collector’s mean actions lie outside \([-1, 1]\). The shrinkage comes from clipping the wide samples, not the means.
  • BC’s learned standard deviation, 0.69 and 0.68, is well below the collector’s 0.93. That is consistent with clipping, which squeezes the recorded values closer together than the samples that produced them.
  • A driver with smaller wheel commands takes longer to get anywhere: BC times out in 62% of episodes, against 55% for the collector’s mean action.
Try it yourself first

Do not take these measurements on trust; they take one short session to repeat. Start python in your lab folder, after your BC run has saved results/lab2/bc_s0.pt:

import numpy as np, torchfrom stable_baselines3 import PPOfrom common import GaussianPolicyd = np.load("data/rover_offline.npz")obs, act = torch.as_tensor(d["obs"]), d["act"]# share of each wheel's actions at exactly +-1print((np.abs(act) == 1.0).mean(axis=0))pol = GaussianPolicy()pol.load_state_dict(torch.load("results/lab2/bc_s0.pt"))ppo = PPO.load("runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/ppo_100000_steps.zip", device="cpu")with torch.no_grad():    bc_mean = pol.mean_net(obs).numpy()    coll = ppo.policy.get_distribution(obs).distribution    # the collector's Gaussian    coll_mean = coll.mean.numpy()# average size of the mean actionprint(np.abs(bc_mean).mean(0), np.abs(coll_mean).mean(0))# average mean action vs recordedprint(bc_mean.mean(0), act.mean(0), coll_mean.mean(0))# learned widthsprint(pol.log_std.exp(), coll.stddev[0])

With the answer key’s file, the lines show about 0.305 and 0.302; sizes 0.141 and 0.169 for BC against 0.211 and 0.244; averages 0.113 (BC), 0.115 (recorded) and 0.164 (collector) on the first wheel; widths 0.689 and 0.676 against 0.942 and 0.923.

So BC did its job perfectly. It imitated the file. The file is not the collector.

An analogy. You learn a song from a recording made on a microphone that flattens every note louder than its limit. You copy the recording faithfully, and your loud passages come out quieter than the singer’s. Where the analogy breaks down: a trained ear can hear clipping as distortion and guess the missing peaks. Nothing in the file lets BC do that: a recorded +1 that was “really” 1.8 looks exactly like a deliberate full-speed command, so the loss has no way to tell them apart.

Keep this in mind for the rest of the lab: AWR trains on exactly the same clipped actions. Whatever it gains over BC, it gains with this same file.

Pitfalls

“BC equals the collector.” BC equals the recorded data. Anything that distorts the recording on the way to disk (clipping, action delays, logging a command instead of what the actuator did) shows up in the clone. On a real robot, check what your log actually stores.

Reading the loss as a score. A training loss of 2.08 against 2.07 says almost nothing about driving. Only the evaluation episodes do.

L2.6 Step 5: the weights

L2.6.1 From “how good” to “how loud”

BC’s ceiling is that every recorded action counts the same. You now have, for each logged step, an advantage \(\hat{A}_i\) that says how much better or worse than usual things went from there. The goal of this step is to turn that number into a volume knob: better steps louder, worse steps quieter.

The obvious first try is to keep only the steps with a positive advantage and clone those. That is a real method, filtered BC, and book Section 4.4.1 lists what is crude about it: the threshold is arbitrary, every step is either fully in or fully out, and a step twice as good as another gets exactly the same treatment. Hold on to that name; you will meet filtered BC again, unexpectedly, in Section L2.9.

The obvious second try is a weight proportional to the advantage. But then a below-average step gets a negative weight, which pushes the policy away from a recorded action, toward some action nobody recorded, which is exactly where an offline method should not go.

Book Section 4.4.3 settles the question without guessing. It asks for the policy with the highest expected advantage that still stays close to the data. Closeness is measured by a KL divergence, a standard measure of how different two probability distributions are (zero when they are identical). The book then solves that problem by hand, and the answer is a target policy:

\[ \pi^*(a \mid s) \;\propto\; \pi_\beta(a \mid s)\, \exp\!\big( A^{\pi_\beta}(s,a) / \beta \big) \]
In plain words

\(\pi^*\) is the best policy that stays close to the data; the star means “the solution”, not a network. \(\pi_\beta(a \mid s)\) is the behavior policy: how likely the collector was to take action \(a\) at state \(s\). \(A^{\pi_\beta}(s,a)\) is the behavior policy’s advantage, which your \(\hat{A}\) estimates. \(\beta \gt 0\) is the temperature. Watch the clash: the subscript in \(\pi_\beta\) names the behavior policy, not the temperature; the clash is standard. \(\exp(\cdot)\) is always positive: above 1 for an above-average action, below 1 for a below-average one. The \(\propto\) (“proportional to”) means the right side is still divided by a normalizing constant, one number per state, so that the probabilities add up to 1. Where the collector never acted, \(\pi_\beta = 0\), so \(\pi^* = 0\) too: the formula reweights; it never invents.

How does that help you? You do not have \(\pi_\beta\) as a formula; you have samples of it, the logged actions. Now look at the ratio of the two policies: \(\pi^* / \pi_\beta\) is exactly the exponential factor \(\exp(\hat{A}/\beta)\), divided by the normalizing constant. So if you give each logged action the weight \(\exp(\hat{A}/\beta)\), the weighted samples behave, in effect, like samples of \(\pi^*\). Maximizing the weighted log-likelihood then fits your network to \(\pi^*\), just as plain BC fits it to \(\pi_\beta\). Book Section 4.4.4 does this change of measure step by step.

That is the answer to “why should cloning logged actions ever beat the collector?”. BC aims at the collector. AWR aims at a tilted version of the collector that favors its better actions, built only from actions the collector really took.

It also says what \(\beta\) prices. A small \(\beta\) makes the tilt sharp and allows the new policy to move far away from the data. A large \(\beta\) keeps it close. At \(\beta = \infty\) the tilt disappears, \(\pi^* = \pi_\beta\), and you are back at BC. Formally \(\beta\) is the Lagrange multiplier of the closeness constraint: the price paid per unit of distance from the data. Section 4.4.3 derives that, and it is also where “why an exponential?” stops bothering you. This lab takes the result as given.

In short, each recorded action’s weight is \(e\) raised to its advantage divided by the temperature. An exponential is always positive, so no step is ever pushed away. And it grows smoothly with the advantage, so better steps get more say. The code adds two practical changes to the textbook weight: it standardizes the advantage first, and it caps the weight. Here is the weight exactly as lab2_awr.py computes it:

\[ \begin{aligned} \tilde{A}_i &= \frac{\hat{A}_i - \operatorname{mean}(\hat{A})}{\operatorname{std}(\hat{A})} \\[4pt] w_i &= \min\!\Big( \exp\big( \tilde{A}_i / \beta \big),\; w_{\max} \Big) \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

\(i\) indexes one logged step. \(\hat{A}_i = G_i - V(s_i)\) is its advantage from Section L2.3. \(\operatorname{mean}(\hat{A})\) and \(\operatorname{std}(\hat{A})\) are the average and standard deviation over all 182,658 steps, so \(\tilde{A}_i\) (A-tilde) is the standardized advantage: how many standard deviations above or below average this step was. \(\beta \gt 0\) is the temperature. It divides before the exponential, so a small \(\beta\) makes differences explode and a large one flattens them; at \(\beta = \infty\) every weight is \(e^0 = 1\), which is BC. (As in the previous box, this \(\beta\) is not the subscript of \(\pi_\beta\).) \(w_{\max}\) is the cap, 20 by default, set with --max-weight; --max-weight 0 removes the \(\min\). Finally the code divides every weight by their average, so the weights average exactly 1.

L2.6.2 Why standardize first

Try the exponential on the raw advantages and watch what happens. The raw \(\hat{A}\) on your file has a standard deviation of 35.4. At \(\beta = 1\), a step at the 90th percentile (\(\hat{A} = +29.5\)) would get \(e^{29.5} \approx 6.5 \times 10^{12}\), and a step at the 10th percentile (\(\hat{A} = -56.6\)) would get \(e^{-56.6} \approx 2.6 \times 10^{-25}\). Every weight is either astronomically large or indistinguishable from zero. To get a sane spread you would need \(\beta\) near 35, and on another dataset with a different reward scale you would need a different number. Book Section 4.4.5’s pitfall box warns about exactly this.

Standardize first, and the same two steps become:

90th percentile:  (29.5 - (-0.59)) / 35.4 =  30.09 / 35.4 =  0.85   ->  exp( 0.85) = 2.3410th percentile: (-56.6 - (-0.59)) / 35.4 = -56.01 / 35.4 = -1.58   ->  exp(-1.58) = 0.206

At \(\beta = 1\) the good step now counts about \(2.34 / 0.206 \approx 11\) times as much as the bad one. That is a strong preference, not an absurd one.

Notice the skew from Section L2.3.6 at work here. The 90th percentile lands only 0.85 standard deviations above the mean, while the 10th percentile lands 1.58 below it: the long tail is on the negative side. And because most advantages are moderately positive, 65% of the steps have a standardized advantage above zero. Keep that 65% in mind; it decides how many steps can reach the cap when \(\beta\) gets small.

Standardizing also gives \(\beta\) a meaning that travels between datasets. A step one standard deviation above average gets \(e^{1/\beta}\) times the weight of an average step: at \(\beta = 3\) that is \(e^{0.333} \approx 1.40\), at \(\beta = 1\) it is \(e^{1} \approx 2.72\), and at \(\beta = 0.3\) it is \(e^{3.33} \approx 28\). The cap binds when \(\tilde{A}_i / \beta\) exceeds \(\log 20 \approx 3.0\), that is, for steps more than \(3.0\beta\) standard deviations above average. On your file that is 0.5% of steps at \(\beta = 1\), 9% at \(\beta = 0.3\), 42% at \(\beta = 0.1\), and 60% at \(\beta = 0.03\). Those last two numbers are the key to Section L2.9.

Of the two operations, dividing by the standard deviation is the one that matters for \(\beta\): it sets the scale on which \(\beta\) is measured. Subtracting the mean only multiplies every weight by the same constant, which the final rescaling removes; it matters only for deciding which steps reach the cap.

L2.6.3 The code

Now replace the ... placeholder in awr_weights. Here is the complete function; the new lines are the else: branch.

def awr_weights(adv: np.ndarray, beta: float, max_weight: float):    """One weight per sample, plus the diagnostics that tell you if beta is sane.​    Returns (weights, info). Weights are float64: exp(5 / 0.05) = exp(100) is a    fine float64 but overflows float32 (whose largest value is about exp(88.7)).    """    adv_std = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)       # zero mean, unit spread    if math.isinf(beta):        w = np.ones_like(adv_std, dtype=np.float64)    else:        log_w = adv_std.astype(np.float64) / beta        if max_weight > 0:            log_w = np.minimum(log_w, math.log(max_weight))   # the cap, applied in log space        # Only RATIOS between weights matter (the loss divides by their mean), so        # subtracting the largest log-weight changes nothing except avoiding overflow.        w = np.exp(log_w - log_w.max())    ess = w.sum() ** 2 / (w ** 2).sum()                      # effective sample size    info = {        "ess": float(ess),        "ess_fraction": float(ess / len(w)),        "fraction_at_cap": (float(np.isclose(w, w.max()).mean())                            if not math.isinf(beta) else 0.0),        "top1pct_weight_share": float(np.sort(w)[-max(1, len(w) // 100):].sum() / w.sum()),    }    return w / w.mean(), info                                # rescale so the mean weight is 1

Line by line:

adv_std is \(\tilde{A}\). The + 1e-8 guards against dividing by zero if every advantage were identical.

log_w = adv_std.astype(np.float64) / beta is the exponent, \(\tilde{A}_i / \beta\), before any exponential is taken.

The cap, in log space. \(\min(e^{x}, 20)\) and \(e^{\min(x,\, \log 20)}\) are the same number, because \(e^x\) only ever increases with \(x\). Capping the exponent means the huge value \(e^{x}\) is never computed at all.

np.exp(log_w - log_w.max()). Subtracting the same number \(m\) from every exponent multiplies every weight by the same factor \(e^{-m}\), so the ratios between weights do not change: \(e^{x-m} / e^{y-m} = e^{x} / e^{y}\). The largest weight becomes exactly \(e^0 = 1\), and nothing can exceed it, so nothing can overflow. The division by w.mean() at the end then sets the scale you actually want.

Why float64 as well. The docstring gives the reason: \(e^{100}\) fits in a 64-bit float but overflows a 32-bit one, whose largest value is about \(e^{88.7}\). And the effective sample size squares the weights, which doubles the exponent. We checked what happens with neither defense: computing the uncapped weights directly as \(e^{\tilde{A}/\beta}\) in float32, the effective sample size comes out as nan at \(\beta = 0.05\) and \(\beta = 0.03\), while float64 gives about 2.8 and 1.4. On this file either defense alone would be enough; together they keep the function safe for any \(\beta\) you type.

L2.6.4 Effective sample size

Once weights differ, “how much data am I training on?” no longer has the obvious answer of 182,658. A step with weight 0.0001 is technically in the loss but contributes almost nothing. You need a number that says how many equally weighted steps your weighted file is worth. That number is the effective sample size:

\[ \mathrm{ESS} \;=\; \frac{\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\Big)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i^{2}} \]
In plain words

\(N\) is the number of logged steps, 182,658, and \(w_i\) is step \(i\)’s weight. The top is the square of the total weight; the bottom adds up the squares of the individual weights. If all \(N\) weights are equal to some \(c\), the top is \((Nc)^2\), the bottom is \(Nc^2\), and ESS \(= N\): every step counts. If one weight is positive and all others are zero, top and bottom are both that weight squared and ESS \(= 1\): one step is the whole training set. Everything else lies in between. Multiplying all weights by the same number cancels, so it does not matter whether ESS is computed before or after the rescaling to mean 1. The code also reports it as a fraction of \(N\), ess_fraction.

An analogy. A class of 30 students votes on a field trip, but a strange rule gives one student’s ballot 1,000 votes. There are 30 ballots and, in effect, one voter. The effective sample size counts voters, not ballots. Where the analogy breaks down: the formula treats every step as an independent opinion. Steps from the same episode are not independent: they share the obstacle layout, the start and the ending. So even 60,000 “effective” steps carry far fewer independent pieces of evidence than the number suggests. Section L2.10 measures how strongly steps within an episode move together.

The other two diagnostics in info are easy to read. fraction_at_cap is the fraction of steps tied for the largest weight: with the cap in place those are the steps sitting at the cap; without a cap it is normally a single step, 1 out of 182,658. top1pct_weight_share sorts the weights, adds up the largest 1% of them (1,826 steps), and divides by the total. For BC it prints as 1.0%: 1,826 of 182,658 steps is a hair under 1%, and with equal weights their share of the weight is the same. If it approaches 100%, a handful of steps own the training signal.

L2.6.5 A worked example: four steps, three settings

These numbers are a toy, chosen for hand calculation, and they are already standardized. Imagine four steps picked out of a large file, whose standardized advantages happen to be \(+2\), \(+0.5\), \(0\) and \(-1\). Work straight from those values; do not standardize them again. (The Try-it box at the end of this subsection explains why that matters when you check the numbers with your code.)

At \(\beta = 1\), the weight is just \(e^{\tilde{A}}\):

weights:   exp(2) = 7.389056   exp(0.5) = 1.648721   exp(0) = 1   exp(-1) = 0.367879sum:       7.389056 + 1.648721 + 1 + 0.367879 = 10.405656shares:    71.0%    15.8%    9.6%    3.5%mean-1:    divide by 10.405656 / 4 = 2.601414  ->  2.8404   0.6338   0.3844   0.1414sum of squares: 54.598150 + 2.718282 + 1 + 0.135335 = 58.451767ESS = 10.405656^2 / 58.451767 = 108.277677 / 58.451767 = 1.852   (of 4, 46%)

Nothing is thrown away: the worst step still has 3.5% of the say. But four steps are worth about 1.85 equally weighted ones.

At \(\beta = 0.1\) with the cap at 20, divide each advantage by 0.1 before exponentiating:

exponents: 2/0.1 = 20     0.5/0.1 = 5     0/0.1 = 0     -1/0.1 = -10exp:       4.85e8         148.41          1             4.54e-5capped:    20             20              1             4.54e-5sum of weights:  41.0000454sum of squares:  400 + 400 + 1 + (tiny) = 801.0000ESS = 41.0000454^2 / 801.000 = 1681.004 / 801.000 = 2.099   (of 4, 52%)

Look at that carefully, because it is the surprise of this lab in miniature. The temperature went down, which should make the weights more extreme, yet the effective sample size went up, from 1.852 to 2.099. The cap flattened the top two steps to the same weight, and two equal weights share the load. The worst step is now effectively gone. What is left is “clone the two good steps, equally, and ignore the rest”: filtered BC.

At \(\beta = 0.1\) without the cap, the weights stay \(4.85 \times 10^{8}\), 148.41, 1 and \(4.54 \times 10^{-5}\). The first is more than three million times the second. ESS \(\approx 1.000\): one step owns everything. That is the book’s dead data: a file full of steps that no longer contribute anything.

So lowering \(\beta\) leads to one of two very different places, depending on a single flag. With the cap, the weights become two-level (at the cap, or nearly zero). Without it, a single winner takes all. Section L2.9 shows both on the real file.

Try it yourself first

Check the three ESS values with NumPy. Do not feed the four numbers to your awr_weights. It standardizes its input again, and these four have a mean of 0.375 and a standard deviation of about 1.08, not 0 and 1. You would get an ESS of 1.981 at \(\beta = 1\) and 1.313 at \(\beta = 0.1\) with the cap, and wrongly conclude that your function or the lesson is broken. Apply the formula directly instead:

import numpy as npz = np.array([2, 0.5, 0, -1.])               # already standardizedfor w in [np.exp(z / 1.0), np.minimum(np.exp(z / 0.1), 20), np.exp(z / 0.1)]:    print(w.sum() ** 2 / (w ** 2).sum())

It should print about 1.852, 2.099 and 1.000 (the last as 1.0000006…).

L2.7 Step 6: the training loop with weights

L2.7.1 One line changed

You already wrote the loop. For AWR, nothing in it changes except the numbers inside w. The loss it minimizes is:

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AWR}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{i \in B} w_i \Bigl( -\log \pi_\theta(a_i \mid s_i) \Bigr) \\[4pt] \text{with}\quad \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_j = 1 \end{gathered} \]
In plain words

This is the BC loss with one multiplier per step. \(B\), \(|B|\), \(i\), \(s_i\), \(a_i\) and \(\pi_\theta\) mean what they meant in Section L2.5.1. \(w_i\) is step \(i\)’s weight from Section L2.6. The second line says the weights are rescaled so that their average over the whole file, all \(N = 182{,}658\) steps indexed by \(j\), is exactly 1. A step with \(w_i = 2.84\) pulls the policy toward its recorded action 2.84 times as hard as an average step; a step with \(w_i = 0.14\) pulls at about a seventh of the usual strength. No step pushes the policy away.

These are the lines of train_policy that carry it:

            idx = perm[start:start + batch_size]            # -log pi(a_i | s_i), one per sample            nll = -policy.log_prob(obs[idx], act[idx])            loss = (w[idx] * nll).mean()

The gradient of that loss is a weighted average of each step’s own gradient. Section L2.4.4 showed what each step’s gradient does: it pulls the mean toward the recorded action and adjusts the width. So a heavy step drags the mean toward its action harder, and a light one barely moves it. That is the whole mechanism by which AWR prefers good actions over bad ones.

L2.7.2 Why the weights average to 1, and why not per batch

There are two reasons to rescale the weights to an average of 1 over the file, and one thing the rescaling does not do.

A loss on BC’s scale. Before the rescaling, the overall size of the weights is arbitrary. The overflow trick in awr_weights sets the largest weight to exactly 1, so the average weight, and with it the printed loss, would shrink or grow by large factors from one \(\beta\) to the next. With mean-1 weights, the printed weighted NLL stays in the same range as BC’s (2.0694 for the \(\beta = 1\) run of Section L2.8.1, against 2.0808 for BC), so a glance at the log tells you training is sane. As the end of this section explains, the two numbers are still not comparable as measures of quality.

An honest minibatch. The loss you really care about is the weighted average over the whole file:

\[ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j} w_j \,\bigl(-\log \pi_\theta(a_j \mid s_j)\bigr) \]

A random minibatch average of \(w_i \cdot \text{nll}_i\) is an unbiased estimate of it: over many random minibatches it averages out to exactly that number. Some minibatches happen to hold heavy steps and pull hard; others hold light steps and pull gently. That variation is correct. It is how the heavy steps get more say.

You may notice that the docstring at the top of the reference lab2_awr.py writes a normalized loss:

\[ -\sum_i w_i \log \pi(a_i \mid s_i) \Big/ \sum_i w_i \]

Mean-1 weights sum to \(N\), so over the whole file that normalized loss and the average above are the same number. That is what mean 1 buys: the minibatch average is an unbiased estimate of exactly the docstring’s loss. The two forms differ only if you apply the normalization inside a single minibatch, and that difference is the pitfall below.

What rescaling does not change: the step size. You might expect that multiplying every weight by 1,000 would make every update 1,000 times larger. With plain gradient descent it would. But this lab uses Adam, which divides each update by a running estimate of the gradient’s recent size. An overall factor on the weights scales the gradient and that running estimate alike, so it mostly cancels. What Adam cannot cancel is a factor that changes from one minibatch to the next, which is why the pitfall below still matters. Mean 1 is about a readable loss and about which loss the minibatch estimates, not about the learning rate.

Pitfall

Dividing each minibatch by its own weight sum. It looks like tidy normalization, and it silently changes the algorithm. A toy with made-up numbers: a minibatch of four steps, each with weight 0.01 and negative log-likelihood 2.0.

mean of w * nll:          (4 x 0.01 x 2.0) / 4 = 0.08 / 4    = 0.02sum(w * nll) / sum(w):    (4 x 0.01 x 2.0) / (4 x 0.01)       = 0.08 / 0.04 = 2.0

The second form gives these four bad steps 100 times the pull the weights intended: full BC strength. At small \(\beta\) without a cap, the weight sits on a few dozen steps, so nearly every minibatch contains none of them, only weights far below 1. Per-batch normalization would make each batch’s own best step its whole training signal, a different and much noisier algorithm.

Two more things to know before you run it. First, the “weighted NLL” printed during training is an average of weighted terms, so it is not comparable across different \(\beta\): a lower number at \(\beta = 1\) than for BC does not mean a better policy. Second, there is another way to apply the same weights: leave the loss unweighted and instead draw each step with probability proportional to its weight. Book Section 4.6.3 explains why that version matters for large networks, and notes that on a small MLP the difference does not matter. This lab weights the loss.

L2.8 Step 7: one AWR run, then the sweep

L2.8.1 One run

With the else: branch of awr_weights written, the same script does AWR. Start with the temperature the book calls typical, \(\beta = 1\), with the default cap of 20.

Run it
python lab2_awr.py --beta 1.0

About 10–25 seconds, like the BC run.

What you should see
awr_b1 seed 0: 182,658 samples, ESS 32.9% of the data, top 1% of samples carry 11.7% of the weight  epoch   0  weighted NLL 2.0836  std [0.686 0.678]  epoch  10  weighted NLL 2.0704  std [0.684 0.679]  epoch  20  weighted NLL 2.0697  std [0.683 0.675]  epoch  29  weighted NLL 2.0694  std [0.685 0.673]  success 38% [29%, 48%]  crash 22%  timeout 40%  return -20.1 [-46.6, 6.4]   (NN s)

As before, NN is the wall-clock time in seconds on your machine.

The weights. The effective sample size is 32.9% of the file, about 60,065 equally weighted steps out of 182,658. The top 1% of steps carry 11.7% of the total weight, against 1.0% for BC. The weighting is strong but far from a takeover.

The loss and the width. The weighted NLL is lower than BC’s, but as Section L2.7.2 warned, that comparison means nothing: the average now leans toward the heavy steps. The learned standard deviations, about 0.685 and 0.673, are close to BC’s.

The score. 38% success [29%, 48%], 22% crashes, 40% timeouts, mean return −20.1. Seed 0 of BC scored 23% [16%, 32%], 15% crashes, 62% timeouts, mean return −55.7. That looks like a clear win, and it is tempting to stop here.

Don’t, for two reasons. The two intervals still overlap, between 29% and 32%. And this is one seed at one temperature. Appendix B’s Rule two says it plainly: a single-seed RL result is noise wearing the costume of a finding. The lab’s question also asked what \(\beta\) does, which one run cannot answer. You need the sweep.

L2.8.2 Optional: run the pilot yourself

Section L2.2.4 told you about the pilot that chose the 100k collector, before you had the scripts to run it. Now you have them. Repeating the pilot matters most if you recorded from checkpoints of your own Lab 1 run, because those may not behave like ours. It is also cheap: one extra recording and six more training runs of 10–25 seconds each, on top of the two you have already done.

There is one trap to know about first, because it bit the answer key itself.

Pitfall

Output names ignore the dataset. run names its files only by \(\beta\), cap and seed, for example results/lab2/bc_s0.json. A run on a second dataset silently overwrites the file from the first. And lab2_plot.py pools every *_s*.json it finds in results/lab2/, whatever produced it. The answer key’s results/pilot/lab2_candidates/ shows the damage: it holds BC and \(\beta = 1\) from the 200k data (58% and 60%) next to \(\beta = 0.3\) and 0.1 from the 100k data (43% and 30%). So move each candidate’s results into a folder of their own before running the next candidate, and make sure results/lab2/ is empty before the sweep.

Run it
# candidate 1: the 100k file you already recorded (BC and beta = 1 are done)python lab2_awr.py --beta 0.3python lab2_awr.py --beta 0.1mkdir -p results/pilot/cand_100k && mv results/lab2/* results/pilot/cand_100k/​# candidate 2: the 200k checkpoint, recorded into a file of its ownpython lab2_collect.py --checkpoint runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/ppo_200000_steps.zip \    --out data/cand_200k.npzpython lab2_awr.py --beta inf --dataset data/cand_200k.npzpython lab2_awr.py --beta 1.0 --dataset data/cand_200k.npzpython lab2_awr.py --beta 0.3 --dataset data/cand_200k.npzpython lab2_awr.py --beta 0.1 --dataset data/cand_200k.npzmkdir -p results/pilot/cand_200k && mv results/lab2/* results/pilot/cand_200k/

The --out flag keeps the second recording from overwriting data/rover_offline.npz. Its summary goes next to it, as data/cand_200k_summary.json.

What you should see

Each training run prints the same kind of lines as before; compare the final success line of each with the pilot table in Section L2.2.4. With the answer key’s checkpoints:

  • the 100k runs give 23%, 38%, 43% and 30% for BC and \(\beta = 1\), 0.3 and 0.1 (they are the same seed-0 runs the sweep repeats);
  • the 200k runs give 58%, 60%, 61% and 58%;
  • the 200k recording reports 134,526 steps, goal, crash and timeout shares of 47%, 33.4% and 19.6%, and an advantage mean of +8.5 with a standard deviation of 40.8.

Read the two sets of numbers the way Section L2.2.4 did. Four scores within a few points of each other, with 100 episodes each (±10 points), say that this setup cannot resolve a difference. A spread like 23% to 43% says there is room for weighting to show what it does.

If your own checkpoints lead the pilot to a different collector, record data/rover_offline.npz again from that checkpoint before the sweep, and pass the same checkpoint to lab2_sweep.py below. Then run ls results/lab2 before the sweep and check that it prints nothing. (If you skipped the pilot, the BC and \(\beta = 1\) files from your single runs can stay: the sweep overwrites them with identical ones. Any other run left in that folder, such as a \(\beta\) you tried on your own, would be pooled into the summary.)

L2.8.3 The sweep script

The sweep answers three questions at once: does weighting beat cloning on the same data; what does \(\beta\) do to the weights; and what happens as \(\beta\) goes toward zero, with the cap and without it. It also scores the collector on the same 100 evaluation episodes, because “AWR beat BC” means little until you know where both stand against the policy that produced the data.

Create lab2_sweep.py. The first chunk defines the grid and the two kinds of job.

import osos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""  # CPU only. Must run before torch is imported​import argparseimport mathfrom concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor​import torchfrom stable_baselines3 import PPO​from common import DATA, RESULTS, ensure_dirs, evaluate, fmt_eval, save_json, sb3_act_fnfrom lab2_awr import run​BETAS = [math.inf, 3.0, 1.0, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03]      # inf first: behavior cloningNO_CAP_BETAS = [1.0, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03]             # the same, with the weight cap removedSEEDS = [0, 1, 2]
def job(args):    beta, max_weight, seed = args    r = run(beta, max_weight, seed, epochs=30, eval_episodes=100,            dataset=str(DATA / "rover_offline.npz"), quiet=True)    return r["name"], seed, r["weights"]["ess_fraction"], r["eval"]​​def score_collector(path):    torch.set_num_threads(1)    model = PPO.load(path, device="cpu")    return {"deterministic": evaluate(sb3_act_fn(model, True), 100),            "stochastic": evaluate(sb3_act_fn(model, False), 100)}

The grid. The temperatures step down by roughly a factor of 3 each time: 3, 1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03. Spacing them by factors rather than by equal differences suits a knob that acts by division inside an exponential; 0.1 and 0.03 are as different as 1 and 0.3. The uncapped list starts at \(\beta = 1\) for a reason you can check in a Python shell: the largest standardized advantage on the file is 3.83, so at \(\beta = 3\) the largest exponent is \(3.83 / 3 \approx 1.28\), far below the cap’s \(\log 20 \approx 3.0\). The cap never binds at \(\beta = 3\), so an uncapped \(\beta = 3\) run would be the same run twice. And BC has no weights to cap.

from lab2_awr import run reuses your function unchanged. This import is where the if __name__ == "__main__": guard in lab2_awr.py earns its keep: importing the file defines run without starting a run.

job runs one setting quietly and returns only what the progress line needs. score_collector loads the collector and scores it both ways on the same 100 evaluation seeds every trained policy faces.

def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--checkpoint", required=True,                   help="the collector used in lab2_collect.py")    p.add_argument("--parallel", type=int, default=10)    a = p.parse_args()    ensure_dirs()​    jobs = ([(b, 20.0, s) for b in BETAS for s in SEEDS]            + [(b, 0.0, s) for b in NO_CAP_BETAS for s in SEEDS])    with ProcessPoolExecutor(a.parallel) as pool:        collector = pool.submit(score_collector, a.checkpoint)        for name, seed, ess, ev in pool.map(job, jobs):            print(f"{name:<16} seed {seed}  ESS {ess:6.1%}  {fmt_eval(ev)}")        collector = collector.result()    save_json({"checkpoint": a.checkpoint, **collector},              RESULTS / "lab2" / "collector_eval.json")    print(f"\ncollector, deterministic: {fmt_eval(collector['deterministic'])}")    print(f"collector, stochastic:    {fmt_eval(collector['stochastic'])}")​​if __name__ == "__main__":    main()

The job list has \(6 \times 3 = 18\) capped runs (BC included) and \(4 \times 3 = 12\) uncapped runs: 30 runs. pool.submit starts the collector’s scoring right away, as one more task in the same pool. pool.map hands out the 30 jobs and gives back their results in job order, so the printed lines come out in the order of the list even though the runs finish in whatever order they like. collector.result() waits for the collector if it is still going. Each worker uses one thread (run calls torch.set_num_threads(1)), so 10 workers fit on a 12-core machine.

Run it
python lab2_sweep.py --checkpoint runs/baseline_s0/checkpoints/ppo_100000_steps.zip

30 training runs plus the collector’s scoring, 10 at a time. The full sweep took about 2 minutes on the reference machine. If you skipped the pilot, it overwrites the bc_s0 and awr_b1_s0 files from your single runs with identical ones.

What you should see
bc               seed 0  ESS 100.0%  success 23% [16%, 32%]  crash 15%  timeout 62%  return -55.7 [-85.4, -26.0]bc               seed 1  ESS 100.0%  success 24% [17%, 33%]  crash 8%  timeout 68%  return -64.3 [-96.6, -31.9]bc               seed 2  ESS 100.0%  success 25% [18%, 34%]  crash 18%  timeout 57%  return -58.7 [-90.2, -27.1]awr_b3           seed 0  ESS  90.2%  success 26% [18%, 35%]  crash 13%  timeout 61%  return -56.4 [-88.1, -24.7]...awr_b1           seed 0  ESS  32.9%  success 38% [29%, 48%]  crash 22%  timeout 40%  return -20.1 [-46.6, 6.4]awr_b1           seed 1  ESS  32.9%  success 31% [23%, 41%]  crash 19%  timeout 50%  return -48.7 [-80.2, -17.2]awr_b1           seed 2  ESS  32.9%  success 41% [32%, 51%]  crash 25%  timeout 34%  return -28.5 [-57.0, -0.1]awr_b0.3         seed 0  ESS  35.7%  success 43% [34%, 53%]  crash 21%  timeout 36%  return -17.4 [-46.7, 11.9]...awr_b0.03        seed 2  ESS  62.4%  success 27% [19%, 36%]  crash 17%  timeout 56%  return -53.4 [-84.5, -22.3]awr_b1_nocap     seed 0  ESS  30.0%  success 41% [32%, 51%]  crash 27%  timeout 32%  return -18.9 [-46.0, 8.1]...awr_b0.3_nocap   seed 0  ESS   0.8%  success 51% [41%, 61%]  crash 45%  timeout 4%  return 10.5 [-13.1, 34.2]awr_b0.3_nocap   seed 1  ESS   0.8%  success 40% [31%, 50%]  crash 32%  timeout 28%  return -24.4 [-53.3, 4.4]awr_b0.3_nocap   seed 2  ESS   0.8%  success 51% [41%, 61%]  crash 38%  timeout 11%  return 8.3 [-18.1, 34.8]...awr_b0.03_nocap  seed 0  ESS   0.0%  success 11% [6%, 19%]  crash 89%  timeout 0%  return -85.6 [-100.2, -71.0]awr_b0.03_nocap  seed 1  ESS   0.0%  success 0% [0%, 4%]  crash 46%  timeout 54%  return -139.4 [-159.9, -118.9]awr_b0.03_nocap  seed 2  ESS   0.0%  success 0% [0%, 4%]  crash 99%  timeout 1%  return -128.1 [-132.7, -123.4]​collector, deterministic: success 33% [25%, 43%]  crash 12%  timeout 55%  return -39.0 [-70.8, -7.1]collector, stochastic:    success 17% [11%, 26%]  crash 38%  timeout 45%  return -74.5 [-96.4, -52.6]

Two things are visible even in the raw lines. First, the ESS is identical for all three seeds of a setting. That is right: the weights depend only on the file and on \(\beta\), never on the seed. Second, seeds of the same setting disagree by 10 points or more (\(\beta = 1\): 38%, 31%, 41%; \(\beta = 0.3\) without the cap: 51%, 40%, 51%), and at the bottom of the list something has clearly gone wrong: 0% success with 99% crashes. The next section reads all of it properly.

L2.9 Reading the results

L2.9.1 Pool the seeds, then plot

Each run was scored on 100 episodes, so each success rate carries an interval of about ±10 points. Three seeds of the same setting give 300 episodes, which narrows the interval to about ±5–6 points. lab2_plot.py does that pooling and draws the two figures. Here is the part of its main() that computes the numbers:

    runs = [json.loads(p.read_text()) for p in sorted((RESULTS / "lab2").glob("*_s*.json"))]    collector = json.loads((RESULTS / "lab2" / "collector_eval.json").read_text())    by_name = defaultdict(list)    for r in runs:        by_name[r["name"]].append(r)​    # ---------- summary numbers ----------    summary = {}    for name, rs in by_name.items():        goals = sum(round(r["eval"]["success_rate"] * r["eval"]["episodes"]) for r in rs)        n = sum(r["eval"]["episodes"] for r in rs)        summary[name] = {            "seeds": len(rs),            "per_seed_success": [r["eval"]["success_rate"] for r in rs],            "pooled_success": goals / n,            "pooled_success_ci": wilson_interval(goals, n),            "mean_crash": float(np.mean([r["eval"]["crash_rate"] for r in rs])),            "mean_timeout": float(np.mean([r["eval"]["timeout_rate"] for r in rs])),            "mean_return": float(np.mean([r["eval"]["mean_return"] for r in rs])),            "ess_fraction": rs[0]["weights"]["ess_fraction"],            "top1pct_weight_share": rs[0]["weights"]["top1pct_weight_share"],            "fraction_at_cap": rs[0]["weights"]["fraction_at_cap"],        }    save_json({"collector": collector, "settings": summary}, RESULTS / "lab2_summary.json")

by_name groups the 30 result files by setting name, so by_name["awr_b1"] holds three runs. round(success_rate * episodes) turns each run’s rate back into a count of goals, the counts are added, and wilson_interval (Lab 0) puts a 95% interval on the pooled rate. The file’s imports are json, defaultdict from collections, numpy, matplotlib (with matplotlib.use("Agg"), as before), and FIGS, RESULTS, plot_style, save_json, wilson_interval from common; main() calls plot_style() before these lines.

One honest limit of pooling: the Wilson interval treats the 300 episodes as one sample from one policy. If the three seeds really produce different policies, the pooled interval understates how uncertain the recipe is. That is why the figure also shows each seed’s own score as a faint dot.

The middle of lab2_plot.py is plotting, and you can copy it from the reference file. It draws Figure L2.4 from seed 0’s runs at \(\beta = 3, 1, 0.3, 0.1\), in a two-by-two grid: each panel is a bar chart of the stored histogram on a logarithmic x-axis, titled with the capped ESS and, where it exists, the uncapped one. It draws Figure L2.3 with one pooled point and interval per setting (blue with the cap, orange without), the per-seed dots, and two horizontal reference lines for the collector. The x-axis of Figure L2.3 follows a fixed order of settings, a constant at the top of the file:

ORDER = ["bc", "awr_b3", "awr_b1", "awr_b0.3", "awr_b0.1", "awr_b0.03"]

The end of main() prints the table you will compare against. It is output, not decoration, so write it yourself:

    # (in the reference file this line sits in the figure code, which also uses d and st)    d, st = (collector["deterministic"]["success_rate"],             collector["stochastic"]["success_rate"])​    print(f"collector: deterministic {d:.0%}, stochastic {st:.0%}")    print(f"{'setting':<18} {'success (pooled)':>18} {'95% interval':>14} "          f"{'crash':>6} {'timeout':>8} {'ESS':>6}")    for name in sorted(summary, key=lambda n: (n.endswith("nocap"),                                               ORDER.index(n.replace("_nocap", "")))):        s = summary[name]        lo, hi = s["pooled_success_ci"]        print(f"{name:<18} {s['pooled_success']:>18.1%} {f'[{lo:.0%}, {hi:.0%}]':>14} "              f"{s['mean_crash']:>6.0%} {s['mean_timeout']:>8.0%} {s['ess_fraction']:>6.1%}")    print(f"wrote {FIGS / 'lab2_weights.png'}, {FIGS / 'lab2_sweep.png'}, "          f"{RESULTS / 'lab2_summary.json'}")

The sort key is a pair. Its first part, n.endswith("nocap"), is False for capped settings and True for uncapped ones, and False sorts first, so all capped settings come before all uncapped ones. Its second part is the setting’s position in ORDER, after removing _nocap from the name, so within each group the temperatures run from BC down to 0.03. In the format strings, <18 left-aligns the text in a field 18 characters wide and >18 right-aligns it, which keeps the columns straight. The inner f-string f'[{lo:.0%}, {hi:.0%}]' builds the interval text first, so that it can be right-aligned as one piece.

Run it
python lab2_plot.py

Here is everything in one place. Success is pooled over 3 seeds × 100 episodes; crash and timeout rates are averaged over the seeds. The effective sample size depends only on the file and \(\beta\), so it is the same for every seed; it is given both as a fraction and in steps.

Per-seed success, for the settings the readings lean on: BC 23, 24, 25; \(\beta = 1\) 38, 31, 41; \(\beta = 0.3\) 43, 33, 36; \(\beta = 0.3\) without the cap 51, 40, 51; \(\beta = 0.1\) without the cap 26, 37, 24; \(\beta = 0.03\) without the cap 11, 0, 0. The reference lines: the collector’s mean action scores 33% [25, 43], its sampled actions 17% [11, 26], each on 100 episodes.

There are six things to read in this table. Take them one at a time.

L2.9.3 Reading one: weighting works on this data

At \(\beta = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.3\), AWR reaches 36.7% and 37.3%. BC reaches 24.0%. That is a gain of about 13 points, and the pooled intervals do not overlap: [31, 42] and [32, 43] against [20, 29].

Section L2.9.1 warned that pooled intervals can understate how uncertain a recipe is, so check the result seed by seed too. It survives: the worst \(\beta = 1\) seed (31%) and the worst \(\beta = 0.3\) seed (33%) both beat the best BC seed (25%). The answer to the first half of the lab’s question is yes. On the same file, with the same network and the same number of updates, weighting the recorded actions by their advantage produced a clearly better driver than copying them.

Both settings also edge past the collector’s own mean action (33%). Do not make much of that. The collector was scored on only 100 episodes, its interval is [25, 43], and the AWR numbers sit inside it. “AWR matched the policy that made the data, starting from a clipped, noisy recording of it” is what the numbers support.

The gain was not free. Timeouts fell from 62% to 41%, and crashes rose from 14% to 22%. AWR learned to drive with purpose, and some of that purpose ends in an obstacle. Section L2.9.9 comes back to that trade.

L2.9.4 Reading two: \(\beta = 3\) is behavior cloning in disguise

At \(\beta = 3\), success is 25.3%, indistinguishable from BC’s 24.0%. The weights explain why: the ESS is 90.2% of the file. On the mean-1 scale every weight lies between about 0.3 and 3.4, and the histogram in Figure L2.4 is a narrow spike around 1. A warm temperature is a gentle tilt, and on this file a gentle tilt is not enough to change the driving.

L2.9.5 Reading three: with the cap, small \(\beta\) turns into filtered BC

Here is the first surprise. The book leads you to expect that lowering \(\beta\) makes the weights ever more extreme and the effective sample size ever smaller. With the cap in place, the opposite happens below \(\beta = 1\). The capped ESS is lowest at \(\beta = 1\), 32.9%, and then goes back up: 35.7% at \(\beta = 0.3\), 54.7% at 0.1, 62.4% at 0.03. And success drifts back down toward BC: 28.3% and 25.7%.

The four-step toy of Section L2.6.5 already showed the mechanism. Here it is again at \(\beta = 0.1\), with standardized advantages of a size that is common on the real file (its standardized advantages run from about −3.3 to +3.8):

A~ = +2.0  ->  exp(+2.0 / 0.1) = exp(20) = 4.85e8  ->  capped to 20A~ = +0.5  ->  exp(+0.5 / 0.1) = exp(5)  = 148     ->  capped to 20A~ = +0.2  ->  exp(+0.2 / 0.1) = exp(2)  = 7.39    (below the cap)A~ = -0.5  ->  exp(-0.5 / 0.1) = exp(-5) = 0.0067  (effectively gone)

As \(\beta\) shrinks, the band of steps that are “above average but still below the cap” gets thinner and thinner. Almost every step with a positive standardized advantage lands exactly at the cap, and almost every step with a negative one gets a weight near zero. The weights become two-level. That is filtered BC: clone the better-than-average steps, all equally, and ignore the rest. Many equal weights make a large effective sample size, which is why the ESS rises. And filtered BC throws away exactly the gradations that made \(\beta = 1\) and 0.3 work: a great step and a barely-above-average step now count the same.

Read Figure L2.4 panel by panel, top row first.

  • At \(\beta = 3\) (top left), a narrow spike around 1 (ESS 90%). No uncapped \(\beta = 3\) run exists, so this title has no parentheses.
  • At \(\beta = 1\) (top right), a spread from a few hundredths up to about 12, with most of the mass near 1 (ESS 33%; 30% without the cap).
  • At \(\beta = 0.3\) (bottom left), a broad spread from about \(10^{-4}\) up to the cap, with a secondary bump at the cap holding 9% of the steps (ESS 36%; 1% without the cap).
  • At \(\beta = 0.1\) (bottom right), 42% of all steps sit at the cap and about 14% at the floor. The rest are spread thinly in between, mostly at low weights: of all the steps below the cap, about 60% get less than a tenth of the average weight, and about half less than a hundredth (ESS 55%; 0% without the cap).

The two-level shape is not complete at \(\beta = 0.1\), but it is getting there. The same histogram at \(\beta = 0.03\), which the figure does not draw (it is in results/lab2/awr_b0.03_s0.json), has only about one step in seven left in the middle bins.

Why does the cap sit at about 2 in the last panel, and not at 20? Because the histogram shows weights after the division by their mean. When 42% of the steps share the cap, the mean weight is large, and the cap divided by it comes out at about 2. At \(\beta = 0.3\), with 9% of the steps at the cap, it lands at about 4.4. At \(\beta = 1\), where only 0.5% of steps reach the cap, the capped weight lands at about 12.

L2.9.6 Reading four: without the cap, the book’s dead data appears exactly as warned

Now look at the orange points. Removing the cap changes little at \(\beta = 1\): 37.7% success, ESS 30.0% (54,775 steps), because only 0.5% of the steps were ever capped there. Below that, the effective sample size collapses:

\(\beta\), no capESS (steps)what it means
154,775a strong but healthy tilt
0.31,447the top 1% of steps carry 83.5% of all weight
0.124about 95% of steps get less than a millionth of the average weight
0.031.4one or two logged steps are the whole training set

At \(\beta = 0.03\) without the cap the policy is trained, in effect, on one or two recorded steps out of 182,658, and nothing constrains what it does anywhere else. It scores 3.7% success with 78% crashes; two of the three seeds reach the goal in zero episodes out of 100, and the mean return is about −117.7. At \(\beta = 0.1\) it still reaches 29% but crashes 65% of the time. This is precisely the failure book Section 4.4.5 describes and Figure 4.3’s “cold” panel draws: the data is still in the file, but it has effectively stopped existing, and the policy overfits the few survivors. You have now watched it happen on your own logs.

L2.9.7 Reading five: the best number sits at the edge of the cliff

Here is the second surprise, and it is the one that most tempts a wrong conclusion. The single highest success rate in the whole sweep is \(\beta = 0.3\) without the cap: 47.3% [42, 53]. It also has the best mean return, about −1.9 (seeds +10.5, −24.4 and +8.3). If you ranked settings by success alone, this is the winner.

Look at what comes with it. It crashes 38% of the time, the highest crash rate of any setting that did not collapse. Its seeds disagree by 11 points, from 40% to 51%, one of the larger spreads in the sweep. (With 100 episodes per seed, do not rank the spreads more finely than that.) Its effective sample size is 1,447 steps, 0.8% of the file. And one step further down the temperature ladder, at \(\beta = 0.1\) without the cap, crashes jump to 65%. This is an aggressive policy built from a small elite of steps. It reaches the goal more often and hits things more often, and it sits right next to the setting where everything falls apart.

The honest reading: the cap trades peak performance for robustness. With the cap, no temperature in the sweep collapsed; the worst capped setting still matched BC.
