Without it, the best result and the worst result are neighbors. So tune \(\beta\) with the effective sample size in view, not success alone. A setting whose ESS has fallen to a fraction of a percent is a setting whose good score may not survive a new seed, a new file, or a new robot.

Pitfalls

Picking \(\beta\) by the top success number. The best-scoring setting here is also the most fragile. Report ESS, crash rate and seed spread beside every success rate, and prefer a setting whose neighbors are also good.

Reading a rising ESS as “safer”. With a cap, a rising ESS at small \(\beta\) means the weights have gone two-level. You are no longer tuning AWR; you are running filtered BC.

L2.9.8 Reading six: the book’s rung E4 is half right

Appendix B rung E4 tells you to normalize the advantages, clip the weights at 20, then push \(\beta\) toward zero and watch Chapter 4’s dead-data failure appear. You now know that on real data this recipe does not show you dead data. With that clip in place (this guide calls it the cap), pushing \(\beta\) down gives filtered BC, and the effective sample size rises. To see dead data you have to remove the cap, as the orange points did.

That is not a mistake in the book’s understanding. The warning about the exponential is right, and the uncapped runs confirmed it to the letter. The recipe simply pairs the warning with the one safety feature that prevents it from happening. It is exactly the kind of thing Appendix B’s Rule three asks you to write down on the “surprise” line of your note, because it is where the mental model you brought in met the data and lost. Something like: with the cap at 20, \(\beta \to 0\) turns AWR into filtered BC (ESS up to 62%); dead data only appears with the cap removed.

L2.9.9 Success against crashes: the trade

Success rate alone hides how each policy fails. Put the three outcome columns side by side and three driving styles appear.

  • Timid: BC, \(\beta = 3\), and the capped \(\beta = 0.03\). Few crashes (13–14%), but about 61–62% of episodes run out of time.
  • Purposeful: capped \(\beta = 1\) and 0.3, and uncapped \(\beta = 1\). Timeouts fall to about 40%, crashes rise to about 22%, and success climbs to about 37%.
  • Aggressive: uncapped \(\beta = 0.3\) and below. Timeouts fall to 6–18% and crashes take over (38–78%).

The capped \(\beta = 0.1\) sits between the first two styles (17% crashes, 55% timeouts), on its way from purposeful back to timid as the weights go two-level.

Which trade is better depends on what a crash costs you. By the environment’s own accounting, where a crash costs 100 reward and every wasted step costs a little, the purposeful policies come out ahead: \(\beta = 1\) averages a return of about −32.4 against about −60 for BC, despite the extra crashes.

Read that gap with care, though. Returns swing a lot from episode to episode: the standard deviation of a single episode’s return is about 148 for \(\beta = 1\) and about 159 for BC (from the evaluation files). Over 300 episodes each, the gap of about 27 has a standard error of about 12.5 (the typical size of the difference that chance alone would produce): \(\sqrt{148^2/300 + 159^2/300} = \sqrt{73.0 + 84.3} \approx 12.5\). So the gap is roughly two standard errors: probably real, not clear-cut.

On a real robot a crash may cost a repair, and the accounting changes. Decide deliberately what you are optimizing, and read the crash column before you celebrate the success column.

On your rig

When you run weighted regression on SO-101 logs, you will not have 300 evaluation episodes per setting. The weight diagnostics are what you will still have: log the effective sample size, the fraction of steps at the cap, and the top-1% weight share for every \(\beta\) you try, and keep the histogram. If ESS rises as you lower \(\beta\) with a cap on, you are in the filtered-BC regime; if it falls to a few hundred steps without one, you are one seed away from a collapse.

L2.10 Why AWR’s weights here are mostly “episode luck”

L2.10.1 The question the results leave open

AWR beat BC by about 13 points, and then it stopped. Its best robust result, about 37%, is roughly where the collector’s own mean action already was. The file contains 77 episodes that reached the goal. Why couldn’t weighting extract more from them?

One suspect is the advantage itself. Recall the warning from Section L2.3.1: \(\hat{A}_t = G_t - V(s_t)\) charges everything that happened after step \(t\) to the action at step \(t\). Put numbers on the reach of that charge. With \(\gamma = 0.99\), a reward \(k\) steps in the future counts \(0.99^k\) as much:

0.99^100 = 0.366   ->  a +100 goal bonus 100 steps later adds 36.6 to G_t0.99^200 = 0.134   ->  the same bonus 200 steps later still adds 13.4

Episodes in this file average about 365 steps. So at most steps, \(G_t\) is dominated by how the episode eventually ended. And how an episode ends depends on many things the action at step \(t\) did not control: the random obstacle layout, the sensor’s dropouts and ghost echoes, a bad decision 150 steps later. If that is what the advantage mostly measures, then the weights mostly measure it too. You can test this directly.

Try it yourself first

Before running anything, make a guess. If you replaced every step’s advantage with the average advantage of its episode, how much of the variation in \(\hat{A}\) across the file would you keep? 10%? 50%? Write the number down. Then write a few lines that compute it: group \(\hat{A}\) by the episode field, and compare the variance of the episode averages (weighted by episode length) with the total variance.

Here is the diagnostic we ran. The advantage array is called adv, because in this chapter a always means an action.

import numpy as npd = np.load("data/rover_offline.npz"); adv = d["ret"] - d["value"]; ep = d["episode"]means = np.array([adv[ep == e].mean() for e in range(ep.max() + 1)])counts = np.bincount(ep)between = np.sum(counts * (means - adv.mean()) ** 2) / len(adv)print("share of advantage variance explained by episode identity: %.2f"      % (between / adv.var()))

means holds each of the 500 episodes’ average advantage, and counts each episode’s number of steps. between is the variance you would get if every step carried its episode’s average instead of its own advantage: each episode’s squared distance from the overall mean, counted once per step. Dividing it by the total variance gives the share of all the variation that is explained purely by which episode a step belongs to. Statisticians call this split between-group and within-group variance.

Run it
python

Start the interactive session in your lab folder, because the path data/rover_offline.npz is relative to it. Paste the snippet above. Keep the same session open for the second snippet below, which reuses d, adv and ep.

What you should see
share of advantage variance explained by episode identity: 0.69

Then split the steps by how their episode ended. The last step of each episode tells you: a reward above 50 means the goal bonus, below −50 means a crash, and an episode that did not terminate timed out.

last = np.flatnonzero(np.r_[ep[1:] != ep[:-1], True])   # index of each episode's last stepfor name, mask in [("goal", d["terminated"][last] & (d["rew"][last] > 50)),                   ("crash", d["terminated"][last] & (d["rew"][last] < -50)),                   ("timeout", ~d["terminated"][last])]:    steps = np.isin(ep, np.flatnonzero(mask))    print("%-8s %3d episodes  mean A %+6.1f  positive %3.0f%%"          % (name, mask.sum(), adv[steps].mean(), 100 * (adv[steps] > 0).mean()))

last finds each episode’s final row: the rows where the next row belongs to a different episode, plus the very last row of the file. mask marks which of the 500 episodes ended each way, and np.isin selects all the steps of those episodes. Paste it into the same session.

What you should see
goal      77 episodes  mean A  +41.9  positive  95%crash    186 episodes  mean A  -44.0  positive  13%timeout  237 episodes  mean A   +4.1  positive  74%

L2.10.2 What it means

69% of the variation in \(\hat{A}\) is explained by which episode a step belongs to. Only 31% is left to distinguish one step from another within the same episode, and that 31% includes all the noise of a partially observed, randomized simulator.

The split makes it concrete. In the 77 episodes that reached the goal, 95% of all steps have a positive advantage, and the mean advantage over all their steps is +41.9: whatever the rover did along the way, nearly every step is marked “better than expected”. In the 186 crash episodes only 13% of steps are positive, and the mean advantage over their steps is −44.0: the sensible steps before the fatal one are marked “worse than expected” along with it. Timeout episodes sit in between, with 74% positive steps and a mean of +4.1.

So on this file AWR’s weights mostly say “this step was in a lucky episode”, not “this action was better than the alternatives at this state”. Weighting still helped, presumably because lucky episodes also contain better driving on average; nothing in this lab measured that directly. But the signal is blurred at exactly the grain AWR needs, the single step. This is the explanation the data supports; we did not run an experiment that isolates it as the cause, so hold it as a well-supported reading rather than a proof.

It also sheds light on Reading three. Timeout episodes run the full 500 steps, so they hold 118,500 of the file’s 182,658 steps, and 74% of those steps have a positive advantage. At the capped \(\beta = 0.03\), about three quarters of the steps sitting at the cap (73.7%) come from episodes that timed out. Timeout episodes hold 65% of all steps, so they are over-represented at the cap, but only modestly. A plausible link, not a proven one: filtered BC clones mostly the “better than expected” steps of drives that never arrived, and it times out about as often as BC does (61% against 62%).

An analogy. Imagine rating every decision a salesperson made during a day by whether the day ended with a big sale. The 9 a.m. phone call gets credit for a deal a walk-in customer closed at 5 p.m. Where the analogy breaks down: a sales day’s outcome may be almost pure luck, whereas on the rover the episode’s ending does depend on the actions, so some of that shared credit is deserved. The 0.69 says how much of the signal lines up with episodes; it does not say how much of it is undeserved.

L2.10.3 Where this leads

If the problem is that the advantage compares an episode’s outcome against a baseline, the fix is an advantage that compares actions at the same state. That is what AWAC does (book Section 4.5). It keeps AWR’s kind of update, weighted regression onto the logged actions, and changes where the advantage comes from: a learned critic \(Q(s, a)\), trained by temporal-difference updates on every transition in the file (learning a value from one step’s reward plus the critic’s own estimate at the next state; Section L3.3 builds it), compared against what the current policy would do at that same state, \(A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - \mathbb{E}_{a' \sim \pi_\theta}[Q(s, a')]\). Lab 3 builds it on the same file and asks whether that sharper signal gets further than AWR did. The next_obs field you stored in Section L2.3, unused so far, is what makes that possible.

Words you will hear

Behavior policy \(\pi_\beta\). Whatever produced the data; here, the 100k checkpoint driving with sampled actions. Filtered BC (also top-k% BC). Behavior cloning on only the samples judged good; capped AWR at small \(\beta\) turns into it. Temperature. The number dividing the advantage before the exponential; low is sharp, high is flat. Effective sample size (ESS). \((\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2\): how many equally weighted samples a weighted set is worth. Bootstrapping at truncation (also partial-episode bootstrapping). Replacing the missing future of a time-limited episode with a value estimate.

Checkpoint
  • Explain why the collector should be mediocre, why this lab used the 100k checkpoint instead of the automatically suggested 200k one, what the pilot measured that the selection rule did not, and why pilot results must be moved out of results/lab2/ (L2.2, L2.8.2).
  • Write down what the offline file stores and why each field is there, and compute \(G_t\) by hand for a short episode that ends by termination and by truncation (L2.3).
  • Compute a Gaussian log-probability for a toy action, and say what the gradient of \(-\log\pi\) does to the mean and to the standard deviation (L2.4).
  • Explain why behavior cloning scored below the collector’s mean action, using the clipping of wide samples (L2.5).
  • Explain why cloning logged actions with weights \(\exp(\hat{A}/\beta)\) aims at a better policy than the collector, compute AWR weights and the effective sample size for a list of standardized advantages, with and without the cap, and explain why a minibatch must not be divided by its own weight sum (L2.6, L2.7).
  • Read the sweep: why weighting beats BC at \(\beta = 1\) and 0.3, why capped small \(\beta\) becomes filtered BC while uncapped small \(\beta\) produces dead data, why the best single number is not the setting to choose, and what the 0.69 episode-luck diagnostic says about AWR’s advantage (L2.9, L2.10).

Where to go deeper. Book Chapter 4 is the theory behind every line of this lab: Section 4.3 for behavior cloning and its ceiling, Section 4.4.3 for why the weight is an exponential, Section 4.4.4 for how weighted cloning fits the target policy, Section 4.4.5 and its pitfall box for the temperature and dead data, and Section 4.5 for AWAC. The AWR paper itself (Peng et al., 2019) is short and readable; its ancestor is reward-weighted regression (Peters & Schaal, 2007). For the Monte Carlo advantage and its noise, reread book Section 3.5.1. Lab 3 continues from the file you recorded here, with AWAC (Nair et al., 2020).

Lab 3 — Give AWR a critic, then let it keep learning (AWAC)

Lab 2 ended on a good result with an uncomfortable footnote. Advantage-weighted regression, trained on nothing but 500 logged episodes, beat plain behavior cloning by about 13 points: 37.3% success against 24.0%, pooled over three seeds. Then the episode-luck check at the end of Lab 2 showed what its weights were mostly made of: 69% of the variance of the advantage was explained by which episode a step belonged to. AWR learned something real, but its teacher was grading luck as much as skill.

This lab keeps AWR’s kind of policy update, weighted regression onto the logged actions, and replaces the teacher. Instead of reading a frozen grade from the file, you will train a critic: a second network that learns, from every recorded transition, how good each action is for the policy you are training right now. The result is AWAC, advantage-weighted actor-critic (Nair et al., 2020; book Section 4.5). Then you will let the policy drive the rover and add its own experience to the same data, which AWR, as you built it in Lab 2, could not do.

The book’s Appendix B has no rung for this lab; it is our addition on top of rung E4. It also brings the most new machinery of the three labs, so the chapter takes it in stages. Sections L3.1 to L3.4 build the ideas without code. Sections L3.5 to L3.8 turn them into one script, lab3_awac.py. Sections L3.9 and L3.10 run it and read the results, including two results that do not flatter AWAC. Section L3.11 carries the lessons to real robots.

What you need from earlier labs:

  • common.py from Lab 0: make_env, evaluate, fmt_eval, set_seed, save_json, ensure_dirs, and the constants DATA, RESULTS and GAMMA, all reused unchanged. The plotting script also uses FIGS, plot_style and wilson_interval.
  • The GaussianPolicy class you added to common.py in Lab 2 (Section L2.4), also reused unchanged.
  • The dataset data/rover_offline.npz, recorded in Lab 2.
  • Lab 2’s results/lab2_summary.json and results/lab2_checkpoints.json, which the final chart reads.

As in Lab 2, write and run everything from inside your own lab folder, labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/, with the virtual environment active. Never save your files in the answer key’s folder, labs/ppo-awr-awac/: your first save would overwrite the reference script you will compare against. The printed outputs in this chapter came from the answer key, so any path they print names that folder instead of yours.

The full run takes about 20 minutes on the CPU.

L3.1 What AWR could not do

Every row of the Lab 2 file carries a state \(s\), the action \(a\) the collector took, and two numbers the collector attached: \(G\), the discounted reward that actually followed, and \(V(s)\), what the collector’s critic expected. AWR’s advantage was \(\hat{A} = G - V(s)\), computed once and turned into one fixed weight per row. Three limits hide in that design.

L3.1.1 The grade describes the collector, and it is frozen

\(G\) is the reward that followed an action while the collector kept driving. The collector was the 100k-step PPO checkpoint, which reached the goal in 15.4% of its recorded episodes. So the advantage is a verdict on the collector’s choices, measured with the collector’s future. As training proceeds, your policy becomes a different driver, yet every weight it trains on is still the grade the collector’s episodes earned. The book says it in one sentence (Section 4.5): a Monte Carlo advantage “is noisy, it wastes partial trajectories, and it does not improve as your policy does.”

L3.1.2 The grade is mostly episode luck

\(G\) at step 40 adds up everything that happened from step 40 to the end of the episode and charges all of it to the one action taken at step 40. A sensible steering command, in an episode whose obstacle layout later traps the rover, gets a bad grade. A careless one, in an episode with an open lane, gets a good grade. (Book Section 3.5.1 walks through this failure with two nearly identical first actions.) Lab 2’s episode-luck check shows how large the effect is on your file:

how the episode endedepisodesmean \(\hat{A}\) of its stepssteps with \(\hat{A} \gt 0\)
goal77+41.995%
crash186−44.013%
timeout237+4.174%

In an episode that reached the goal, 95% of the steps got a positive advantage, the hesitant ones included. In a crash episode, 87% got a negative advantage, the good ones included. So AWR’s weights mostly said “this step was in a lucky episode”, rarely “this action was better than the alternatives here”. The weighting still helped, because lucky episodes do contain more good actions. But it was a blunt instrument.

L3.1.3 New experience has nowhere to go

Suppose your AWR policy drives 100 new episodes. The collector’s critic cannot grade them, because it estimates the collector’s future, not this policy’s. Using them would require a critic for the new policy, which means the Lab 2 pipeline starts over, and starts over again each time the policy changes. AWR as you built it is one-shot: one file in, one policy out.

L3.1.4 The question for this lab

All three limits come from one decision: the advantage was computed once, from finished episodes, by someone else’s critic. So this lab asks:

If the advantage comes from a learned Q-function instead of the collector’s frozen Monte Carlo estimate, and the policy keeps collecting its own data, does it improve beyond AWR?

Keep its two halves apart, because the results answer them differently. Offline: on the same file, with no new data, does a learned critic give better weights than \(G - V\)? Online: once the policy drives and adds its own experience, does it keep improving?

L3.2 The idea in one picture

AWAC’s recipe fits in one sentence: keep AWR’s actor update, weighted regression onto logged actions, and change where the advantage comes from. (This lab’s version also changes a few settings of that update. L3.7 shows them, and Reading 2 in L3.10.3 checks that they are not what makes the difference.) Figure L3.1 shows the whole loop.

The solid arrows are what every update does. In the offline phase they are all that happens, and no environment is involved. The replay buffer is the Lab 2 file loaded into memory: 182,658 transitions, each holding a state, an action, a reward, the next state, and a flag saying whether the episode really ended there. Every update draws a random batch of 256.

The batch goes two ways. At the top it trains the critics, two networks that estimate \(Q(s,a)\), the future reward that follows from taking action \(a\) in state \(s\). Section L3.3 shows how they learn it and L3.4 why there are two, plus two slow copies. To build the critics’ training targets, the slow copies score an action that the policy samples at each next state; that is the arrow labeled “a’ at s’” on the right. In the middle, the batch meets the critics again to produce an advantage, and from it a weight, for each logged action. On the right the policy, called the actor in this family of methods, does what it did in Lab 2: it raises the log-probability of each logged action in proportion to its weight.

The dashed arrows are the online phase. After 50,000 offline updates the policy drives the rover, each step it takes is appended to the same buffer, and one update follows every step. The update itself never changes; only the buffer grows. That is what “off-policy” buys: the critics and the actor learn from any transition, whoever produced it.

L3.2.1 The advantage, computed from the critic

AWR compared what happened with what was expected. AWAC compares the logged action with what the current policy would typically do in the same state, both scored by the critic:

\[ \begin{aligned} A(s,a) &= Q(s,a) - V(s), \\ V(s) &\approx \frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=1}^{4} Q(s, a'_k), \qquad a'_k \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s). \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

\(s\) is a state from the buffer (15 observation numbers) and \(a\) the action logged with it (two wheel speeds). \(Q(s,a)\) is the critic’s estimate of the discounted reward that follows if the rover takes \(a\) in \(s\) and then drives the way the current policy \(\pi\) drives. \(V(s)\) is the same estimate when the first action is also chosen by \(\pi\). We build it on the spot: draw four candidate actions \(a'_1, \dots, a'_4\) from the policy at \(s\) (\(\sim\) means “sampled from”), ask the critic about each, and average. The advantage \(A(s,a)\) is positive when the logged action looks better than what the policy would usually do here, negative when it looks worse.

Book Section 4.5 writes this advantage \(\hat{A}(s,a)\), with the hat that marks an estimate. This chapter drops the hat, only to keep it visually apart from Lab 2’s \(\hat{A} = G - V(s)\).

This is the whole point of the lab, so take it one piece at a time. Both terms are evaluated at the same state, and two separate effects then work in AWAC’s favor.

Effect one: the critic stores averages, not one episode’s outcome. The critic is trained toward an expected value. Its estimate for a state and an action is learned over many transitions, so the later luck of one particular episode, such as a dropout or a ghost echo 150 steps later, is averaged away inside \(Q\). That luck is never written into one row as its grade, the way \(G\) was.

Effect two: subtracting \(V(s)\) removes how good the state is overall. If the sensors show an obstacle close ahead, every action there is worth less, so \(Q(s,a)\) and \(V(s)\) both drop. Their difference is left to say only how the logged action compares with the policy’s usual choice. This cancels only as far as the critic is accurate. Lab 2’s \(G - V(s)\) also subtracted a value for the state; effect one is the part AWR lacked.

A toy with made-up numbers shows effect one, using the setup of book Section 3.5.1. Two rows in the file have nearly the same state and nearly the same action. In the first row’s episode the rover found a clear lane and reached the goal, and its return was \(G = +180\). In the second, an obstacle blocked the path, the rover detoured and ran out of time, and \(G = -20\). Suppose the collector’s critic said \(V(s) = 80\) at both states.

  • AWR grades the first row \(\hat{A} = 180 - 80 = +100\) and the second \(\hat{A} = -20 - 80 = -100\). Same situation, same action, opposite grades.
  • A critic trained on both rows sees nearly the same inputs twice, so it cannot give them different values. It learns one \(Q(s,a)\) for that pair, somewhere between the two outcomes, and the policy’s samples give one \(V(s)\) for that state. Both rows get the same advantage, whatever it turns out to be. Neither is rewarded or punished for its episode’s luck.

And because \(V\) comes from the current policy’s samples on every update, the baseline moves as the policy changes. On paper, then, AWAC addresses L3.1.1 and L3.1.2, and the online phase addresses L3.1.3. Whether the real critic is accurate enough for this is what L3.10 tests.

Pitfall

Two different primes. Here, \(a'_k \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s)\) is drawn at the same state \(s\), to estimate \(V(s)\). In the critic’s target (L3.3), \(a' \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s')\) is drawn at the next state \(s'\), to estimate the future. Same policy, different state. Papers overload the prime the same way. The code keeps them apart as a_pi and next_act.

An analogy. AWR graded moves the way you might grade a chess game after the tournament: every move in a won game gets credit, every move in a lost game gets blame. AWAC grades moves the way a chess engine annotates a game: at each position it compares the move played with the moves a reasonable player would consider there. A strong move in a lost game gets the credit it deserves.

Where the analogy breaks down: a chess engine gets its evaluations by searching ahead with the exact rules of the game. The critic has no rules to search with. It learns its evaluations from the same logged transitions, and it can be confidently wrong exactly where the data is thin. Section L3.4 exists because of that difference.

L3.3 Q-learning from zero, simply

The critic is the genuinely new piece, so this section builds it from nothing: what \(Q(s,a)\) means on the rover, how to learn it from single transitions, and what to do when an episode ends.

L3.3.1 What Q(s, a) means for the rover

You know \(V(s)\) from PPO: one number per state, the discounted reward the policy expects from here on. The action-value function \(Q(s,a)\), or Q-function, takes the action as an extra input. For the rover it answers: “if the rover, in this sensor situation, sends these two wheel-speed commands for one 0.2-second step, and from then on drives the way \(\pi\) drives, how much discounted reward will it collect?” (The randomized action delay and motor lag spread a command’s effect over the next few steps, so the command matters beyond its own step. The Q-function’s answer includes that.)

Picture the rover 1.5 m from the goal with an obstacle slightly to its right. \(Q(s, [0.8, 0.8])\), both wheels forward, and \(Q(s, [0.2, 0.9])\), a curve to the left, are two different numbers. If curving keeps clearance at little cost in progress, the second is higher. \(V(s)\), by contrast, is one number for the state: the average of \(Q(s,a)\) over the actions \(\pi\) tends to pick there.

For scale: with \(\gamma = 0.99\), a common rule of thumb reads \(1/(1-\gamma) = 100\) steps, about 20 simulated seconds, as the horizon a value “sees”. The large rewards are the +100 at the goal and −100 at a crash; the per-step terms are small but add up.

L3.3.2 The obvious way to learn it, and why it fails here

The obvious way is Lab 2’s: regress the critic onto the discounted return that actually followed each logged action. It fails for two reasons you have now seen. That return was produced by the collector driving afterwards, so it measures the collector’s future, not the future of \(\pi\). And it carries the whole episode’s luck. We need a way to learn \(Q\) for the current policy from single transitions, without waiting for episodes to finish and without caring who drove.

L3.3.3 The fix: one real step, then trust the estimate

Use the idea behind the TD residual \(\delta_t\) you computed in Lab 1 (book Section 3.5.2): take one real reward and let the critic estimate everything after it. A stored transition says that in state \(s\) the action \(a\) was taken, reward \(r\) arrived, and the rover landed in \(s'\). What happens after \(s'\) is, by the definition of \(Q\), up to the policy. So we ask the policy what it would do at \(s'\), ask the critic what that is worth, and put the real reward in front. The result is the TD target, the number the critic is trained to output for \((s,a)\):

\[ y = r + \gamma\,(1 - d)\,Q(s', a'), \qquad a' \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s') \]
In plain words

\(y\) is the target: the value \(Q(s,a)\) should have. \(r\) is the reward logged for this one transition. \(\gamma = 0.99\) is the discount, the constant GAMMA every lab uses. \(s'\) is the next state stored with the transition. \(a'\) is a fresh action sampled from the current policy at \(s'\), not read from the file. \(Q(s',a')\) is the critic’s own estimate of what follows from there. \(d\) is the terminated flag, 1 if the episode really ended at this step (goal or crash) and 0 otherwise, so \((1-d)\) switches the future off when there is none. The critic is nudged toward \(y\) by a squared-error loss, with \(y\) held fixed as a label.

Two choices inside the equation matter.

The next action comes from \(\pi\), not from the file. The buffer holds the action the collector took at \(s'\), but plugging that in would learn the value of the collector continuing to drive, Lab 2’s problem again. Sampling \(a'\) from the current policy makes the target describe the future of \(\pi\), even though someone else recorded every transition. That makes the critic off-policy: it learns about one policy from data generated by another (book Section 4.1).

The target uses the critic’s own estimate. Training a value against targets built from other value estimates is called bootstrapping (book Section 4.2). It is what lets single transitions teach. The +100 at the goal enters the target of the final transition directly; on later updates it flows into the target of the transition before, and so on backwards through the buffer. Every transition contributes, including those from crashed and timed-out episodes. Bootstrapping is also the source of both dangers in L3.4.

L3.3.4 Terminated is not the same as truncated

The flag \(d\) looks like a detail, and it is one of the most common bugs in hand-written Q-learning.

A rover episode ends in one of three ways: at the goal, in a collision, or when the 500-step time limit fires. Gymnasium reports the first two as terminated=True and the third as truncated=True. A goal or a crash is a real ending: no more reward comes, so the future is truly worth zero. A timeout ends the experiment, not the world. At step 500 the rover is in an ordinary state, and its 15 observations contain no clock.

So a truncated transition keeps its bootstrap term. Setting \(d = 1\) there would teach the critic that some ordinary-looking states are worth only their immediate reward, while identical-looking states met at step 200 are worth much more. The critic cannot tell them apart, so it would learn a muddle of both. You have seen this reasoning twice already. Lab 2’s compute_returns bootstrapped \(G\) at the time limit, and SB3’s PPO adds \(\gamma V\) of the final observation to the last reward of a truncated episode. The code therefore stores only terminated. A truncated step enters with \(d = 0\), and its \(s'\) is the real final observation.

L3.3.5 Worked example: three targets for one transition

The numbers are made up for teaching; the arithmetic is exact. An ordinary transition has logged reward \(r = -0.05\), and the critic’s estimate at the next state is \(Q(s',a') = 11.2\). With \(\gamma = 0.99\) and \(d = 0\):

\[ \begin{aligned} y &= -0.05 + 0.99 \times (1 - 0) \times 11.2 \\ &= -0.05 + 11.088 \\ &= 11.038. \end{aligned} \]

If the critic currently says \(Q(s,a) = 10.0\), the squared error is \((10.0 - 11.038)^2 = (-1.038)^2 = 1.077444\), and the gradient step raises \(Q(s,a)\) a little toward 11.038.

Now suppose the same step had reached the goal, with \(r = 100.4\) and \(d = 1\):

\[ y = 100.4 + 0.99 \times (1 - 1) \times 11.2 = 100.4 + 0 = 100.4. \]

Nothing is added, because nothing comes after a goal. Finally, suppose it was step 500 and the time limit cut the episode. That is truncation, so \(d = 0\) and the bootstrap stays: \(y = r + 0.99 \times 11.2\), which with \(r = -0.05\) is again \(-0.05 + 11.088 = 11.038\). From the critic’s side, nothing special happened.

An analogy for the TD target: a navigation app that keeps an estimate of the remaining travel time from every intersection. It does not wait until you arrive to correct them. To correct its estimate for the intersection you just left, it takes the time you actually spent on that block and adds its current estimate from the intersection you reached. That sum is the new target for the old intersection. The block you drove plays the part of \(r\), and the estimate from the intersection you reached plays the part of \(\gamma\,Q(s',a')\).

Where the analogy breaks down: the app’s estimates for later segments come from live traffic data, measured independently of your trip. The critic’s estimate at \(s'\) comes from the critic itself, trained by this very process. If it is too high, the error is copied into the target for \(s\), and nothing independent checks it. The next section deals with that self-reference.

L3.4 Why two critics and slowly moving target copies

Bootstrapping makes the critic its own teacher, and two things can go wrong when a network trains against its own outputs. Each has a cheap, standard fix, and lab3_awac.py uses both.

L3.4.1 Problem one: flattering errors get selected

A neural critic is a little wrong everywhere, in random directions. It is most wrong where it has little or no data: at states and actions no transition in the buffer resembles. Papers call that extrapolation error, the critic’s error where it has to guess beyond its data. On its own, random error would average out. But the actor gives larger weights to actions with higher \(Q\), so the policy leans toward them. The next targets then sample \(a'\) from that policy. So among actions of equal true worth, the ones whose \(Q\) happens to be too high are the ones that get picked and queried.

A made-up micro-example: two actions at some state are truly worth 10 each, and the critic says 12 for the first and 8 for the second. The policy drifts toward the first, the targets sample it, and the 12 flows backwards into the targets of earlier states. The −2 error on the second action never matters, because nobody asks about it any more. Over many states and updates, the surviving errors are systematically the flattering ones. Book Section 4.2.2 puts it in one line: “extrapolation error is random in sign, but the optimizer specifically hunts for the positive errors.” The result is called overestimation.

L3.4.2 The fix: two critics, trust the lower one

Train two critics, \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\), from different random initial weights, and whenever you need a value, take the smaller of their answers. A flattering error in one is unlikely to be matched by the same error in the other, so the minimum tends to discard it. This is the clipped double-Q trick. You will meet it in most off-policy actor-critic code, including the critic of your HIL-SERL pipeline. That pipeline’s learner is in the style of SAC, soft actor-critic: an off-policy method that trains a Q-function alongside a Gaussian actor rewarded for staying random (book Section 4.5). Book Chapter 13 calls taking the minimum over an ensemble of critics “a deliberate pessimism that keeps the bootstrap from inflating itself.”

Now you can see where the 11.2 in L3.3.5 came from. In that example the two critics answered 12.0 and 11.2 at \((s',a')\), and the target used \(\min(12.0,\ 11.2) = 11.2\), giving 11.038. Trusting the first critic would have given \(-0.05 + 0.99 \times 12.0 = -0.05 + 11.88 = 11.83\).

An analogy: before listing a house, you ask two agents what it will sell for and plan your budget on the lower quote.

Where the analogy breaks down: two agents are independent people with independent information. The two critics see the same batches and are trained toward the same targets; they differ only in their random starting weights. Their errors are partly correlated, so the minimum reduces optimism without removing it. And where both critics are right on average but noisy, the minimum still comes out a little low, which is the price of the trick.

L3.4.3 Problem two: chasing a moving target

In ordinary regression the labels sit still while the network moves toward them. Here the label \(y\) contains \(Q\) itself. A gradient step that changes \(Q(s,a)\) also changes \(Q\) at nearby states and actions. That changes the targets of other transitions, and so it changes the next step. The network is chasing a target that moves whenever the network moves. A feedback loop like that can oscillate, or run away, instead of settling.

L3.4.4 The fix: target copies that follow slowly

Keep a second copy of each critic, called a target network, and compute \(y\) with the copies. The copies are never trained by gradients. After every update they move a tiny step toward the live critics, slowly enough that the live critics can catch up.

With both fixes in place, this is the target the code computes:

\[ \begin{aligned} y &= r + \gamma\,(1-d)\,\min\!\big(Q^{\text{targ}}_1(s',a'),\; Q^{\text{targ}}_2(s',a')\big), \\ a' &\sim \pi(\cdot \mid s'), \quad \text{clamped to } [-1, 1]. \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

This is the L3.3 target with two changes. \(Q^{\text{targ}}_1\) and \(Q^{\text{targ}}_2\) are the slow copies of the two critics, not the critics being trained, and \(\min(\cdot,\cdot)\) keeps the lower of their answers at the next state. As before, \(r\) is the logged reward, \(\gamma = 0.99\), \(d\) is the terminated flag, and \(a'\) is sampled from the current policy at \(s'\). The sample is clamped into \([-1, 1]\) because every logged wheel command lies inside that box. Both live critics, \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\), are trained toward this same \(y\).

The slow following is Polyak averaging, also called a soft target update. After every gradient update, each target parameter becomes a mix of its old value and the live critic’s value:

\[ \phi^{\text{targ}} \leftarrow (1 - \tau)\,\phi^{\text{targ}} + \tau\,\phi, \qquad \tau = 0.005 \]
In plain words

\(\phi\) (phi) is one parameter, a single weight or bias, of a live critic, and \(\phi^{\text{targ}}\) is the same parameter in its target copy. \(\leftarrow\) means “replace with”. \(\tau\) (tau) is the step size of the following: with \(\tau = 0.005\), each update keeps 99.5% of the old target value and mixes in 0.5% of the live value. The rule is applied to every parameter of both copies, once per gradient update.

L3.4.5 Worked example: how slow is “slow”?

Suppose the live critic changes a parameter and holds it there. The gap between target and live value shrinks by the factor \(1 - \tau = 0.995\) per update: 0.995 of it remains after one update, \(0.995^2 = 0.990025\) after two, \(0.995^n\) after \(n\). Half the gap is gone when \(0.995^n = 0.5\). Take logarithms:

\[ \begin{aligned} n &= \frac{\ln 0.5}{\ln 0.995} \\ &= \frac{-0.693147}{-0.0050125} \\ &= 138.3 \text{ updates.} \end{aligned} \]

So the copies trail the live critics with a half-life of about 138 updates. After 1,000 updates, \(0.995^{1000} \approx 0.0067\) of the gap is left. At about 5 ms per update, 138 updates take under a second, and the offline phase alone is 50,000 updates. Over the whole run, then, the targets are never stale for long. Yet from one gradient step to the next they barely move, and that is what damps the chase.

An analogy from your day job: a service built against a library you are editing at the same time. If the service tracks the library’s latest commit, every edit breaks the build you are debugging, so you pin a release and bump the pin now and then. The target network is the pinned release.

Where the analogy breaks down: a pin jumps in discrete bumps and is frozen in between, which matches another style of target network, a full copy every so many updates. Polyak averaging never freezes and never jumps: it slides 0.5% of the way toward the live critic on every update, so target and live critic are never equal.

Words you will hear

TD target: the bootstrapped label \(r + \gamma(1-d)Q(s',a')\); the TD error is its gap to \(Q(s,a)\), and one update toward it is a backup. Extrapolation error: a critic’s error at states or actions its data barely covers. Support: the region of states and actions the data actually covers; a policy that drifts “off support” asks the critic about places it never saw. Target network: a slowly updated critic copy used only for targets; Polyak averaging or soft update is the \(\tau\)-mixing that moves it. Clipped double-Q: two critics, use the minimum. Offline-to-online fine-tuning: pretrain on a fixed dataset, then keep training while the policy collects more. Update-to-data ratio (UTD): gradient updates per environment step; this lab uses 1.

L3.5 Step 1: the critic network and the replay buffer

Create lab3_awac.py next to your common.py in your own folder, labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/, and write it top to bottom in the order of the next four sections. Every chunk is the reference script’s own code and comments; when you finish, compare your file with the answer key’s labs/ppo-awr-awac/lab3_awac.py.

The first three lines hide the GPU before PyTorch is imported, for the reason Lab 0 gave: Adam’s step() opens a CUDA context of about 386 MB even for CPU tensors, and parallel runs next to a busy GPU die with CUDA error: out of memory. Three seeds in parallel are exactly that situation.

import os# CPU only. Must run before torch is imported: see common.pyos.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""​import argparseimport copyimport time​import numpy as npimport torchimport torch.nn as nnimport torch.nn.functional as F​from common import (DATA, GAMMA, RESULTS, GaussianPolicy, ensure_dirs, evaluate, fmt_eval,                    make_env, save_json, set_seed)

Three imports are new compared with lab2_awr.py:

  • copy provides deepcopy, which creates the target networks.
  • torch.nn, imported as nn, provides the layers of the critic network, QNet.
  • torch.nn.functional, imported as F, provides F.mse_loss for the critics.

The script also takes GAMMA and make_env from common.py; you last used them in lab2_collect.py. (lab2_awr.py’s math import is not needed here.) Reusing Lab 2’s GaussianPolicy unchanged means any difference from Lab 2’s policies comes from how the network was trained, not from a different network.

L3.5.1 The critic network

A critic answers “how good is this action in this state?”, so it needs both as input. The simplest way is to glue them together: 15 observation numbers plus 2 action numbers make 17 inputs, and one number comes out.

class QNet(nn.Module):    """Q(s, a): state (15) and action (2) in, one number out."""​    def __init__(self, obs_dim=15, act_dim=2, hidden=256):        super().__init__()        self.net = nn.Sequential(            nn.Linear(obs_dim + act_dim, hidden), nn.ReLU(),            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.ReLU(),            nn.Linear(hidden, 1),        )​    def forward(self, obs, act):        return self.net(torch.cat([obs, act], dim=-1)).squeeze(-1)

nn.Sequential stacks three linear layers with ReLU activations between them: 17 to 256, 256 to 256, 256 to 1. torch.cat([obs, act], dim=-1) joins a batch of observations, shape (256, 15), and actions, shape (256, 2), into (256, 17). The network returns (256, 1), and .squeeze(-1) drops the trailing axis to leave (256,), one value per sample.

That last shape matters. Rewards come out of the buffer as (256,). Adding a (256, 1) tensor to them would broadcast into a (256, 256) matrix without raising an error, and the TD target would be corrupted. The only symptom is a warning, printed when F.mse_loss compares the critic’s output with that target:

UserWarning: Using a target size (torch.Size([256, 256])) that is different to the input size (torch.Size([256, 1])). This will likely lead to incorrect results due to broadcasting. Please ensure they have the same size.

It scrolls by easily and the script keeps running. If you ever see it, check the .squeeze(-1).

The critic is much wider than the policy. Count its parameters (weights plus biases): \(17 \times 256 + 256 = 4{,}608\) in the first layer, \(256 \times 256 + 256 = 65{,}792\) in the second, and \(256 + 1 = 257\) in the last. That is 70,657 in total, against 5,316 for Lab 2’s policy. The size is this lab’s choice, and a common one for off-policy critics. A critic has the harder job: its output depends on both state and action, and its targets keep moving.

L3.5.2 The replay buffer

The buffer must hand out random batches of the Lab 2 file and, online, accept new transitions one at a time. The simplest structure that does both is a set of numpy arrays allocated once at their final size, plus a counter of filled rows.

Try it yourself first

Write sample(batch_size) before reading the class. Given arrays obs, act, rew, next_obs, terminated and a count size of filled rows, return five PyTorch tensors holding the same batch_size random rows of each; rows may repeat. Hints: np.random.randint(low, high, size=n) draws n integers from low up to but not including high, and a numpy array can be indexed with an array of row numbers.

class ReplayBuffer:    """Fixed-size numpy arrays. Starts full of offline data; online steps are appended."""​    def __init__(self, data, capacity):        n = len(data["rew"])        self.obs = np.zeros((capacity, 15), np.float32)        self.act = np.zeros((capacity, 2), np.float32)        self.rew = np.zeros(capacity, np.float32)        self.next_obs = np.zeros((capacity, 15), np.float32)        self.terminated = np.zeros(capacity, np.float32)        self.obs[:n], self.act[:n], self.rew[:n] = data["obs"], data["act"], data["rew"]        self.next_obs[:n], self.terminated[:n] = data["next_obs"], data["terminated"]        self.size, self.capacity = n, capacity​    def add(self, obs, act, rew, next_obs, terminated):        i = self.size        self.obs[i], self.act[i], self.rew[i] = obs, act, rew        self.next_obs[i], self.terminated[i] = next_obs, terminated        self.size += 1​    def sample(self, batch_size):        idx = np.random.randint(0, self.size, size=batch_size)        return (torch.as_tensor(self.obs[idx]), torch.as_tensor(self.act[idx]),                torch.as_tensor(self.rew[idx]), torch.as_tensor(self.next_obs[idx]),                torch.as_tensor(self.terminated[idx]))

__init__ creates five zero-filled float32 arrays of length capacity and copies the n offline transitions into the first rows. The file stores terminated as booleans, and assigning them into a float32 array turns them into 1.0 and 0.0, the form \((1-d)\) needs. The file’s other fields, truncated, episode, value and ret, are not copied. A truncated step is treated like any non-terminal one (L3.3.4), and value and ret are the collector’s grades, the very thing this lab replaces.

add writes one transition into row size and advances the counter. There is no wrap-around: the script sets the capacity to exactly the offline size plus the online steps, 282,658 rows (about 38 MB) with the defaults. Adding one transition too many would raise an IndexError, which is how you want such a bug to surface.

sample draws row numbers uniformly from 0 to size - 1, with replacement, and returns the rows as float32 tensors. Because sampling is uniform over the filled rows, offline and online transitions are drawn in proportion to how many of each the buffer holds; L3.8.4 comes back to that.

Run it

Check both classes before building on them. With the imports, QNet and ReplayBuffer written, save this as check_lab3.py in your folder, labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/, and run python check_lab3.py there:

import numpy as npfrom common import DATA, set_seedfrom lab3_awac import QNet, ReplayBuffer​data = dict(np.load(DATA / "rover_offline.npz"))buffer = ReplayBuffer(data, capacity=len(data["rew"]) + 100_000)print("size", buffer.size, "capacity", buffer.capacity)print("terminated steps in the file:", buffer.terminated[:buffer.size].sum())set_seed(0)obs, act, rew, next_obs, terminated = buffer.sample(256)print(obs.shape, act.shape, rew.shape)print(next_obs.shape, terminated.shape)print("Q output:", QNet()(obs, act).shape)
What you should see
size 182658 capacity 282658terminated steps in the file: 263.0torch.Size([256, 15]) torch.Size([256, 2]) torch.Size([256])torch.Size([256, 15]) torch.Size([256])Q output: torch.Size([256])

263 terminated steps means 77 goals plus 186 crashes; the other 237 episodes were truncated and add none. A count of 500 means the terminated flag your buffer copied also includes truncation: check ReplayBuffer and, if needed, the flags your Lab 2 collection script saved. A Q output of [256, 1] means the .squeeze(-1) is missing.

L3.6 Step 2: the critic update

The heart of the algorithm is one method, update(batch), which takes one gradient step for the critics, one for the policy, and one Polyak step for the target copies. It lives in a class that owns all the networks.

class AWAC:    def __init__(self, beta=1.0, max_weight=20.0, lr=3e-4, tau=0.005, n_action_samples=4):        self.policy = GaussianPolicy()        self.q1, self.q2 = QNet(), QNet()        self.q1_target, self.q2_target = copy.deepcopy(self.q1), copy.deepcopy(self.q2)        self.pi_opt = torch.optim.Adam(self.policy.parameters(), lr=lr)        self.q_opt = torch.optim.Adam(            list(self.q1.parameters()) + list(self.q2.parameters()), lr=lr)        self.beta, self.max_weight, self.tau, self.k = beta, max_weight, tau, n_action_samples​    def sample_actions(self, obs):        return self.policy.distribution(obs).sample().clamp(-1.0, 1.0)  # the env clips too

Networks. self.policy is Lab 2’s Gaussian (Section L2.4): a 15→64→64→2 tanh network for the means, plus a learned log standard deviation per wheel starting at −0.5. self.q1 and self.q2 get different random initial weights from PyTorch, which L3.4.2 relies on. copy.deepcopy makes target copies that start equal to the live critics but share no memory with them, so training the live critics does not move the copies.

Optimizers. pi_opt updates only the policy. q_opt updates both critics from one combined parameter list. That is equivalent to two separate Adams, for two reasons: Adam keeps its statistics per parameter, and each critic’s parameters get gradient only from that critic’s own loss term. The target copies have no optimizer at all; only Polyak averaging moves them. Every learning rate is \(3 \times 10^{-4}\).

Knobs. The other arguments are the settings of L3.2 to L3.4: the temperature beta (1.0), the cap max_weight (20, as in Lab 2), tau (0.005), and the four action samples for \(V(s)\), stored as self.k.

Sampling. sample_actions draws one action per state and clamps it into \([-1, 1]\). The comment gives the reason: the environment clips actions, so every buffered action lies inside the box. A raw Gaussian sample often does not. Take the starting standard deviation, \(e^{-0.5} \approx 0.61\), and a made-up wheel mean of 0.8. The value 1 lies \((1 - 0.8)/0.61 \approx 0.33\) standard deviations above that mean, and a normal distribution exceeds its mean by more than 0.33 standard deviations about 37% of the time. (In Python, 0.5 * math.erfc(0.33 / math.sqrt(2)) gives 0.3707.) So more than a third of that wheel’s raw samples would fall outside the box. Asking the critic about a wheel speed of 1.4 is exactly the out-of-data question that book Section 4.2 warns a critic will answer with confident nonsense.

.sample() passes no gradient back to the policy, and none is needed. The policy learns only through the log-probability of logged actions (L3.7).

Try it yourself first

Write the first half of update(self, batch) from the key equation in L3.4.4. The batch is the five tensors from ReplayBuffer.sample. Compute the target inside with torch.no_grad():, then the loss for both critics, then one optimizer step. You need self.sample_actions, torch.min(x, y) (element-wise minimum of two tensors), GAMMA, and F.mse_loss(prediction, target), the mean of squared differences.

    def update(self, batch):        obs, act, rew, next_obs, terminated = batch​        # ---- critic: one TD backup ----------------------------------------        with torch.no_grad():            next_act = self.sample_actions(next_obs)            next_q = torch.min(self.q1_target(next_obs, next_act),                               self.q2_target(next_obs, next_act))            # (1 - terminated): after a goal or a crash there is no future to add.            # Truncation is NOT terminal - the rover could have kept driving.            target = rew + GAMMA * (1.0 - terminated) * next_q        q_loss = F.mse_loss(self.q1(obs, act), target) + F.mse_loss(self.q2(obs, act), target)        self.q_opt.zero_grad()        q_loss.backward()        self.q_opt.step()

Match each line to the equation. Apart from observations, actions and the scalar loss, every tensor here has shape (256,).

  • next_act is \(a'\), one fresh clamped action per sample at \(s'\).
  • next_q is \(\min(Q^{\text{targ}}_1, Q^{\text{targ}}_2)\) at \((s', a')\), asked of the target copies, compared sample by sample.
  • target is \(y\); (1.0 - terminated) is \((1-d)\): 0 for goal and crash steps, 1 for all others, truncated steps included.
  • q_loss sums one mean squared error per live critic, both against the same target.

Why torch.no_grad(). It makes the target a true label. We want to move \(Q(s,a)\) toward \(y\), never \(y\) toward \(Q(s,a)\). As a bonus, no computation graph is built for three forward passes whose gradients nobody needs: the policy at \(s'\) and the two target critics.

Why summing the losses is safe. Each term depends on one critic’s parameters only, so backward() gives each critic exactly the gradient of its own error. Then zero_grad() clears the previous update’s gradients, backward() computes new ones, and step() moves both critics.

Trace L3.3.5 through the code. A row with rew = -0.05, terminated = 0 and target copies answering 12.0 and 11.2 gets next_q = 11.2 and target \(= -0.05 + 0.99 \times 1 \times 11.2 = 11.038\). The goal row, rew = 100.4 and terminated = 1, gets \(100.4 + 0.99 \times 0 \times 11.2 = 100.4\).

L3.7 Step 3: the actor update

The actor’s job is unchanged from Lab 2: raise \(\log \pi(a \mid s)\) for logged actions in proportion to a weight. What changes is how the weight is computed, and when.

Lab 2’s awr_weights ran once, before training, and produced weights that never changed. Here the critics change on every update, and so does the policy that defines \(V(s)\). So the advantage must be recomputed for every batch.

That raises a practical problem. The scale of \(Q\) is unknown in advance, and it drifts as the critic learns. An exponential, meanwhile, is extremely sensitive to scale: \(e^{1} \approx 2.7\), but \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\). This is how the lab handles it:

\[ \begin{aligned} w_i &= \min\!\Big(\exp\!\Big(\frac{A_i}{\beta\,\sigma_A}\Big),\; 20\Big), \\ L_\pi &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \,\log \pi(a_i \mid s_i). \end{aligned} \]
In plain words

\(i\) numbers the \(N = 256\) samples of the batch. \(A_i\) is sample \(i\)’s advantage from L3.2, computed with \(\min(Q_1, Q_2)\) for the logged action and for four sampled actions. \(\sigma_A\) (sigma) is the standard deviation of the batch’s 256 advantages. \(\beta = 1\) is the temperature; smaller \(\beta\) makes weights more extreme, as in Lab 2. \(w_i\) is sample \(i\)’s weight: \(\exp\) turns the scaled advantage into a positive number, and \(\min(\cdot, 20)\) caps it at 20. \(s_i\) and \(a_i\) are the logged state and action, and \(\log \pi(a_i \mid s_i)\) is the policy’s log-probability of that action, summed over both wheels. \(L_\pi\), the actor loss, is the average weighted negative log-likelihood: Lab 2’s weighted regression.

Continue update(), directly below self.q_opt.step(), at the same indentation:

        # ---- actor: AWR's weighted regression, advantage from Q ------------        with torch.no_grad():            q_data = torch.min(self.q1(obs, act), self.q2(obs, act))  # Q(s, a_logged)            v = torch.zeros_like(q_data)            for _ in range(self.k):  # V(s) ~ mean_k Q(s, a'_k)                a_pi = self.sample_actions(obs)                v += torch.min(self.q1(obs, a_pi), self.q2(obs, a_pi)) / self.k            adv = q_data - v            weights = (torch.exp(adv / (self.beta * (adv.std() + 1e-6)))                       .clamp(max=self.max_weight))        pi_loss = -(weights * self.policy.log_prob(obs, act)).mean()        self.pi_opt.zero_grad()        pi_loss.backward()        self.pi_opt.step()

L3.7.1 Reading the code line by line

The weight computation sits inside torch.no_grad() because the weights are labels, fixed numbers saying how much each sample counts. Gradient should flow only through log_prob into the policy.

q_data is \(\min(Q_1, Q_2)\) at the logged action. It uses the live critics, updated a few lines earlier; the target copies serve only the TD target.

The loop builds v, the estimate of \(V(s)\). It starts from zeros of shape (256,). Each of the four passes draws a fresh action per state, keeps the lower of the two critic answers, and adds a quarter of it. adv is then \(A = Q(s,a) - V(s)\), one number per sample.

weights is the key equation’s first line. adv.std() is \(\sigma_A\) for this batch, and the 1e-6 keeps the division finite if all advantages were ever equal. .clamp(max=self.max_weight) replaces every value above 20 with 20. There is no lower bound, so a very negative advantage gives a weight near 0.

pi_loss is the second line: Lab 2’s log_prob of the logged actions, multiplied by the weights, averaged, and negated because the optimizer minimizes. The step uses pi_opt, so only the policy moves.

Two things to notice. First, the policy is regressed onto logged actions only; its own samples feed nothing but the baseline.

Second, unlike Lab 2, the weights are not rescaled to mean 1 over the dataset. There is no dataset-wide set of weights to rescale: each batch computes its own, and the loss simply averages over the batch. If you remember Section L2.7.2, a question follows. The batch’s mean weight is no longer fixed. It floats from batch to batch, depending on how the advantages fall and how many weights hit the cap, and the actor’s effective step size floats with it. Is that a problem?

Not in this lab. Take Lab 2’s reasons one at a time.

  • Lab 2 rescaled so that the printed loss stayed on BC’s scale at every \(\beta\) of its sweep, and so that each minibatch estimated one fixed whole-file loss. This lab does not sweep \(\beta\), and its weights are recomputed on every batch from critics that keep changing, so there is no fixed whole-file loss to estimate.
  • Batches with heavier weights pull harder. L2.7.2 called that behavior correct: it is how heavy samples get more say.
  • The pitfall Lab 2 warned about, dividing by the batch’s own weight sum, is still avoided. The loss is .mean() over the batch, not a sum divided by weights.sum().

Adam softens the rest. It scales each parameter’s step by a running estimate of that parameter’s gradient size, so a loss that is steadily larger by a constant factor does not take proportionally larger steps.

L3.7.2 Why four sampled actions

Averaging four samples is a Monte Carlo estimate of an expectation. Its noise shrinks with the square root of the sample count, so halving it takes four times as many samples, and each sample costs two more critic evaluations on the whole batch. Four is this lab’s compromise. The book describes the same idea (Section 4.5): “Averaging \(Q(s,a')\) over a handful of such draws is precisely an estimate of \(V^{\pi_\theta}(s)\).”

L3.7.3 Dividing by the batch standard deviation: this lab’s choice

You will not find this line in the paper. The AWAC paper (Nair et al., 2020) uses \(\exp(A/\lambda)\) with a temperature \(\lambda\) tuned per task. (That \(\lambda\) is a temperature, unrelated to the GAE \(\lambda\) of Lab 1.) Dividing by the batch standard deviation is this lab’s practical choice, made so that \(\beta\) means what it meant in Lab 2. There, the advantages were standardized, so at \(\beta = 1\) an advantage one standard deviation above zero multiplied its weight by \(e \approx 2.718\), whatever the reward units. Dividing by \(\sigma_A\) keeps that reading.

How much did it matter on these runs? At each evaluation, the script saved the last batch’s \(\sigma_A\) (the field adv_std in results/lab3/awac_s*.json). Across those 45 saved batches, three seeds times 15 evaluations, it stayed between 0.40 and 1.14. Without the division, at \(\beta = 1\), an advantage one standard deviation above zero would have been weighted anywhere from \(e^{0.40} \approx 1.49\) to \(e^{1.14} \approx 3.13\), depending on the batch, instead of a steady \(e \approx 2.72\).

So on these runs the effect was moderate. The division matters more when the critic’s scale is far from 1, and you cannot know that scale in advance. Lab 2’s \(G - V\), for comparison, had a standard deviation of 35.4. On that scale, without any division, an advantage one standard deviation above zero would get \(e^{35.4} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{15}\) before the cap.

Notice that the line divides by the standard deviation but does not subtract the batch mean, as Lab 2 did. Here the baseline is already inside the advantage, because \(V(s)\) is subtracted state by state. So the sign keeps its meaning: positive still means “better than what the current policy would typically do here”.

L3.7.4 The cap, and ESS per batch

The cap at 20 is Lab 2’s, for Lab 2’s reason: it stops a few samples from owning the loss. It binds regularly here. In 22 of the 45 saved batches, the saved field weight_max is exactly 20.00. That does not mean heavy capping: it means that at least one of that batch’s 256 weights hit the cap.

The script also reports each batch’s effective sample size, with Lab 2’s formula \((\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2\), divided by 256. It is the ESS column of the log.

L3.7.5 Worked example: three rows of one batch

The numbers are made up for teaching; the arithmetic is exact. Take \(\beta = 1\) and a batch standard deviation \(\sigma_A = 0.5\), inside the range the real runs recorded. That 0.5 is set by all 256 advantages of the batch, not by the three rows below, so do not expect these three alone to have a standard deviation of 0.5.

Row 1. The critics’ lower answer for the logged action is \(Q(s,a) = 11.0\), and the four sampled actions get 12.0, 10.0, 11.5 and 12.5:

\[ \begin{aligned} V(s) &\approx \frac{12.0 + 10.0 + 11.5 + 12.5}{4} = \frac{46.0}{4} = 11.5, \\ A &= 11.0 - 11.5 = -0.5, \\ w &= \exp\!\Big(\frac{-0.5}{1 \times 0.5}\Big) = \exp(-1) = 0.368. \end{aligned} \]

The logged action looks slightly worse than the policy’s usual choice, so it counts for about a third of a sample whose advantage is exactly zero (weight \(e^0 = 1\)).

Row 2. The critics give \(Q(s,a) = 9.6\) for the logged action, and the four sampled actions average to \(V(s) = 9.0\), computed the same way as in row 1:

\[ \begin{aligned} A &= 9.6 - 9.0 = +0.6, \\ w &= \exp\!\Big(\frac{0.6}{1 \times 0.5}\Big) = \exp(1.2) = 3.320. \end{aligned} \]

Row 3. The critics give \(Q(s,a) = 14.1\), and the four sampled actions average to \(V(s) = 12.5\). Call the weight before the cap \(\tilde w\):

\[ \begin{aligned} A &= 14.1 - 12.5 = +1.6, \\ \tilde w &= \exp\!\Big(\frac{1.6}{1 \times 0.5}\Big) = \exp(3.2) = 24.53, \\ w &= \min(\tilde w,\ 20) = \min(24.53,\ 20) = 20. \end{aligned} \]

Row 3 now pulls the policy \(20 / 0.368 \approx 54\) times as hard as row 1. The effective sample size of the three weights is:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{ESS} &= \frac{(0.368 + 3.320 + 20)^2}{0.368^2 + 3.320^2 + 20^2} \\ &= \frac{23.688^2}{0.135 + 11.023 + 400} = \frac{561.12}{411.16} = 1.36 \text{ of } 3. \end{aligned} \]

The log’s ESS column is the same calculation over a batch’s 256 weights.

L3.7.6 Why asking the critic about sampled actions is survivable

If L3.4.1 made you uneasy, that is the right reaction. The advantage queries the critic at actions the policy chose for itself, which is the pattern that inflates values in offline Q-learning. The book’s answer (Section 4.5) is that the actor is trained by weighted regression onto logged actions. That pins the policy to the data, so its samples stay where the data can answer the critic’s questions. The book is equally clear about the limit: “the safety is conditional, not structural. Set \(\beta\) low enough, or fine-tune long enough with a stale critic, and AWAC drifts off support like anything else.” The support here is the region of states and actions the data actually covers. A policy that drifts off support asks the critic about places no transition shows, which is where extrapolation error lives.

L3.8 Step 4: the target update, the loops, and evaluation

L3.8.1 The target update and the diagnostics

Try it yourself first

Write the Polyak update for both critics from the key equation in L3.4.4.

Hints: zip(net.parameters(), tgt.parameters()) pairs matching tensors of two identical networks, and PyTorch methods ending in an underscore work in place: t.mul_(c) multiplies t by c, t.add_(x) adds x.

These are the last lines of update(), directly below self.pi_opt.step(), at the same indentation:

        # ---- slowly move the target critics toward the live ones -----------        with torch.no_grad():            for net, tgt in ((self.q1, self.q1_target), (self.q2, self.q2_target)):                for p, tp in zip(net.parameters(), tgt.parameters()):                    tp.mul_(1 - self.tau).add_(self.tau * p)​        return {"q_loss": q_loss.item(), "pi_loss": pi_loss.item(),                "q_mean": q_data.mean().item(), "adv_std": adv.std().item(),                "weight_max": weights.max().item(),                "ess_fraction": (weights.sum() ** 2 / (weights ** 2).sum()                                 / len(weights)).item()}

The outer loop visits each (live critic, target copy) pair. A deepcopy lists its parameters in the same order as the original, so zip pairs every weight matrix and bias with its twin. tp.mul_(1 - self.tau) multiplies the target parameter by 0.995 in place, and .add_(self.tau * p) adds 0.005 times the live one: \(\phi^{\text{targ}} \leftarrow (1-\tau)\phi^{\text{targ}} + \tau\phi\).

Two details matter. First, the update must be in place: tp = (1 - self.tau) * tp + self.tau * p would only rebind the name tp and leave the network untouched. Second, it must sit inside torch.no_grad(). The copied parameters still have requires_grad=True, and PyTorch refuses in-place changes to such tensors while it tracks gradients.

Within one call of update, the order is: the critics step, then the actor steps using the freshly updated critics, then the targets follow.

The return line reports six numbers about this one batch (.item() turns a one-element tensor into a Python float):

keywhat it is
q_loss, pi_lossthe two losses just minimized
q_meanmean of \(\min(Q_1, Q_2)\) at the logged actions
adv_std\(\sigma_A\) for this batch
weight_maxlargest weight; 20 when the cap bound
ess_fractioneffective sample size divided by the batch size

The log prints q_mean and ess_fraction; the JSON keeps all six at every evaluation. Each describes only the last batch before that evaluation, so read them as noisy snapshots.

Run it

With update complete, check that it runs, that the target copies really move, and that sampled actions stay inside the box. Save this as check_lab3_update.py in your folder, labs/my-ppo-awr-awac/, and run it there:

import numpy as npfrom common import DATA, set_seedfrom lab3_awac import AWAC, ReplayBuffer​data = dict(np.load(DATA / "rover_offline.npz"))buffer = ReplayBuffer(data, capacity=len(data["rew"]))set_seed(0)agent = AWAC()p0 = agent.q1_target.net[0].weight.clone()   # a target weight before any updatefor _ in range(3):    stats = agent.update(buffer.sample(256))print(sorted(stats))print(0 < stats["ess_fraction"] <= 1, stats["weight_max"] <= 20.0)print("target moved:", (agent.q1_target.net[0].weight - p0).abs().max() > 0)obs, act, rew, next_obs, terminated = buffer.sample(256)print("sampled actions inside the box:", agent.sample_actions(obs).abs().max() <= 1.0)
What you should see
['adv_std', 'ess_fraction', 'pi_loss', 'q_loss', 'q_mean', 'weight_max']True Truetarget moved: tensor(True)sampled actions inside the box: tensor(True)

The loss values themselves mean nothing yet after three updates on random networks. What matters is that the call runs, returns six keys, and keeps the weights in range. net[0] is the first linear layer of the target copy; .clone() saved its weights before training. If they have not changed, your Polyak update rebinds a name instead of working in place. Without the clamp, the last line prints tensor(False).

L3.8.2 Arguments and setup

def main():    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)    p.add_argument("--beta", type=float, default=1.0)    p.add_argument("--offline-steps", type=int, default=50_000,                   help="gradient updates on the dataset only")    p.add_argument("--online-steps", type=int, default=100_000,                   help="environment steps (1 update each)")    p.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=256)    p.add_argument("--eval-every", type=int, default=10_000)    p.add_argument("--eval-episodes", type=int, default=50)    p.add_argument("--dataset", default=str(DATA / "rover_offline.npz"))    p.add_argument("--tag", default="awac")    args = p.parse_args()    ensure_dirs()    set_seed(args.seed)    torch.set_num_threads(1)​    data = dict(np.load(args.dataset))    n_offline = len(data["rew"])    buffer = ReplayBuffer(data, capacity=n_offline + args.online_steps)    agent = AWAC(beta=args.beta)    curve = []  # one row per evaluation
flagdefaultwhat it controls
--seed0seeds Python, numpy (batch sampling) and torch (initial weights, action sampling)
--beta1.0temperature \(\beta\)
--offline-steps50,000gradient updates on the dataset alone
--online-steps100,000environment steps online, one update after each
--batch-size256transitions per update
--eval-every10,000updates (offline) or env steps (online) between evaluations
--eval-episodes50episodes per intermediate evaluation; the final one uses 100
--datasetdata/rover_offline.npzthe Lab 2 file
--tagawacprefix of the output file names

ensure_dirs() creates the output folders if needed. torch.set_num_threads(1) keeps each run on one core, so parallel seeds do not compete for cores; the 5 ms per update quoted in this chapter is for one thread. dict(np.load(...)) reads every array of the .npz archive into memory. curve collects one dictionary per evaluation, which becomes the raw material of the JSON file and the plot.

L3.8.3 Evaluation and the offline loop

    def evaluate_now(phase, grad_steps, env_steps, stats):        ev = evaluate(lambda o: agent.policy.act(o, deterministic=True),                      n_episodes=args.eval_episodes)        row = {"phase": phase, "grad_steps": grad_steps, "online_env_steps": env_steps,               "total_env_steps": n_offline + env_steps, "eval": ev, **stats}        curve.append(row)        print(f"[{phase:>7}] grad {grad_steps:>7,}  env {env_steps:>7,}  {fmt_eval(ev)}  "              f"Q {stats.get('q_mean', 0):6.1f}  ESS {stats.get('ess_fraction', 0):.0%}")​    t0 = time.time()    stats = {}    # ---------------- phase 1: offline ----------------    for step in range(1, args.offline_steps + 1):        stats = agent.update(buffer.sample(args.batch_size))        if step % args.eval_every == 0:            evaluate_now("offline", step, 0, stats)

evaluate_now is defined inside main, so it can see agent, args, curve and n_offline. It scores the policy with Lab 0’s evaluate, driving with the mean action, the same way Lab 2 scored BC and AWR. evaluate always starts from seed 1,000,000. So every evaluation of every seed faces the same obstacle layouts and goals, and a difference between two points comes from the policy, not from the maps.

The row it records holds the counters, the evaluation result, and the six batch statistics (**stats unpacks the dictionary into the row). total_env_steps counts the file’s steps plus the online ones; the plotting script adds the collector’s 100,000 PPO steps later.

The print line packs in several format codes:

  • {phase:>7} right-aligns the phase name in 7 characters, which is why online lines read [ online].
  • {grad_steps:>7,} right-aligns a number in 7 characters with commas between thousands.
  • fmt_eval(ev) is Lab 0’s summary of success, crash, timeout and return.
  • :6.1f prints the Q mean with one decimal, and :.0% prints the ESS fraction as a whole percentage.

The offline loop never touches the environment. It samples 256 transitions, updates, and evaluates every 10,000 updates. With the defaults that is 50,000 updates, about \(50{,}000 \times 0.005 = 250\) seconds of compute, plus five evaluations.

L3.8.4 The online loop

    # ---------------- phase 2: online -----------------    env = make_env()    obs, _ = env.reset(seed=2_000_000 + args.seed)    episode = 0    for env_step in range(1, args.online_steps + 1):        action = agent.policy.act(obs, deterministic=False)          # explore by sampling        next_obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)        buffer.add(obs, action, reward, next_obs, float(terminated))        obs = next_obs        if terminated or truncated:            episode += 1            obs, _ = env.reset(seed=2_000_000 + args.seed * 10_000 + episode)        stats = agent.update(buffer.sample(args.batch_size))        if env_step % args.eval_every == 0:            evaluate_now("online", args.offline_steps + env_step, env_step, stats)​    final = evaluate(lambda o: agent.policy.act(o, deterministic=True), n_episodes=100)    print(f"final (100 episodes): {fmt_eval(final)}   total {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")    out = {"args": vars(args), "offline_samples": n_offline,           "curve": curve, "final_eval": final}    save_json(out, RESULTS / "lab3" / f"{args.tag}_s{args.seed}.json")    torch.save(agent.policy.state_dict(),               RESULTS / "lab3" / f"{args.tag}_s{args.seed}_policy.pt")​​if __name__ == "__main__":    main()

Seeds. Online episodes are seeded from 2,000,000 upward (2_000_000 + args.seed first, then 2_000_000 + args.seed * 10_000 + episode). The dataset used seeds 0 to 499 and evaluation uses seeds from 1,000,000, so the policy never trains on the layouts it is scored on.

Exploration. The policy drives with deterministic=False: it samples from its Gaussian instead of using the mean. That is where exploration comes from. To learn which actions are better, the buffer needs different actions tried in similar situations, and weighting cannot choose between actions that were never tried. It is the same reason Lab 2’s collector sampled. act returns a numpy action already clamped to \([-1, 1]\).

Storing, then resetting. The transition enters the buffer with float(terminated), and truncated is deliberately not stored, so a timed-out step is non-terminal (L3.3.4). The order matters. The transition is stored first, with the real next_obs that step returned, which Gymnasium provides even when the time limit fires. Only then does the loop reset if the episode ended. The observation reset returns belongs to a new episode and must never become the \(s'\) of the previous transition.

One update per step. Each environment step is followed by one update on a batch drawn from the whole buffer, an update-to-data ratio of 1. Because sampling is uniform, the batches stay mostly offline data for a long time. After 10,000 online steps, the policy’s own transitions are \(10{,}000 / 192{,}658 = 5.2\)% of the buffer. At the end of the run they are \(100{,}000 / 282{,}658 = 35.4\)%.

Output. Evaluations happen every 10,000 environment steps, labeled with the total update count, 50,000 + env_step. After the last step comes a 100-episode evaluation and the total time. The results go to results/lab3/awac_s0.json (arguments, offline sample count, curve, final evaluation), and the policy weights to results/lab3/awac_s0_policy.pt; other seeds change the number in the name.

Pitfalls
  • Storing terminated or truncated as the flag: the critic learns that the last states of timed-out episodes are nearly worthless, and 47.4% of Lab 2’s episodes timed out. Check: L3.5’s check prints 263, and your buffer.add passes float(terminated) alone.
  • Dropping .clamp(-1.0, 1.0): the critic gets queried at wheel speeds no transition contains. Check: the last line of L3.8.1’s check.
  • Resetting before storing, so the next episode’s first observation is saved as next_obs. Check: in your loop, buffer.add comes before env.reset.
  • Updating targets with tp = ... instead of in place: the copies never move, so the critics chase targets from their random start forever. Check: target moved in L3.8.1’s check.
  • Background runs without python -u: the logs stay empty until the run ends. Check: the log is still empty minutes after launch.

L3.9 Step 5: run it

L3.9.1 A smoke test first

Before committing three cores for 20 minutes, check that loading, updates, evaluation and saving all work, with a short offline-only run.

Run it
cd labs/my-ppo-awr-awacsource ../../.venv/bin/activatepython -u lab3_awac.py --offline-steps 3000 --online-steps 0 --tag smoke

--offline-steps 3000 runs 3,000 updates, about \(3{,}000 \times 0.005 = 15\) seconds. --online-steps 0 skips the online loop, because range(1, 1) is empty. --tag smoke writes results/lab3/smoke_s0.json instead of overwriting awac_s0.json; the plotting script only reads awac_s*.json, so the smoke files never reach the figure.

What you should see

Exactly one line. Since 3,000 is below --eval-every, there is no intermediate evaluation, only the final one on 100 episodes. The line begins final (100 episodes): success, has the same fields as the log lines in L3.10, and ends with the total seconds.

When we ran a smoke test with 3,000 offline updates, it scored 43% [34, 53] on 100 episodes. That is anecdotal: one short run, which could land quite differently on another attempt, and 100 episodes alone carry about ±10 points. Do not compare your number with ours. The smoke test only tells you the pipeline runs and learns something; a random policy scores 0% on these evaluation seeds (Lab 0).

L3.9.2 The full run: three seeds in parallel

Rule two of the book’s Appendix B applies with full force: “a single-seed RL result is noise wearing the costume of a finding.” So the real run is three seeds, launched together, one core each.

Run it
for s in 0 1 2; do python -u lab3_awac.py --seed $s > runs/awac_s$s.log 2>&1 & done; wait

for s in 0 1 2; do ... done repeats the command with $s set to 0, 1 and 2. > runs/awac_s$s.log sends the output to one log per seed, and 2>&1 sends errors to the same file. The trailing & starts each command in the background so all three launch at once, and wait blocks until they finish. runs/ exists from Lab 1; the shell needs it before Python starts.
