Keep the -u. When output goes to a file, Python buffers it, and the log looks empty until the run ends. The runs behind this chapter were launched without -u and behaved exactly that way. -u writes each line the moment it is printed.

What you should see

In the terminal, almost nothing. Your shell may print a job number and process ID for each run as it starts; after that it stays quiet until wait returns, about 20 minutes later. All the output goes to the three log files.

Each log grows by one line per evaluation, every 10,000 updates offline and every 10,000 environment steps online. A finished log has 16 lines. The last begins final (100 episodes): and ends with the total time; our three seeds printed total 1175 s, total 1168 s and total 1170 s. Seed 0’s complete log is shown and read in L3.10.1.

Time. Each seed took about 1,170 seconds (19.5 minutes) on one core, so the three together take about 20 minutes. You can account for most of it. The 150,000 updates at 5 ms each take \(150{,}000 \times 0.005 = 750\) seconds. The remaining 420 seconds or so cover the 100,000 environment steps and the 16 evaluations: 15 of 50 episodes and one of 100, or 850 episodes in all.

Watching progress. Run tail -f runs/awac_s0.log in another terminal; Ctrl+C stops tail, not the run. The first line appears after 10,000 updates, about 50 seconds of updates plus one evaluation.

L3.9.3 The plot

The plotting script is mostly matplotlib boilerplate, so copy lab3_plot.py from the answer key, labs/ppo-awr-awac/, into your own folder rather than typing it, and read it there. Its logic is short. It loads your three awac_s*.json files, plus lab2_summary.json (best capped AWR, BC, the collector’s mean action) and lab2_checkpoints.json (PPO from scratch).

The top panel plots success against AWAC’s gradient updates. The bottom panel switches the x-axis to environment steps, the cost that matters on a real robot. It reads the collector’s training steps from the checkpoint’s file name (ppo_100000_steps.zip gives 100,000), adds the 182,658 recorded steps, and places AWAC’s offline result and the best capped AWR at that total. AWAC’s online points sit further right by their own online steps. Finally, the script pools the three final evaluations: \(48 + 65 + 62 = 175\) goals in 300 episodes, 58.3%, with a Wilson interval of [52.7%, 63.8%].

Run it
python lab3_plot.py
What you should see

The seeds also fail differently at the end. Seed 0 crashed in 17% of its final episodes and timed out in 35%, for a mean return of −67.0. Seed 1 crashed in 31% and timed out in only 4% (mean return +4.2). Seed 2 had 21% crashes and 17% timeouts (−13.2). Pooled, the final success rate is 58.3% [52.7, 63.8]: 175 goals in 300 episodes.

L3.10.3 Seven readings

Each reading was checked against the numbers; where a reading is an explanation rather than a measurement, it says so. The table lists all seven; the paragraphs below give the evidence.

readingwhat it saysstatus
1On the same file, offline AWAC ended at 48 to 58% (pooled 54% [46, 62]); the best capped AWR reached 37% [32, 43]measured
2Longer AWR training does not close the gap; with AWAC’s actor update but Lab 2’s Monte Carlo advantage, success stays near 34%measured
3AWR’s advantage is weak here because it mostly measures episode lucksupported, not proven
4The offline-to-online handoff did not crashmeasured, one evaluation per 10,000 steps
5Online fine-tuning did not measurably improve the policy within 100,000 stepsmeasured; the reason offered is not proven
6On a cheap simulator, PPO from scratch is the better deal in total environment stepsmeasured
7One seed alone would have told one of three different stories about online fine-tuningmeasured

Reading 1: same file, far better policy. Offline AWAC reached 52 to 66% success after only 10,000 updates, fewer than AWR’s roughly 10,700, and ended the offline phase at 48 to 58%. On the same 182,658 transitions, the best capped AWR reached 37% [32, 43], BC 24%, and the collector’s own mean action 33%.

Check that against the noise before believing it. Each end-of-offline number comes from only 50 episodes. Seed 2’s 48% [35, 61] overlaps AWR’s interval, and seed 1’s 56% [42, 69] just touches it; only seed 0’s 58% [44, 71] clears it. Pooled, though, the three seeds reached the goal in \(29 + 28 + 24 = 81\) of 150 end-of-offline episodes. That is 54%, and wilson_interval(81, 150) returns about (0.460, 0.618), an interval of [46, 62], clearly above AWR’s [32, 43]. The comparison is also on shared maps: the 50-episode evaluations use the first 50 of the same 100 evaluation layouts behind Lab 2’s numbers.

That answers the offline half of the question: on this data, AWAC trained far better policies than AWR from the same file. It does not yet say why, because the two recipes differ in more than where the advantage comes from. AWAC’s Adam uses a learning rate of \(3 \times 10^{-4}\) instead of \(10^{-3}\), and batches of 256 instead of 512. It divides advantages by each batch’s standard deviation instead of standardizing them once over the whole file, and it does not rescale the weights to mean 1. Reading 2 rules out training length, then holds the actor update identical and swaps only the advantage. Reading 3 gives the mechanism the data points to, and says how far it is proven.

Reading 2: not a training-length artifact, and not the actor’s settings. AWAC’s offline phase ran 50,000 updates against AWR’s 10,700, so perhaps AWR simply stopped too early. We checked. AWR was re-run on seed 0 with 70 epochs (24,990 updates) and with 150 epochs (53,550 updates), each scored on 100 episodes (results/pilot/awr_long_*.json). At \(\beta = 1\) it scored 28% and 30%; at \(\beta = 0.3\), 33% both times; BC with 150 epochs scored 19%. More updates do not close the gap.

That leaves the other differences Reading 1 listed: the learning rate, the batch size and the per-batch weight formula. So we ran one more check, an ablation: an experiment that swaps exactly one ingredient to see what that ingredient was doing. It trains a fresh GaussianPolicy with AWAC’s actor update exactly as L3.7 wrote it: Adam at \(3 \times 10^{-4}\), batches of 256, 50,000 updates, and the weight \(\min(\exp(A/(\beta\,\sigma_A)), 20)\) with \(\beta = 1\). The one swap is the advantage. \(A\) is Lab 2’s Monte Carlo \(\hat{A} = G - V(s)\), read from the file, instead of the critics’ \(Q(s,a) - V(s)\). The script and its results sit in the answer key’s results/pilot/ folder (ablation_awr_with_awac_actor.py and ablation_awr_awac_actor_s0.json to _s2.json).

After 10,000 updates the three seeds scored 34, 30 and 38% (50 episodes each). After 50,000 updates they scored 35, 36 and 31% (100 episodes each): 102 goals in 300 episodes, 34.0% [28.9, 39.5]. AWAC’s offline phase, with the same actor update, stood at 66, 56 and 52% after 10,000 updates and at 58, 56 and 48% after 50,000, pooled 54% [46, 62] over 150 episodes. With the actor update held identical, the Monte Carlo advantage stays at AWR’s level and the learned critic’s advantage reaches about 54%. On this data, the source of the advantage accounts for the gap. It is still one dataset and one environment.

Reading 3: why AWR’s advantage is weak on this data. L3.1.2 showed that 69% of the variance of \(G - V\) comes from episode identity, so AWR’s weights mostly flag lucky episodes. AWAC’s \(Q(s,a) - V(s)\) compares actions at the same state against what the current policy would do there, learned by TD from every transition. That matches book Section 4.5’s argument about Monte Carlo advantages. Reading 2’s ablation shows that the source of the advantage makes the difference. It does not show which property of the Monte Carlo advantage is to blame. Episode luck is the explanation the data supports, but we ran no experiment that isolates it, so do not treat it as a proven cause.

One more observation fits, with its own caveat. In the 45 batches the script saved, AWAC’s within-batch \(\sigma_A\) ranged from 0.40 to 1.14 (L3.7.3), against 35.4 for Lab 2’s \(\hat{A}\) over the whole file. Remember that Lab 2’s \(\hat{A} = G - V(s)\) also subtracted a value for each state, so the subtraction is not what differs. What differs is that AWR used the sampled return \(G\), which carries the episode’s later luck, while AWAC uses the critic’s expected value \(Q(s,a)\) (effect one in L3.2.1). A much smaller spread is what you would expect if that swap removes episode-level swings.

It is also what you would expect from a critic whose values are simply compressed, varying less from state to state than real returns do, or from one that only weakly tells one action from another. These numbers cannot tell those explanations apart.

Reading 4: the offline-to-online handoff did not crash. Book Section 4.5 names the absence of a performance crash at the handoff as AWAC’s selling point. Last offline versus first online evaluation: 58% to 60%, 56% to 48%, 48% to 50%, all within the ±14-point noise of 50 episodes.

“Did not crash” holds at the resolution you measured, and that resolution is coarse. With one evaluation every 10,000 steps, a brief dip that recovered within those steps would be invisible. To check the handoff closely, evaluate more often around it, for example with --eval-every 2000 on one seed. That flag applies to both phases, so the run then evaluates five times as often throughout and takes considerably longer.

Reading 5: online fine-tuning did not measurably improve the policy within 100,000 steps. The mean of each seed’s last three online evaluations is 46%, 63% and 54%, around the offline level. The final evaluations say the same once their noise is allowed for.

A plausible reason comes from Lab 2’s checkpoint table. On this environment, with networks of these sizes, PPO itself reaches only 62 to 70% mean-action success at 1,000,000 steps, and offline AWAC already sits near that ceiling. That is plausible, not proven. Seeing a gain of a few points would also take far more evaluation episodes: even 300 pooled episodes carry an interval of about ±5 to 6 points.

Reading 6: robot-time honesty. In the bottom panel of Figure L3.2, the x-axis counts every environment step a result cost. PPO from scratch reaches 58, 60 and 54% mean-action success at 150,000 steps (Lab 2’s checkpoint scores, results/lab2_checkpoints.json). AWAC’s offline result cost \(100{,}000 + 182{,}658 = 282{,}658\) steps: the collector’s training plus the recording. On a cheap simulator, PPO from scratch is the better deal in total steps.

This does not cancel Reading 1; it tells you where Reading 1 is worth something. The case for offline methods is data you already have and cannot cheaply collect again: real-robot logs, teleoperation, old runs. That is exactly book Chapter 4’s motivation. It is not beating PPO on a simulator that runs about 12,000 random-action steps per second.

Reading 7: variance. The seeds end at 48, 65 and 62%. With only one seed, comparing the end of offline training with the final evaluation, you would have concluded “online fine-tuning hurt, 58% to 48%” from seed 0, “it helped, 56% to 65%” from seed 1, and “it helped a lot, 48% to 62%” from seed 2. Three stories, each within the evaluations’ noise: Rule two of the book’s Appendix B in action.

L3.10.4 What the Q and ESS columns tell you

Q starts near −8 at 10,000 updates (−8.2, −8.3 and −6.8 for the three seeds), falls to about −25 by 40,000 to 50,000 updates, and then stays between about −22 and −31. Its level is hard to read on its own. It is a discounted estimate, made pessimistic by the minimum of two critics, at states from the collector’s episodes, many of which were heading for a crash or a timeout. Read its trend instead. A steady climb far above anything the rover earns in an episode would be the overestimation of L3.4.1 appearing in your log. Here the value settles into a band.

ESS fluctuates between 23% and 62% of the batch. Lab 2’s capped AWR kept 32.9% of the dataset at \(\beta = 1\) and 35.7% at \(\beta = 0.3\), so AWAC’s weighting lives in a similar range. That is a rough comparison: Lab 2’s number covers all 182,658 weights of the file, while each of these covers a single batch of 256. Still, the weighting is clearly not uniform, and in none of the 45 logged batches did it collapse onto a handful of samples. The swings from line to line are expected, because each value comes from one batch.

L3.10.5 The answer to the lab’s question

Offline: yes. With the same file and no new data, AWAC’s three freshly initialized policies reached 48 to 58% at the end of the offline phase, against 37% for the best capped AWR; both were trained from scratch on that file, and longer AWR training does not close the gap. With the actor update held identical, Lab 2’s Monte Carlo advantage stays near 34%, so on this file the gap comes from where the advantage comes from (Reading 2). That episode luck is the mechanism is the explanation the data supports, not a proven one (Reading 3). Online: not measurably, in 100,000 steps on this environment; the handoff was smooth, but the policy did not clearly climb further. And on a cheap simulator, PPO from scratch remains the better deal in total environment steps.

L3.11 What to carry to real robots

L3.11.1 When offline data is the only data

On the simulator, new data is nearly free, which is why PPO wins the bottom panel of Figure L3.2. On hardware, that axis means something else. Book Section 4.1 prices a one-million-step on-policy run on your SO-101: once 15-second human resets are counted, it comes to about 16.2 hours of wall clock for one run, and 81 hours for five seeds. And on-policy learning discards those hours after each update. In the book’s words: “You are renting your data, not owning it.”

The logs you already own are valuable because, again in the book’s words, “nothing about the data’s origin makes its content less true.” Teleoperation, pad interventions and old checkpoints’ rollouts all record real physics and real outcomes. In that world, learning from logged data is often the only affordable option. This lab showed, on a small scale, that what you do with such data matters: on the same file, AWAC’s learned-critic recipe produced a much better policy than AWR’s episode-outcome weights, and the ablation of Reading 2 traced the gap to the advantage, not to the actor’s settings. That holds for one dataset on one environment, and why the Monte Carlo advantage falls short is supported, not proven.

L3.11.2 Offline first, then online

Book Section 4.5 describes the workflow AWAC is built for: “pretrain offline on demonstrations and logged data, then fine-tune online, still reusing everything in the replay buffer.” Your runs showed the handoff without a crash. They could not show the fine-tuning paying off. Plausibly that is because offline AWAC already sat near what PPO reaches on this task (Reading 5), though we did not test it. On a robot, check those two things separately, and plan enough evaluation episodes to detect a change of the size you care about.

Carry the book’s warning with you too. AWAC’s protection against a critic’s bad extrapolation comes from the actor staying near the data, and that protection is “conditional, not structural”.

On your rig

Your HIL-SERL pipeline answers the same data problem with a different actor. Book Section 4.5 calls it “RLPD-family — off-policy Q-learning in the style of SAC”, over a buffer mixing demonstrations, pad interventions and autonomous rollouts. RLPD (Ball et al., 2023) is the off-policy learner your pipeline runs; SAC is the soft actor-critic of L3.4.2. Book Chapter 13 writes its critic target with \(a'\) “resampled from the current policy”, takes \(\min_i Q_i\) over an ensemble of critics, and uses a high update-to-data ratio. One visible difference: its batches are drawn half from the demonstration-and-intervention buffer and half from the online buffer, a fixed proportion, where this lab samples uniformly. The deeper difference is the actor: AWR-style regression trades some per-sample efficiency, in the book’s words, for “total indifference to the policy’s architecture.”

That phrase is the bridge to the rest of the book. The critic you built only ever needed samples from the policy, and the actor only a supervised loss on logged actions. Book Section 4.6 explains why that pair of requirements is what survives when the policy stops being a small Gaussian network.

Checkpoint
  • You can explain why Lab 2’s \(G - V\) grades the collector, not your policy, and mostly measures episode luck. (L3.1)
  • You can compute the TD target for an ordinary, a terminated and a truncated step, say what two critics and slow target copies each fix, and compute the Polyak half-life. (L3.3–L3.4)
  • You can write the critic update, and say why its target is computed under no_grad with the target copies and why QNet squeezes its output. (L3.5–L3.6)
  • You can compute an AWAC weight from four sampled actions, and say that dividing by \(\sigma_A\) is this lab’s choice, not the paper’s. (L3.7)
  • You can say what the online loop stores, in which order, with which flag. (L3.8)
  • You can state what the results show and do not: offline AWAC far above AWR on the same file, a gap the ablation traces to the advantage source, with episode luck a supported but unproven mechanism; a smooth handoff; no measurable online gain; PPO cheaper in total steps here. (L3.10)

Where to go deeper. Book Section 4.5 is AWAC in one section, and Section 4.2 explains in detail why offline Q-learning inflates its own values, the failure that the two critics, the target copies and the weighted-regression actor all guard against. Book Chapter 13 shows the same critic machinery inside the HIL-SERL pipeline you run on the SO-101. The original method is Nair et al. (2020), AWAC: Accelerating Online Reinforcement Learning with Offline Datasets; read it knowing the one place this lab departs from it on purpose: the paper weights by \(\exp(A/\lambda)\) with \(\lambda\) tuned per task, while this lab divides by the batch standard deviation so that \(\beta\) reads as it did in Lab 2.

Two notes on this list.

  • The collector is chosen by hand. lab2_pick_checkpoint.py automatically suggests the first seed-0 checkpoint with 30–60% stochastic success, which was the 200k checkpoint. The guide uses the 100k checkpoint instead. A single-seed pilot showed that with the 200k collector, weighting added nothing that 100 evaluation episodes could resolve (BC 58%, AWR 58–61% at the three settings tried), while the 100k collector left room (Section L2.2.4).
  • Use python -u for anything whose output goes to a file. Without it, Python buffers the output and the log looks empty until the run finishes.

Total compute for all three labs is under an hour on this machine. For a sense of scale: a single PPO run alone runs at about 3,600 environment steps per second, and the raw environment at about 12,000 random steps per second.

A.3 Reading PPO curves

This sheet summarizes Lab 1. Section L1.9 has the same patterns seen in Lab 1’s runs, with the evidence behind each; this sheet adds the book’s guidance next to them. The rightmost column says where each pattern comes from: Lab 1 means it was seen in these runs; book 3.6 means it is the book’s Section 3.6 guidance and these labs did not test it. Read the curves as a set, never one at a time.

Watch the sign of the entropy curve. TensorBoard shows entropy_loss, which is minus the entropy. So when the book says entropy falls, your curve rises, and the other way round. Every row below is written in terms of the curve you actually see, with the book’s wording in parentheses.

What you seeLikely causeWhat to trySource
approx_kl around 0.5–2 from the start (about 100 times the baseline) and spiking to 10–87; reward rises faster than baseline, then collapses; entropy_loss rises fastest (entropy collapses; action std about 0.2 against 0.5)The clip is not binding: clip_range far too large (10 in Lab 1)Restore clip_range=0.2Lab 1 (L1.6)
clip_fraction near zero (about 0.003) while the run is unstableclip_fraction only counts ratios outside \(1 \pm\) clip_range; with a huge window almost none areTrust approx_kl over clip_fraction; check clip_rangeLab 1 (L1.6)
clip_fraction near zero and approx_kl small, in a run whose reward is not collapsingThe clip never binds: the learning rate is too timid, or learning has convergedLet the reward curve decide whichbook 3.6
Lowest value_loss and, for two of three seeds, the highest explained_variance, yet reward, level with baseline for about the first 0.4M steps, then plateaus far lower; clip_fraction about 2 times baseline; approx_kl about 2 times\(\lambda\) too low (gae_lambda=0): the critic is graded against targets it builds from its own predictions, so its metrics look good while its advantages are weakRestore gae_lambda=0.95; never read low value_loss alone as a healthy criticLab 1 (L1.7)
value_loss rising early (about 100 to 500 in PPO_9’s first 0.4M steps) while reward climbsHealthy on this rover: returns grow from about −140 to +100 as the rover starts reaching goals, so the critic’s targets grow tooNothing. The generic advice “value loss should fall early” does not hold hereLab 1 (L1.2)
entropy_loss rising smoothly (−2.8 to +0.9 over PPO_9’s 5M steps)Healthy: entropy_loss is minus the entropy, so it rises as the policy slowly becomes more certainNothingLab 1 (L1.2)
entropy_loss shooting up in the first 10% of training (entropy dropping off a cliff)The policy went deterministic before it found anything worth being confident aboutRaise ent_coefbook 3.6
entropy_loss falling steadily (entropy climbing)Usually a broken advantage signalCheck how advantages are computedbook 3.6
KL spiking with clip_fraction above 0.4Updates too largeLower the learning rate, or cut n_epochsbook 3.6
Seeds of one configuration disagree as much as different configurations doSeed noiseRun more seeds before diagnosing anythingbook B.1

Healthy numbers on this rover. The three 1M-step baseline runs: median approx_kl 0.0059–0.0062, median clip_fraction 0.062–0.067, final explained_variance 0.65–0.69, final action std 0.51–0.53. Your 5M-step PPO_9: approx_kl rising slowly from 0.005 to 0.017, clip_fraction from 0.05 to 0.195, explained_variance about 0.76 at 0.5M steps and settling near 0.55. Notice that the healthy 1M-step baselines sit below the book’s rule-of-thumb band (KL 0.01–0.03, clip fraction 0.1–0.3) and still learn well. A band is a starting point, and your own healthy runs are the better reference.

What SB3 actually logs (checked in the stable-baselines3 2.9 source):

  • train/value_loss is the mean squared error between the critic and the TD(\(\lambda\)) returns (advantages plus values), not Monte Carlo returns. train/explained_variance is measured against the same targets.
  • train/entropy_loss is minus the mean entropy.
  • train/approx_kl is the mean of \((\rho - 1) - \log \rho\) over the last epoch’s minibatches, where \(\rho\) is the probability ratio.
  • train/clip_fraction is the fraction of samples with \(|\rho - 1| \gt\) clip_range, over all epochs. A nonzero value at clip_range=10 means some ratios exceeded 11: the new policy made a logged action more than 11 times as likely as the policy that collected it.

Your hand-computed GAE disagrees with SB3’sThe two disagree about what follows the last stepUse an episode that ended for real (the script picks a goal episode) with \(V = 0\) after its last step; ours matched to 0.00e+00L1.8
The last steps of timed-out episodes look worthlessTruncation treated as terminationReturns: \(G_T = r_T + \gamma V(s_{T+1})\) at a truncation. Critic target: multiply by \((1 - \text{terminated})\) onlyL0.4.5, L2.3.4, L3.3.4
Advantage weighting has nothing to choose betweenA deterministic collector records one action per situationCollect with deterministic=FalseL2.3
Weights become inf or nan\(\exp(100)\) is fine in float64 but overflows float32, whose largest value is about \(\exp(88.7)\)Compute weights in float64, apply the cap in log space, and subtract the largest log-weight before exponentiatingL2.6
Minibatches full of low-weight samples train as hard as good onesThe loss was divided by each batch’s own weight sum, which re-inflates low-weight batchesRescale weights to mean 1 over the whole dataset, then take a plain mean over the batch. (The module docstring of lab2_awr.py still writes the loss with a division by \(\sum w\); the code does the mean-1 version.)L2.7
Behavior cloning scores below the collector’s own mean action (24% against 33%), with many timeoutsNot a bug. The collector’s std is about 0.93 per wheel, so about 30% of logged actions sit clipped at ±1; BC imitates those recorded actions, which are pulled toward zeroKnow what your dataset stores: the action the wheels receivedL2.5
AWR barely beats BC on your dataThe collector is already near PPO’s plateau (the 200k collector: BC 58%, AWR 58–61%)Pilot two candidate collectors on a few settings before the full sweepL2.2
Pushing \(\beta\) toward zero does not produce dead dataWith the cap at 20, small \(\beta\) turns AWR into filtered BC: good samples all sit at the cap, bad ones near zero, and ESS goes back upRemove the cap (--max-weight 0) to see the collapse; tune \(\beta\) with ESS in viewL2.8, L2.9
AWAC’s success jumps by 10 points between evaluationsEvaluations of 50 episodes carry about ±14 points of noiseRead trends across several evaluations and seeds; the final evaluation uses 100 episodesL3.10

A.5 All headline numbers

Success rates are from evaluate() on the fixed evaluation seeds, with 95% Wilson intervals. Remember the widths: about ±14 points at 50 episodes, ±10 at 100, ±6 at 300 pooled. Those widths hold near a 50% success rate; near 0% or 100% the intervals are narrower (BC’s pooled 24% has [20, 29]). And a pooled interval covers map luck, not seed luck: read the per-seed numbers beside it (Section L0.8.3).

A.6.2 Notation collisions

The same letter means different things in different places. These are the collisions you will actually meet.

  • \(\lambda\). In this guide \(\lambda\) is always GAE’s parameter. The AWAC paper (Nair et al., 2020) uses \(\lambda\) for the temperature, writing its weight as \(\exp(A/\lambda)\). The book’s Section 4.4.3 uses \(\lambda\) for the Lagrange multiplier that makes the probabilities add up to 1; the multiplier of its KL leash is \(\beta\), which is why the temperature is called \(\beta\). This guide writes the temperature as \(\beta\) in both Lab 2 and Lab 3.
  • \(\beta\) in Lab 3 is not the paper’s temperature. Lab 3’s weight is \(\exp\big(A / (\beta\, \sigma_A)\big)\), where \(\sigma_A\) is the batch’s standard deviation of \(A\). Dividing by \(\sigma_A\) is this lab’s practical choice, so that \(\beta = 1\) means what it meant in Lab 2, where advantages were standardized. It is not in the paper.
  • \(\beta\) as a subscript. Book Chapter 4 also writes the behavior policy as \(\pi_\beta\). The subscript is unrelated to the temperature.
  • \(\epsilon\). PPO’s clip parameter (clip_range). The code also adds tiny constants such as 1e-8 and 1e-6 to avoid dividing by zero; those are not \(\epsilon\) in any formula.
  • \(\delta\). The TD error \(\delta_t\) in Lab 1, but the KL leash radius \(\delta\), with no subscript, in book Section 4.4.2, which flags the clash itself.
  • \(d_t\). The true distance to the goal in Lab 0’s reward formula, but the done flag in Lab 1’s GAE formulas and, written \(d\), in Lab 3’s TD target.
  • \(\hat{A}\), \(\tilde{A}\), \(A\). Lab 1’s GAE advantage and Lab 2’s \(G - V(s)\) wear a hat; Lab 2’s standardized advantage wears a tilde; Lab 3’s critic-based advantage wears neither, although book Section 4.5 writes it \(\hat{A}(s, a)\).
  • \(k\). The wheel index in Lab 2’s log-probability, the sampled-action index in Lab 3’s estimate of \(V(s)\), and, in the book, also a diffusion noise-level index (Chapter 6).
  • \(\tau\). The Polyak rate in Lab 3, but a trajectory in the book’s notation table.
  • “Clip”, three ways. PPO clips the probability ratio (clip_range). AWR and AWAC cap the weights at 20 (--max-weight); the guide says “cap” for this one. And the environment, the collector and the policies clip actions to [−1, 1].
  • “Return”, two ways. \(R\), an episode’s plain sum of rewards (what evaluate and ep_rew_mean report), and \(G_t\), the discounted reward-to-go from one step (Lab 2’s ret).
  • “std”, four ways. The policy’s action standard deviation (log_std.exp(), TensorBoard’s train/std, written \(\sigma\) in the Gaussian log-probability); the spread used to standardize advantages over the whole file in Lab 2; the spread of one batch’s advantages in Lab 3, written \(\sigma_A\); and return_std, the spread of episode returns in evaluate, written \(\sigma_R\). The subscripts keep the last two apart from the policy’s \(\sigma\). One code name also collides: adv_std holds the standardized advantages \(\tilde{A}\) in lab2_awr.py, but the batch spread \(\sigma_A\) in lab3_awac.py’s saved statistics.
  • \(s\). Always the observation (state) in this guide. Other textbooks often write a sample standard deviation as \(s\); this guide writes the spread of returns as \(\sigma_R\) instead, to keep \(s\) free.
  • “Target”, two ways. The target networks q1_target and q2_target (slow copies of the critics), and the TD target \(y\) that the live critics regress onto. The target networks are used to compute the TD target.
